Combined with visual synthesis and camera-anchored action conversion, TouchBridge produces robot-domain demonstrations for fine-tuning a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) model. Across four real-world contact-rich tasks, policies fine-tuned solely on TouchBridge-converted human demonstrations achieve a 72.5% average success rate, compared with 77.5% using an equal number of teleoperated robot demonstrations, while human demonstration collection is 7.0x faster. Under the same policy and training setup, Tac-Retarget outperforms DexPilot and UniDex by 25.0 and 42.5 percentage points, respectively.

智能产业研究院 (AIR).title: PhysInsert: Physically Plausible Object Insertion with Geometric Priors and Bidirectional Object-Scene Interactions
智能产业研究院 (AIR).authors_text: Yue Gong, Le Zhang, Rui Chen, Song Chang, Xiaochao Qu
智能产业研究院 (AIR).summary: PhysInsert is a framework that enhances physically plausible object insertion by integrating geometric priors and bidirectional interactions, improving fidelity and adaptability across varying scenes.
智能产业研究院 (AIR).debug_abstract: We present PhysInsert, a framework for physically plausible reference-based object insertion that jointly adapts objects and their surrounding scenes. Existing methods often rely on masked inputs, generation-based pairs, or training pairs with limited viewpoint variation, leaving pose and illumination adaptation and bidirectional object-scene interactions insufficiently constrained. We construct the Insert World dataset with strictly aligned Blender-rendered counterfactual pairs and object references across viewpoints and lighting conditions. Building on these data, Geometry-Guided Adaptation couples a VGGT geometry stream with image and text streams under target-scene feature supervision to guide spatially consistent insertion. Complementary 2D Object-Scene Spatial Supervision jointly supervises object occupancy and environmental changes while grounding spatial instructions in object regions through image-text attention. We introduce PhysInsert-Bench with dedicated cross-environment and cross-view cases requiring illumination and pose adaptation beyond appearance copying. Experiments on PhysInsert-Bench and DreamBooth demonstrate improved image fidelity; a user study further shows more accurate placement and improved lighting integration, perspective, and pose plausibility.

智能产业研究院 (AIR).title: BURGER: Benchmarking and Understanding Robotic Generalization via Embodied Drawing
智能产业研究院 (AIR).authors_text: Xiangyu Xu, Bangshuai Peng, Ziyi Liu, Mengjie Zhao, Chenhao Lu
智能产业研究院 (AIR).summary: BURGER is a novel benchmark for evaluating vision-language-action models in robotic drawing, highlighting their generalization capabilities through diverse, scalable datasets and multimodal behaviors.
智能产业研究院 (AIR).debug_abstract: How effectively can vision-language-action (VLA) models learn diverse language-conditioned behaviors as training data scales? Investigating this question requires large and varied robot datasets, whose collection on physical robots remains costly. We introduce BURGER, a language-conditioned robotic drawing benchmark with a scalable, prompt-driven pipeline for generating continuous drawing trajectories, both in simulation and the real world. In BURGER, an agent starts from the same blank canvas and controls a robot arm to draw the object or spatial composition specified by language, while each instruction allows an open-ended variety of valid drawings and stroke orders. Using 28,200 simulated demonstrations spanning 282 drawing tasks, we evaluate five representative VLA models across data scales, language grounding, and multimodal behavior. BURGER supports fine-grained analysis of language grounding, spatial composition, and action generation, revealing distinct failure patterns across VLA models. Our experiments suggest that some VLA models can benefit from greater task diversity and demonstration scale, capture multimodal drawing behaviors, and generalize to unseen compositions of familiar objects. Finally, we deploy a trained policy on a Franka Panda arm, demonstrating the ability to draw reactively under human intervention. Project homepage and code can be found at https://siyingzhao.github.io/BURGER/.

智能产业研究院 (AIR).title: What Should a Navigator Remember? Spatiotemporal Memory for Zero-Shot Vision-Language Navigation
智能产业研究院 (AIR).authors_text: Yuhang Peng, Zhikai Wang, Ziyi Wang, Jiaru Zhong, Xiaoji Zheng
智能产业研究院 (AIR).summary: This paper presents a zero-shot vision-language navigation system that optimally organizes spatiotemporal memory to enhance navigation performance without specific training, achieving superior real-world success rates.
智能产业研究院 (AIR).debug_abstract: Zero-shot vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires an agent to use past observations without navigation-specific training. We study what information an 8B-scale navigation system should retain and how it should be organized for subsequent decisions. Our agent combines instruction progress, hierarchically compressed observation history anchored to poses, and accumulated geometry in complementary task, temporal, and spatial memories. An 8B observer summarizes observations, and an 8B reasoner uses the memories to select waypoint intents or request additional views, a geometric controller executes the selected targets. A semantic information perspective motivates the distinction between retaining evidence, making it accessible to the reasoner, and acquiring further observations. On R2R-CE val-unseen, the complete system achieves the highest among the evaluated Qwen3-based zero-shot baselines. Removing temporal memory reduces SR and sharply increases average path length from 16.9 to 39.1m, removing the spatial-map and planning component reduces SR as well. Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 show that our zero-shot method achieves higher success rates than the post-trained baseline in both corridor and office environments, suggesting better transfer to the evaluated real-world settings. As a complementary evaluation, LAW2 uses paired instruction interventions to examine behavioral responses, instruction following ability beyond endpoint success. These results support preserving task progress, observation history, and geometry in structured memory for zero-shot navigation with smaller open models.

智能产业研究院 (AIR).title: AEM: Adaptive Entropy Modulation for Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning
智能产业研究院 (AIR).authors_text: Haotian Zhao, Songlin Zhou, Yuxin Zhang, Stephen S. -T. Yau, Wenyu Zhang
智能产业研究院 (AIR).summary: AEM introduces a supervision-free method for adaptive entropy modulation in multi-turn reinforcement learning, enhancing exploration-exploitation balance and improving performance across various tasks.
智能产业研究院 (AIR).debug_abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has substantially improved the ability of large language model (LLM) agents to interact with environments and solve multi-turn tasks. However, effective agentic RL remains challenging: sparse outcome-only rewards provide limited guidance for assigning credit to individual steps within long interaction trajectories. Existing approaches often introduce dense intermediate supervision, such as process reward models or auxiliary self-supervised signals, which increases supervision and tuning complexity and may limit generalization across tasks and domains. We present AEM, a supervision-free credit assignment method that adaptively modulates entropy dynamics during RL training to improve the exploration-exploitation trade-off. Since in agentic RL the environment is typically affected by a complete response, rather than an individual token, our analysis lifts entropy dynamics from the token level to the response level, aligning uncertainty estimation with the effective action granularity of LLM agents and reducing sensitivity to token-level sampling noise. We further show that entropy drift under natural-gradient updates is governed by the interaction between the sampled-response advantage and its relative surprisal. Motivated by this result, AEM derives a practical response-level uncertainty proxy and uses it to rescale advantages, leveraging the evolving balance between positive and negative samples to naturally transition from exploration to exploitation. Extensive experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SWE-bench-Verified with models ranging from 1.5B to 32B demonstrate that AEM consistently improves strong RL baselines, including a +1.4\% gain when integrated into a state-of-the-art software-engineering RL training framework.

智能产业研究院 (AIR).title: LaWAM: Latent World Action Models for Efficient Dynamics-Aware Robot Policies
智能产业研究院 (AIR).authors_text: Jialei Chen, Kai Wang, Kang Chen, Shuaihang Chen, Feng Gao
智能产业研究院 (AIR).summary: LaWAM introduces a Latent World Action Model that enhances robot control by predicting future dynamics through compact latent visual subgoals, achieving state-of-the-art performance with low latency.
智能产业研究院 (AIR).debug_abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) leverage large-scale vision-language pretraining for semantic robot control, but often lack explicit foresight into how robot actions change the scene. World-Action Models (WAMs) address this limitation by conditioning policies on predicted futures, yet existing approaches typically rely on computationally expensive video generation with substantial pixel-level redundancy. We present LaWAM, a Latent World Action Model that exposes predictive dynamics to robot policies through compact latent visual subgoals instead of reconstructed future video. At the core of LaWAM is a latent-action-conditioned Latent World Model (LaWM). We obtain LaWM by training a latent action model in the latent space of a pretrained vision foundation model and repurposing its forward decoder to predict future observation features for scene evolution. LaWAM then conditions action generation on these predicted latent visual subgoals to enable dynamics-aware robot control. LaWAM achieves state-of-the-art or competitive success rates (SRs) across LIBERO (98.6% SR), RoboTwin (91.22% SR), and real-world manipulation tasks while retaining low-latency inference. LaWAM runs in 187 ms per action-chunk prediction and achieves up to 24x lower wall-clock latency than pixel-space WAMs.

智能产业研究院 (AIR).title: ElasticFormer: Detecting Objects in HRW Shots via Elastic Computing Vision Transformer
智能产业研究院 (AIR).authors_text: Wenxi Li, Jingchen Huang, Chenyang Lyu, Moran Liu, Haozhe Lin
智能产业研究院 (AIR).summary: ElasticFormer introduces a dynamic sparse backbone for detecting objects in gigapixel HRW shots, improving efficiency and accuracy by adapting resource allocation based on foreground density.
智能产业研究院 (AIR).debug_abstract: Recent advances in gigapixel-level imaging have brought High-Resolution Wide shots to the forefront of research. However, these images present significant challenges: extreme sparsity of foreground, gigapixel-level resolutions and diverse target counts. This makes traditional close-up detectors inaccurate and slow as they are overwhelmed by the background. Although previous research has explored sparse backbones, their fixed sparsity patterns lack the adaptability required to handle diverse target numbers. To address this, we introduce ElasticFormer, a sparse backbone that dynamically allocates computational resources based on foreground proportion. After scoring windows based on variance, proposed ElasticSelector module will predict the foreground proportion for top-k selection. The mechanism guides the model to select target-containing windows, scaling resources in areas where objects are clustered. We introduce a novel loss function combined with the 3-phase training strategy for ElasticSelector, allowing it to function properly when bounding box annotations are missing. A WSOD study is carried on PASCAL VOC 2007 to evaluate its extensibility. Further, ElasticNet is created to verify its backbone-agnostic nature. In experiments on the PANDA gigapixel benchmark, ElasticFormer reduces backbone FLOPs by 80% while achieving a significant improvement in AP50 when compared to fixed-ratio sparse methods.

智能产业研究院 (AIR).title: SG^2SLAM: Spatial Geometry-Informed 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM for Monocular Outdoor Navigation
智能产业研究院 (AIR).authors_text: Ziang Guo, Didar Seyidov, Yixiao Zhou, Xuefeng Zhang, Ali Alridha Abdulkarim
智能产业研究院 (AIR).summary: SG^2SLAM enhances monocular outdoor navigation by integrating streaming spatial geometry with ray-conditioned 3D Gaussian Splatting for improved tracking and mapping consistency.
智能产业研究院 (AIR).debug_abstract: Monocular outdoor navigation requires robust camera motion estimation and a dense, navigable map, where 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM serves this task through an explicit differentiable parameterization and closed-form projection. However, typically, the geometry is recovered by associating 2D pixels with 3D points, so a modular SLAM system absorbs tracking error into the map, leading to cascading degradation. To address these gaps, we present SG^2SLAM, which couples streaming spatial geometry with a ray-conditioned 3DGS kernel. Streaming spatial geometry replaces the per- frame cross-dimensional correspondence with a chunk-level metric prior that supervises tracking and mapping from one source. A ray-conditioned kernel extends each primitive with a viewing-direction subspace that senses the monocular camera viewpoints. The joint optimization over spatial geometry and poses ensures a globally consistent map and trajectory outcome. Experiments on the KITTI and Waymo Open datasets show that our SG^2SLAM surpasses the per-frame association baselines in the monocular outdoor navigation task. Code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

智能产业研究院 (AIR).title: OmniBrain-0: A Unified Agentic Model for Embodied Intelligence
智能产业研究院 (AIR).authors_text: Xiaomi Embodied Intelligence Team, Yuechen Luo, Chong He, Fang Li, Shaoqing Xu
智能产业研究院 (AIR).summary: OmniBrain-0 is a lightweight unified agent that integrates manipulation and navigation skills through a shared decision model, enhancing task performance while minimizing overhead.
智能产业研究院 (AIR).debug_abstract: General-purpose embodied intelligence requires robots to coordinate diverse skills over long horizons, track task progress, and recover from failures. Specialist policies alone do not ensure task-level reliability, while powerful multimodal agents rely on costly reasoning and external experience that compact models struggle to reproduce. We introduce OmniBrain-0, a lightweight unified embodied agent that coordinates manipulation and navigation through a shared high-level decision model, integrating task understanding, planning, progress tracking, and feedback-driven recovery. Our progressive training framework combines embodied pretraining, domain-specialized agent distillation, and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). It distills powerful teachers' interaction experience into manipulation and navigation experts, then consolidates their decision capabilities into OmniBrain-0. Unification therefore occurs within the learned decision model rather than only at the tool interface. We further introduce Rubric-Guided Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI), a data flywheel in which a Meta-Agent turns execution evidence into refined rubrics, step-level reminders, and verified trajectories for domain-expert updates before their reconsolidation into OmniBrain-0 through MOPD. We evaluate OmniBrain-0 on LIBERO-Pro, LIBERO-Plus, RoboCasa365, RoboTwin 2.0, and R2R-CE Val-Unseen, as well as multiple real-world manipulation tasks. OmniBrain-0 combines strong cross-domain task performance with substantially lower inference and execution overhead than its closed-source teacher, demonstrating efficient transfer and consolidation of embodied capabilities into a compact unified agent.

智能产业研究院 (AIR).title: From Solver Trajectories to Teaching Trajectories: Cognition-Aligned Reasoning Distillation
智能产业研究院 (AIR).authors_text: Yashuo Luo, Qianren Mao, Ziqi Qin, Junnan Liu, Haitao Li
智能产业研究院 (AIR).summary: The paper introduces Cognition-Aligned Reasoning Distillation (CARD), an RL-based method that optimizes teacher trajectories for effective knowledge transfer to smaller models.
智能产业研究院 (AIR).debug_abstract: Knowledge distillation from large reasoning models (LRMs) often uses raw teacher trajectories as supervision. However, this practice creates a mismatch between the goal of distillation and the nature of teacher trajectories. Advanced LRMs typically improve their reasoning capabilities through reward-driven post-training, such as RLHF. This training optimizes them as strong solvers, rather than as teachers that produce reasoning processes smaller models can easily learn. Since smaller models have different "cognitive capacities" compared to their larger teachers, directly imitating raw teacher trajectories can sometimes be ineffective and often requires a substantial number of high-quality samples. To bridge this mismatch, we propose Cognition-Aligned Reasoning Distillation (CARD), an RL-based framework that transforms solver trajectories into teaching trajectories aligned with the student's cognition. Avoiding expensive resampling, our framework directly transforms existing trajectories. We optimize CARD with two reward signals: (1) a Distribution Alignment Reward that matches the student's predictive distribution, and (2) a Logical Coherence Reward that reduces misleading failed reasoning steps. Comprehensive evaluations across multiple student models and settings demonstrate that CARD outperforms distillation from raw teacher trajectories in in-domain settings while achieving substantial gains in out-of-distribution performance. Code is available at https://github.com/LiteSSLHub/CARD.

智能产业研究院 (AIR).title: A generalist policy for muscle-driven control across individual musculoskeletal models
智能产业研究院 (AIR).authors_text: Bozhao Wang, Yinglei Zhu, Zhengqing Li, Zhiyuan Zhang, Weiming Kang
智能产业研究院 (AIR).summary: MyoAcross enables effective muscle-driven control across diverse musculoskeletal models by integrating morphology-conditioned policy learning and virtual model augmentation, achieving high tracking accuracy without fine-tuning.
智能产业研究院 (AIR).debug_abstract: Differences in musculoskeletal morphology challenge policy reuse across individual models. Here we present MyoAcross, a framework that combines individual musculoskeletal model construction, morphology-conditioned policy learning and virtual model augmentation to enable muscle-driven reference-motion tracking without individual fine-tuning. Across 31 held-out individual models, MyoAcross achieves 99.24% completion and reduces tracking error by 22.60% relative to an unconditioned multilayer perceptron. Policy reuse extends to models of 22 held-out individuals constructed from single-image shape estimates, measured height and body mass, and, with asymmetry augmentation, to models with unilateral lower-limb shortening. Comparisons with measurements from 120 additional individuals show agreement in vertical ground reaction force waveforms and channel-dependent agreement between simulated muscle activations and electromyography. These results establish a common control framework for comparative simulations of movement across individual musculoskeletal models.

智能产业研究院 (AIR).title: OctWorld: Long-Range World-Consistent Video Generation with Octree-Based 3D Mapping
智能产业研究院 (AIR).authors_text: Zelong Lv, Sicheng Xu, Jianfeng Xiang, Ruicheng Wang, Yue Dong
智能产业研究院 (AIR).summary: OctWorld is a video generation framework that utilizes an adaptive octree-based 3D memory to create consistent, high-fidelity scenes along extended camera paths.
智能产业研究院 (AIR).debug_abstract: We present OctWorld, a video diffusion framework with persistent 3D memory for generating explorable, world-consistent, and high-fidelity visual scenes. Given a single image, OctWorld performs stable autoregressive world generation along user-specified camera trajectories. We focus on long-range generation, characterized by extended camera paths and wide viewpoint coverage, where preserving spatial consistency is particularly challenging when previously generated regions are revisited. To address this problem, we introduce OctMap, an extensible and spatially adaptive 3D memory that progressively fuses generated visual observations and their corresponding depth maps into a global representation. OctMap employs TSDF fusion within a dynamic sparse octree whose spatial resolution adapts to image evidence. This design preserves geometric and appearance details across diverse scene scales while maintaining low memory overhead. Experiments demonstrate that OctWorld generates long-range, spatially consistent videos and outperforms prior methods on both existing benchmarks and challenging long-range generation settings. OctMap also provides clear advantages over point-based caches and fixed-resolution TSDF volumes. Project page: https://github.com/microsoft/OctWorld

智能产业研究院 (AIR).title: DIP-CAD: A Design-Intent-Preserving Agent Harness for Parametric CAD Modeling
智能产业研究院 (AIR).authors_text: Xi Cheng, Chenxi Zhai, Hang Cheng, Mingyu Fan, Pingfa Feng
智能产业研究院 (AIR).summary: DIP-CAD is a novel framework that enhances parametric CAD modeling by preserving design intent through explicit geometry references and constraints, improving shape generation and parameter editing accuracy.
智能产业研究院 (AIR).debug_abstract: Parametric CAD modeling requires not only matching the target shape, but also preserving design intent under parameter edits. However, most existing methods focus on improving static shape generation accuracy, while the dependencies that govern later edits are often overlooked. To tackle this issue, we present DIP-CAD, a design-intent-preserving agent harness for generating parametric CAD models from images. DIP-CAD combines vision-language model reasoning with CAD kernel operations to establish dependencies that encode the design intent. In parametric CAD, these dependencies are mainly established through geometry references in modeling commands and constraints in parametric sketches. At the command level, ID-based explicit geometry reference binds modeling commands to selected faces, edges, or vertices. At the sketch level, a local-coordinate bridge ensures accurate sketch placement, providing the basis for correctly establishing sketch constraints. Constraints among sketch primitives and constraints to external projected geometry further preserve both internal sketch relationships and dependencies on existing geometry. To provide a more comprehensive data foundation for parametric CAD modeling tasks, we introduce the Geometry Explicit Reference Dataset (GERD), whose structured data format links stepwise modeling commands to intermediate CAD models through explicit geometry references. On GERD-EVL and a DeepCAD test subset, DIP-CAD improves mIoU for static model generation by 11.1% and 5.6%, respectively. In parameter-editing evaluations, the corresponding mIoU improvements are 7.0% and 4.2%. Case studies further demonstrate how parameter edits drive shape updates while preserving design intent.

智能产业研究院 (AIR).title: When the Critic Falls Behind: Co-Evolving Rubrics and Harnesses for Continual Agent Self-Improvement
智能产业研究院 (AIR).authors_text: Hao Chen, Yukun Yan, Ziyu Han, Ye He, Chuanzhe Guo
智能产业研究院 (AIR).summary: RuHarness is a co-evolution framework that enhances autonomous agents' self-improvement by dynamically updating rubrics and harnesses based on evolving behavioral weaknesses during execution.
智能产业研究院 (AIR).debug_abstract: Autonomous agents increasingly depend on harnesses that govern interaction, memory, tools, and execution around large language models (LLMs). While recent work has begun to evolve these harnesses from execution experience, the supervision used to guide evolution often remains relatively static, making it difficult to track changing behavioral weaknesses across rounds and potentially limiting generalization to unseen tasks. To address this issue, we propose RuHarness, a rubric--harness co-evolution framework for continual agent self-improvement. RuHarness continually discovers and reassesses behavioral criteria from execution trajectories, prioritizes the most relevant unresolved weaknesses, and uses them to guide targeted harness updates while keeping the task objective fixed. Extensive experiments across diverse agent tasks and backbone models show that RuHarness outperforms strong harness-evolution baselines, particularly on unseen held-out tasks. Further analyses show that adaptive rubric prioritization tracks shifting weaknesses and supports more sustained improvement and stable generalization across evolution rounds.

智能产业研究院 (AIR).title: Trace-WAM: Learning to Act via 3D Motion Prediction for World Action Models
智能产业研究院 (AIR).authors_text: Xu Hu, Changjie Wu, Linzhe Shi, Hang Zhang, Chen Yang
智能产业研究院 (AIR).summary: Trace-WAM enhances robot control by integrating future 3D motion prediction with video-action learning, improving manipulation performance and generalization across diverse tasks.
智能产业研究院 (AIR).debug_abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) learn representations for robot control by coupling future visual prediction with action generation. Successful manipulation depends primarily on how the robot and task-relevant objects evolve, whereas future-video prediction must also reconstruct the appearance and background of the entire scene. We therefore propose Trace-WAM, which augments video-action learning with future 3D motion prediction as an auxiliary objective. This objective supervises temporal point correspondence together with image-plane displacement and depth change, directly describing the interaction dynamics and spatial changes involved in manipulation. To this end, we adopt a three-branch Mixture-of-Transformer (Tri-MoT) architecture to jointly learn video prediction, motion prediction, and action generation. The motion expert predicts future trajectories from current visual features, allowing motion supervision to shape the representations used for action generation. Because the action expert does not consume predicted trajectories, inference retains the current-observation policy path: a single visual forward pass followed by action denoising. Experiments on RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus demonstrate strong in-distribution performance and out-of-distribution generalization, with particularly clear gains over Fast-WAM under limited demonstrations and distribution shifts.

智能产业研究院 (AIR).title: How Much Can Best-of-N Help a World Action Model? Measuring Selectable Headroom and Realizing It in Closed Loop
智能产业研究院 (AIR).authors_text: Haojia Gao, Yue Cao, Yumin Liu, Haohua Que, Mingkai Liu
智能产业研究院 (AIR).summary: This paper presents a novel protocol for measuring and realizing selectable headroom in world action models, enhancing task success rates through improved action selection strategies.
智能产业研究院 (AIR).debug_abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict the visual consequences of the actions they generate, which makes test-time selection a natural way to improve a fixed policy: imagine the futures of candidate actions and execute the best one. The benefit of selection is bounded by the selectable headroom, how much better the best candidate truly is, but the standard estimate, which executes each candidate once and keeps the best outcome, conflates candidate quality with the randomness of everything that follows. We introduce a denoised counterfactual protocol, based on bitwise-reproducible branching, repeated continuations, held-out oracles, and common random numbers, that measures the headroom a selector can realize, and use its measurements to build a fail-gated selector. Across four WAMs, two benchmarks, over 100,000 branched rollouts, and pre-registered tests, we find that (i) the standard estimate overstates the selectable headroom of native samples: bounds from 17 continuations per candidate place its selectable share between 24% and 66% for three WAMs; (ii) structured action perturbations create up to 16 points of selectable headroom; and (iii) in both WAMs with action-conditioned imagination, imagined futures carry candidate-outcome information with no detectable loss relative to real futures, information that the value head of Cosmos Policy leaves unused. Deviating from the policy chunk only when a readout of the WAM predicts failure, the selector raises closed-loop task success from 76.9% to 81.6% on held-out episodes of training tasks, with the largest gain where the policy fails most often, and from 62.6% to 69.8% on unseen tasks.

智能产业研究院 (AIR).title: Does Your Generalist Skill Optimizer Really Incentivize Agentic Tasks? Rethinking Skill Optimization via Bipartite Attribution
智能产业研究院 (AIR).authors_text: Jiawei Zhou, Bo Peng, Yuxuan Huang, Ming Zhang, Youbang Sun
智能产业研究院 (AIR).summary: The paper critiques existing skill optimizers, introducing BiPA to evaluate their effectiveness and revealing that learned skills show minimal improvement over hand-written seeds.
智能产业研究院 (AIR).debug_abstract: Skill optimizers adapt an agent to long-horizon tasks, such as repairing a terminal environment, by rewriting its skill, a natural-language procedure in its context, and keeping the edits that raise success on a small dev set. On such tasks success is noisy, so a gain on a small dev set does not show that an edit helps, and a success score does not show what the edit costs. We introduce BiPA, which replays an optimizer's acceptance rule on candidates identical to its seed to measure what selection alone reports, and records each episode as a bipartite graph of turns and the text they read to trace extra input tokens to the behavior behind them. Across three optimizers, three agentic benchmarks and two models, the learned skills succeed about as often as their hand-written seed, 0.1 points higher on average. Their dev gains vanish on test: keeping the best of several candidates on at most 30 tasks reports gains this large even when none changed. They read about 16% more input tokens: the optimizers almost always add rules, half to re-check work and some to act one call at a time, and the agent follows them as extra turns, each re-sending the whole conversation. Four principles follow: accept an edit only if its gain exceeds what selection alone reports; charge it for the turns it adds, not for its length; let the editor delete and merge rules; show it what earlier rules cost. Code is available at https://github.com/valleysprings/BiPA.git.

智能产业研究院 (AIR).title: GameVerse: A Minute-Scale Gameplay Dataset for Long-Horizon Interactive World Modeling
智能产业研究院 (AIR).authors_text: Kang He, Wenshuo Peng, Chuanhao Li, Zihui Gao, Xiaojie Xu
智能产业研究院 (AIR).summary: GameVerse is a comprehensive minute-scale gameplay dataset designed to enhance long-horizon interactive world modeling, featuring 69.7K clips and superior annotations compared to existing datasets.
智能产业研究院 (AIR).debug_abstract: Recent advances in interactive world models have made it possible to generate controllable, dynamic environments from action inputs. Yet current models struggle to maintain coherence beyond roughly one minute of rollout, a limitation rooted not in model capacity but in the scarcity of long-horizon training data. Existing gameplay video datasets typically consist of clips under ten seconds, with captions that describe whole clips in coarse and undifferentiated text, which is insufficient for controllable long-horizon generation. We address this with GameVerse, a minute-scale gameplay video dataset purpose-built for long-horizon interactive world modeling. GameVerse contains 69.7K clips spanning 1,655 hours and 349.6 million frames across diverse first- and third-person gameplay, including 1,358 hours of continuous two-minute sequences, an order of magnitude longer than prior datasets. Clips pass through a unified pipeline of scene-consistent segmentation, quality filtering, camera pose estimation, and event-based caption annotation. Each clip is paired with a temporally stable camera trajectory that remains coherent across minutes, together with captions that separate static scene context from dynamic foreground events and align to event boundaries rather than fixed time windows. Comprehensive analysis shows that GameVerse surpasses existing public datasets in scale, diversity, and annotation quality. Experiments further demonstrate that training on GameVerse substantially extends the temporal horizon of interactive world models.

智能产业研究院 (AIR).title: Ego-CEVR: Learning Cross-Embodiment Visual Representations from Human Egocentric Videos
智能产业研究院 (AIR).authors_text: Keru Zhou, Zhirui Fang, Xinrun Xu, Yaopeng Lou, Zeyuan He
智能产业研究院 (AIR).summary: Ego-CEVR is a framework that leverages egocentric videos to learn hierarchical visual representations for robot manipulation, enhancing task understanding and action alignment.
智能产业研究院 (AIR).debug_abstract: As egocentric video becomes increasingly available for embodied learning, an important research question is how to turn this low-cost, scalable source of data into robot manipulation capabilities. Egocentric videos naturally provide rich context for high-level task understanding, while real-robot demonstrations with wrist observations and action annotations provide supervision for fine-grained action alignment. We present Ego-CEVR, a data-native framework for hierarchical visual representation learning that assigns distinct learning objectives to global and interaction representations. The global module learns object relations, task state, and temporal progress through future prediction on egocentric video. The Interaction module interprets wrist observations in global context and learns local alignment and contact cues through robot action supervision. Separate residual paths expose both representations to the action policy, preserving direct access to task context alongside fine-grained execution information. Ego-CEVR supports independent pretraining of its global video module on large-scale human egocentric videos and videos from diverse robot embodiments, without requiring robot action labels or paired wrist observations.

智能产业研究院 (AIR).title: Doubly Robust Alignment for Large Language Models
智能产业研究院 (AIR).authors_text: Erhan Xu, Kai Ye, Hongyi Zhou, Luhan Zhu, Francesco Quinzan
智能产业研究院 (AIR).summary: The paper introduces a doubly robust preference optimization algorithm for aligning large language models via reinforcement learning from human feedback, enhancing performance despite model misspecifications.
智能产业研究院 (AIR).debug_abstract: This paper studies reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) for aligning large language models with human preferences. While RLHF has demonstrated promising results, many algorithms are highly sensitive to misspecifications in the underlying preference model (e.g., the Bradley-Terry model), the reference policy, or the reward function, resulting in undesirable fine-tuning. To address model misspecification, we propose a doubly robust preference optimization algorithm that remains consistent when either the preference model or the reference policy is correctly specified (without requiring both). Our proposal demonstrates superior and more robust performance than state-of-the-art algorithms, both in theory and in practice. The code is available at https://github.com/DRPO4LLM/DRPO4LLM

智能产业研究院 (AIR).title: FTP-1: A Generalist Foundation Tactile Policy Across Tactile Sensors for Contact-Rich Manipulation
智能产业研究院 (AIR).authors_text: Chengbo Yuan, Zicheng Zhang, Mingjie Zhou, Wendi Chen, Yi Wang
智能产业研究院 (AIR).summary: FTP-1 is a pioneering generalist tactile policy that enables transferable manipulation skills across diverse sensors, improving performance in contact-rich tasks by significant margins.
智能产业研究院 (AIR).debug_abstract: Despite the success of vision-based generalist robotic policies, existing tactile-based policies remain tied to fixed embodiments and sensor setups. This is because tactile signals are highly heterogeneous across hardware, making cross-sensor generalization difficult. We present FTP-1,the first generalist foundation tactile policy pretrained to acquire transferable tactile manipulation abilities across diverse sensors and embodiments. FTP-1 supports varied tactile inputs, including image-, array-, and state-based signals, by using heterogeneous encoders to project them into unified morphology-aware latent tokens that are jointly modeled by a shared tactile Transformer expert. Pretrained on around 3,000 hours of tactile manipulation data aggregated from 26 data sources, spanning human and robot demonstrations across 21 sensors, FTP-1 learns tactile skills that transfer beyond the sensors seen during pretraining. Across downstream finetuning experiments spanning 5 hardware configurations, FTP-1 improves contact-rich manipulation on seen sensor setups by +17.2% and, surprisingly, transfers to two previously unseen tactile-sensor setups, achieving a +31% gain in success rate. FTP-1 establishes the first unified foundation baseline for tactile manipulation, providing future tactile policies with a shared model-level starting point. Pretrained models, datasets, training code and more visualization at https://ftp1-policy.github.io.

智能产业研究院 (AIR).title: Understanding Human-Robot Collaboration through Joint Action
智能产业研究院 (AIR).authors_text: Chengwen Zhang, Jianyang Wang, Chang Liu, Yukun Wang, Yuan Xu
智能产业研究院 (AIR).summary: This systematic review synthesizes 83 empirical studies on human-robot collaboration using Joint Action theory, identifying key constructs and gaps for future research.
智能产业研究院 (AIR).debug_abstract: Human-robot collaboration requires partners to coordinate interdependent contributions toward a shared goal. Joint Action theory provides concepts for understanding this coordination, but how these concepts are instantiated and combined across empirical research remains fragmented. We conducted a systematic review following PRISMA 2020, identifying 83 empirical papers published between 2021 and 2026. Through theory-driven framework analysis, we organized the literature into nine constructs across three capacities: Representation, Prediction, and Integration. We analyze how these constructs are distributed and co-occur across studies, revealing where empirical evidence concentrates and where it is absent. By mapping empirical HRC research onto a unified Joint Action framework, this review offers a coherent overview of HRC studies, identifies gaps in current evidence, and provides guidelines for future research.

智能产业研究院 (AIR).title: VideoLVR: Latent Visual Reasoning over Grounded Video Evidence
智能产业研究院 (AIR).authors_text: Shilong Li, Xingyuan Bu, Hao Shi, Yun Xing, Weixin Feng
智能产业研究院 (AIR).summary: VideoLVR enhances multimodal large language models' video understanding by integrating latent visual evidence during reasoning, improving accuracy without significantly increasing context size.
智能产业研究院 (AIR).debug_abstract: Chain-of-thought reasoning has substantially advanced video understanding in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, language-based reasoning traces do not provide a reliable mechanism for models to revisit relevant visual evidence, leading to visual forgetting and impairing their ability to reason over video content. Existing approaches maintain visual grounding during reasoning in two main ways: they either refer to evidence using textual coordinates, which specify symbolic locations rather than the visual content itself, or reinsert cropped regions or frames into the multimodal context, preserving visual details at the cost of substantial context expansion. To address these limitations, we introduce VideoLVR, which constructs latent visual evidence from local regions at relevant video moments, thereby providing visual support for intermediate reasoning steps. To supervise latent visual evidence generation, we introduce a visual token prediction objective that formulates visual token reconstruction as prediction over a vocabulary derived from the input video, thereby unifying visual evidence reconstruction and text generation within the same token prediction framework. This shared prediction framework enables MLLMs to reason over interleaved text tokens and latent visual states while integrating evidence from different moments. We further extend VideoLVR to reinforcement learning by treating sampled visual tokens as actions alongside text tokens and jointly optimizing the policy using final-answer rewards. By efficiently revisiting task-relevant visual information during reasoning, VideoLVR improves video understanding without substantially expanding the multimodal context. Experiments on multiple video benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness, especially on tasks requiring fine-grained visual evidence.

SU Lab.title: SceneAnything: Agentic Reconstruction of Large-Scale Mesh Scenes from a Single Video
SU Lab.authors_text: Bowen Xue, Saeed Hadadan, Fabrice Rousselle, Zahra Montazeri, Ravi Ramamoorthi
SU Lab.summary: SceneAnything automates 3D mesh scene reconstruction from videos, enhancing fidelity and content similarity through coordinated agents and a structured reconstruction protocol.
SU Lab.debug_abstract: Reconstructing an editable 3D scene from video requires matching visible structure while plausibly completing unseen surfaces. Agents can write scene-construction programs, but direct reconstruction attempts often produce errors in layout, scale, and lighting. We introduce SceneAnything, an automated system for reconstructing mesh scenes from real and generated videos, enabling text-to-scene construction when paired with video generation. A software harness coordinates agents, pretrained vision models, and graphics tools through an explicit reconstruction protocol. Shared camera, depth, and segmentation estimates ground component construction: a scene-owner agent plans the environment and briefs authors, who write parameterized Blender programs. A visibility- and fit-based level-of-detail rule selects the construction level, while unseen regions are completed and marked as inferred. Assembled scenes use fitted lighting and supported motion, and revisions undergo programmatic checks and independent visual comparisons. Accepted programs and lessons are reused across scenes. We evaluate on 100 scenes; subset comparisons show improved original-view fidelity over direct-agent reconstruction and higher novel-view content similarity than the compared video-to-3D methods. We will release the harness, agent instructions, reusable libraries, and scenes.

SU Lab.title: From Questions to Decisions: Benchmarking How LLM Agents Acquire Decision-Relevant Information from Human Beings
SU Lab.authors_text: Yuhan Tang, Ke Fan, Xinkai Zou, Baichuan Mo, Kangxin Cui
SU Lab.summary: The paper introduces Ask2Decide, a benchmark assessing LLM agents' ability to acquire crucial decision-making information from humans, revealing significant shortcomings in their planning efficacy.
SU Lab.debug_abstract: LLM agents are increasingly asked to make plans for people, such as scheduling drivers or assigning nurses. However, people's requests are often incomplete, and the supporting information for decision-making may be outdated, requiring agents to ask for clarification. Existing benchmarks typically provide fully specified problems or rely on uncalibrated LLM-simulated users, leaving this ability insufficiently tested. We introduce Ask2Decide, a benchmark of 43 planning tasks that evaluates whether agents ask for missing information that matters for their decisions. An operator holds facts absent from the agent's request and records, and optimization solvers determine which facts change the optimal plan. We also include similarly worded facts that leave the optimal plan unchanged to test whether agents distinguish useful information from irrelevant details. We collect 79 interaction sessions from 19 participants and find that, after an incorrect plan, human replies omit the correcting fact far more often than replies from an uncalibrated simulated user (43% versus 7%). Using these interactions, we calibrate a simulated operator that more closely matches human reply patterns. Evaluating four frontier LLMs, we find that their initial plans are infeasible on 58-98% of tasks when information is missing, compared with 5-28% when all facts are provided upfront. Agents uncover facts that change the optimal plan only slightly more often than facts that leave it unchanged (39-52% versus 32-41%). These results show that obtaining decision-relevant information through interaction remains a major bottleneck for LLM planning. This is ongoing work and will be updated. The date of this version is shown on the first page.

SU Lab.title: Generative OOD-regularized Model-based Policy Optimization
SU Lab.authors_text: Aysin Tumay, Jiahe Huang, Elise Jortberg, Rose Yu
SU Lab.summary: The paper introduces GORMPO, a density-regularized offline RL algorithm that integrates generative models to prevent out-of-distribution actions, enhancing policy performance in sparse state-action spaces.
SU Lab.debug_abstract: We study sequential decision-making with offline reinforcement learning (RL). Traditional offline RL policies may result in out-of-distribution (OOD) actions when training relies only on sparse offline representations. To ensure safe offline policies in a sparse state-action space, we explore how density estimation models can be integrated into model-based RL methods to avoid OOD regions. Generative models are capable of explicitly modeling the density in sparse state-action spaces. Building on this, we introduce Generative OOD-regularized Model-based Policy Optimization (GORMPO), a density-regularized offline RL algorithm that uses generative density modeling to restrict policy updates to high-density areas of the dataset. Furthermore, we examine whether better OOD detection corresponds to better model-based offline policies. We compare (1) the OOD detection capabilities of various density estimators and (2) their performance within the GORMPO framework on a real-world medical dataset and sparse offline RL datasets. We provide theoretical guarantees bounding GORMPO's performance gap in terms of density estimation error, ensuring near-optimal policies under imperfect density estimates. Empirically, GORMPO remains competitive in reward and improves clinical metrics compared to state-of-the-art clinical RL models, and outperforms state-of-the-art offline RL models in offline RL benchmarks. Our empirical findings show that better OOD detection generally results in improved policies in environments with stable dynamics, while conservative penalties with poor density estimation are favored when dynamics are uncertain. Code, checkpoints, sparse, and OOD D4RL datasets are available at https://github.com/Rose-STL-Lab/GORMPO.

SU Lab.title: BunshinRL: Splitting Live Agent Workspaces for Memory-Efficient Agentic RL
SU Lab.authors_text: Yutong Huang, Vikranth Srivatsa, Alex Asch, Yiying Zhang
SU Lab.summary: BunshinRL introduces a memory-efficient agentic RL system utilizing memory sharing, caching, and speculative execution to significantly reduce memory usage and rollout latency.
SU Lab.debug_abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) rollouts interleave model reasoning with tool calls in persistent workspaces. Scaling these rollouts incurs substantial memory costs for concurrent environments, while slow tool calls delay entire rollout batches. We present BunshinRL, an agentic RL rollout system that exploits shared environment state and recurring tool calls through three techniques: memory sharing across environments, tool-prefix caching, and speculative tool execution. These techniques build on BunshinFork, a novel live whole-workspace forking mechanism for containers. BunshinFork reconstructs process trees, shares memory copy-on-write, and preserves file, communication, and GUI state, enabling cached-state reuse and rollback after incorrect speculation. We implement BunshinRL and BunshinFork through Linux kernel module and CRIU modifications. BunshinRL reduces peak memory by up to 43%, total memory consumption by up to 51%, and end-to-end rollout latency by 23%.

SU Lab.title: HiLo-WAM: Decoupling Long-Horizon Task Evolution and Local Dynamics in World Action Models
SU Lab.authors_text: Xingyu Wang, Yanjiang Guo, Zhijing Ding, Jiaxin Fang, Zeyu Lai
SU Lab.summary: HiLo-WAM enhances robotic manipulation by decoupling long-horizon task evolution from local dynamics, achieving high success rates and efficiency through a dual-DiT architecture.
SU Lab.debug_abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) improve robotic manipulation by jointly modeling visual dynamics and robot actions. However, most existing WAMs model dense short-horizon visual dynamics, capturing local interactions but providing limited long-range task context. Extending prediction horizons increases uncertainty and computation while entangling task-level evolution with fine-grained local dynamics, obscuring their dependencies and distinct roles in action generation. We propose HiLo-WAM, which decouples long-horizon task evolution from local visual dynamics while jointly modeling their interaction with robot actions. A sparse long-horizon visual stream captures historical task context and future evolution, while a dense local dynamics visual stream models short-horizon robot-object interactions. The two streams operate at different temporal scales within a unified dual-DiT architecture and guide actions through structured cross-stream attention. Progressive inference further reduces unnecessary computation through stream-wise partial denoising, joint denoising, and dynamic skipping. Experiments demonstrate strong long-horizon manipulation performance: HiLo-WAM achieves a 93.70% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 and a 17.43 progress score on RoboDojo long-horizon tasks, with robust in-domain and OOD performance on the Fourier GR-3 robot. Ablations confirm the complementary contributions of long-horizon task evolution and local interaction dynamics, while temporal-scale analyses highlight the importance of balancing temporal coverage and resolution. Progressive inference further achieves a 2.93x speedup while improving performance.

SU Lab.title: Towards General Continuous Memory for Vision-Language Models
SU Lab.authors_text: Wenyi Wu, Zixuan Song, Kun Zhou, Yifei Shao, Zhiting Hu
SU Lab.summary: The paper introduces CoMEM, a method leveraging continuous memory in vision-language models to enhance performance on complex multimodal reasoning tasks with minimal parameter use.
SU Lab.debug_abstract: Language models (LMs) and their extension, vision-language models (VLMs), have achieved remarkable performance across various tasks. However, they still struggle with complex reasoning tasks that require multimodal or multilingual real-world knowledge. To support such capabilities, an external memory system that can efficiently provide relevant multimodal information is essential. Existing approaches generally concatenate image and text tokens into a long sequence as memory, which, however, may drastically increase context length and even degrade performance. In contrast, we propose using continuous memory, a compact set of dense embeddings to more effectively and efficiently represent multimodal and multilingual knowledge. Our key insight is that a VLM can serve as its own continuous memory encoder. We empirically show that this design improves performance on complex multimodal reasoning tasks. Building on this, we introduce a data-efficient and parameter-efficient method to fine-tune the VLM into a memory encoder, requiring only 1.2% of the model's parameters and a small corpus of 15.6K self-synthesized samples. Our approach CoMEM utilizes VLM's original capabilities to encode arbitrary multimodal and multilingual knowledge into just 8 continuous embeddings. Since the inference-time VLM remains frozen, our memory module is plug-and-play and can be flexibly integrated as needed. Extensive experiments across eight multimodal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Infinite Gaze Generation for Videos with Autoregressive Diffusion
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Jenna Kang, Colin Groth, Tong Wu, Finley Torrens, Patsorn Sangkloy
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: This paper introduces an autoregressive diffusion model for infinite-horizon gaze prediction in videos, enhancing long-range spatio-temporal accuracy and trajectory realism beyond traditional methods.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Predicting human gaze in video is fundamental to advancing scene understanding and multimodal interaction. While traditional saliency maps provide spatial probability distributions and scanpaths offer ordered fixations, both abstractions often collapse the fine-grained temporal dynamics of raw gaze. Furthermore, existing models are typically constrained to short-term windows ($\approx$ 3-5s), failing to capture the long-range behavioral dependencies inherent in real-world content. We present a generative framework for infinite-horizon raw gaze prediction in videos of arbitrary length. By leveraging an autoregressive diffusion model, we synthesize gaze trajectories characterized by continuous spatial coordinates and high-resolution timestamps. Our model is conditioned on a saliency-aware visual latent space. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing approaches in long-range spatio-temporal accuracy and trajectory realism.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: WEVO: World Model-Enabled VLA Optimization for Whole-Body Loco-Manipulation
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Qianzhong Chen, Muyuan Lin, Yuyin Sun, Mac Schwager, Cheng-Hao Kuo
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: WEVO enhances whole-body humanoid VLA policies using a video world model, improving real robot task success rates by integrating simulated and real-world data.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve vision-language-action (VLA) policies beyond imitation, but humanoid exploration is unsafe and simulator RL can exploit residual sim-to-real gaps. We present WEVO, a teleoperation-free framework for post-training a whole-body humanoid VLA in an action-conditioned video world model (WM). Simulated manipulation and locomotion play data improve contact-dynamics and viewpoint-change prediction. A VLA trained on synthetic demonstrations collects 20 autonomous real robot rollouts per task to align the WM with deployment observations. The VLA, whole-body controller (WBC), and video WM then form a closed-loop RL environment with dense progress rewards. Across three real robot tasks, play data improves every evaluated WM metric and downstream policy success; video WM RL raises mean success from 23.3% to 75.0%, compared with 48.3% for real robot RL. We therefore leverage the complementary strengths of both environments: simulation provides policy initialization and broad coverage, while the video WM offers a deployment-aligned environment for policy improvement. Project website: https://qianzhong-chen.github.io/wevo.github.io/.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: PRIO: Pre-trained Representation for Interactive Objects in 4D Worlds
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Shixun Huang, Lifu Wei, Yue Chang, Chen Geng, Heng Zhang
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: PRIO is a pre-trained representation that enables real-time interaction with objects in 4D worlds by predicting their dynamic configurations from static geometry.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: 3D worlds can now be captured, reconstructed, and generated at scale, yet the objects in them stay still: a pressed pillow does not compress, and a pulled door does not swing. Bringing these objects into interactive 4D world models requires a representation of how they can move, deform, and respond physically to user actions in real time. We present PRIO, a pre-trained representation for interactive objects. Given static geometry, PRIO predicts an object-specific configuration space in a single forward pass. This space provides generalized coordinates for Lagrangian mechanics, allowing physical laws and user actions to govern motion. Configurations are linear in these coordinates, allowing the quantities needed by the dynamics to be precomputed. Dynamics then run at interactive rates without further network inference. Pre-trained on diverse 4D trajectories, PRIO learns priors over object configurations that generalize to unseen shapes. It supports meshes, point clouds, and 3D Gaussians, bringing objects in reconstructed and generated scenes into interaction. We demonstrate its use in real-to-sim workflows and robot manipulation. In addition, compared with existing 4D generation methods, PRIO generates dynamics faster and follows user actions more faithfully.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: WeightCode: Installing New Capabilities into Neural Networks via Weight-Space Programming
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Bo Li, Taoyong Cui, Bob Zhang, Mengran Li, Chengyang Zhang
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: WeightCode introduces Weight-Space Programming to enhance neural networks' capabilities by directly modifying weights with executable programs, achieving significant performance improvements without retraining.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Neural networks encode learned capabilities in their weights, yet extending those capabilities with explicit task knowledge remains a fundamental challenge. Here we show that Weight-Space Programming (WSP), in which executable programs read, construct or modify a network's weights directly, can install new capabilities within trained neural networks. WeightCode, a WSP framework, uses a frozen language model to write executable weight programs that install new computations into trained neural networks using task knowledge and their existing weights, without gradient-based training. Once installed, the new capabilities run independently of the language model. Given a grammar or eight demonstrations, weight programs enable previously unseen command compositions (0% to 99.8% exact match) and a new pickup action (0% to 98.4% success), while preserving the original command and navigation capabilities. On ImageNet, four weight programs achieve net gains of 8.84-17.62 points while preserving clean accuracy, outperforming the best of eight fine-tuning methods under matched examples, checks, and retention constraints. In a Vision Transformer, causal interventions show that installed noise-correction gates drive robustness gains, while their selective activation preserves clean accuracy. Rerun on five independently trained Vision Transformers without further language model calls, ten weight programs retain 83-110% of their source-network gains on average, whereas copying their fixed weight edits yields negligible gains. Six programs written for an already edited network add 5.23-14.50 points of contrast robustness while retaining the previously installed noise gain. Together, these results establish WSP as a new route to acquiring and accumulating capabilities in trained neural networks through reusable weight programs.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: One Prior, Two Dynamics: Repurposing Video Diffusion Transformers for Self-Supervised Latent Action Learning
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Yuxin Jiang, Wenqiang Sun, Jiaqi Li, Yuchao Gu, Lvmin Zhang
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: O$^{2}$LaF repurposes pretrained video diffusion transformers for self-supervised latent action learning, achieving state-of-the-art performance in few-shot action probing and zero-shot transfer.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Videos reveal how the world changes, but rarely the actions that cause those changes. Latent action learning recovers such supervision from visual transitions, yet often learns the underlying dynamics largely from scratch. We ask whether a pretrained video generator can instead provide the prior for both inverse and forward dynamics. We introduce O$^{2}$LaF, built on a simple principle: one prior, two dynamics. We initialize both models from the same pretrained video DiT and adapt them to their distinct roles: a feed-forward transition encoder with learnable action queries for inverse dynamics, and a causal, action-conditioned video generator for forward dynamics. By controlling information access and optimizing both dynamics end-to-end through a compact bottleneck, O$^{2}$LaF learns transferable actions from unlabeled videos. Across navigation and robotic manipulation, O$^{2}$LaF sets a new state of the art in few-shot action probing and enables stronger zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and embodiments. Beyond generative video priors, we further extend our framework to predictive representation priors such as V-JEPA2, achieving competitive performance. Our findings suggest a broader paradigm for latent-action learning: repurposing pretrained video models to discover transferable actions and predict their consequences.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Bridging Structure and Language: Graph-Based Visual Reasoning for Autonomous Road Understanding
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Lena Wild, Katie Z Luo, Marco Pavone
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: The paper presents the Combined Road Substrate (CRS), a graph-based framework that integrates geometric road structure with open-vocabulary semantics for improved autonomous road understanding and reasoning.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Structured road understanding of lane geometry, topology, and traffic element relationships is foundational to safe autonomous driving. While vision-language models (VLMs) offer promising semantic flexibility, they lack the geometric and relational grounding required for precise road reasoning. Conversely, traditional modular systems, e.g., HD maps and topological road graphs, provide structural precision but remain semantically rigid. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Combined Road Substrate (CRS), a graph-grounded framework that makes geometric road structure and open-vocabulary semantics jointly executable in a single representation. CRS enables the automatic generation of compositionally complex and linguistically varied question-answer pairs via recursive graph queries, augmented with a "grounding for free" mechanism that ensures logical traceability to specific map elements, and procedurally extracted chain-of-thought supervision traces. We demonstrate that state-of-the-art VLMs - including large, closed-source models - struggle significantly with structured road reasoning, yet training a small 2- or 4-billion-parameter model with as few as 20 to 80 CRS-enriched scenes yields stable gains in compositional reasoning tasks of varying depth. Analysis of model behavior via verifiable reasoning traces reveals a systematic shift in failure modes: whereas baseline models fail at relational scene understanding, CRS-trained models reduce failures to attribute recognition, suggesting that for structured road reasoning tasks, the lack of structured supervision is a greater limitation than model scale. Project page: https://kth-rpl.github.io/CRS/

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: SPROUT: The Open-Source Soft Growing Robot for Search and Rescue
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Antonio Alvarez Valdivia, Ciera McFarland, Robert Reeve, Ankush Dhawan, Chad Council
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: SPROUT is an open-source soft robot designed for versatile search and rescue operations, featuring modular hardware and software for various challenging environments and tasks.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Soft robotic systems have long been theorized as ideal candidates for use in search and rescue operations; however, there have been significant barriers to entry in graduating soft robotic systems from the laboratory to the field. To address this gap in replicable, reliable soft robot systems, we present the designs for SPROUT, the Soft Pathfinding Robotic Observation Unit. The system has matured over years of interaction with professional urban search and rescue communities, with the goal of operating in dusty, wet, and isolated conditions. This manuscript contains supplementary material, including code, parts manifests, CAD assemblies, and build instructions to allow the broader robotics research community to build their own SPROUT systems. The modular hardware and ROS 2-based software stack support task-specific payloads and control functions, allowing SPROUT to be adapted for applications beyond search and rescue, including infrastructure inspection and archaeology. Here, we demonstrate SPROUT performing a variety of challenging inspection and traversal tasks in collapsed structure training sites used by first responders. The main project page is available online at https://sprout-mitll.github.io/sprout/.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Recoverability, Not Invariance: Certified Safety for Robots at the Limits of Performance
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Thomas A. Berrueta, Joshua D. Ibrahim, Gilchrist X. Johnson, John Lathrop, Soon-Jo Chung
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: This paper introduces recoverability as a safety certification method for robots, enabling certified recovery from aggressive maneuvers without relying on forward invariance.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Safety certification in robotics typically rests on forward invariance of the deployed controller, a property that demands high-fidelity models at the edge of the operating envelope, exactly where models are least reliable and robots perform best. As a result, many of the behaviors we most want robots to run, from learned policies to aggressive maneuvers at the limits of traction, cannot be certified at all. We introduce recoverability, a contraction-theoretic safety concept that resolves this tension by certifying a robot's ability to reengage a trusted recovery mode rather than the invariance of a deployed behavior. We prove that switching to the recovery mode from anywhere inside a certified tube guarantees exponential convergence, even under disturbances and model error. To decide when to switch, we derive the contraction insertion gradient, the first-order effect of a recovery insertion on the certificate, and embed it in a switching-time program in which feasibility alone guarantees safety and optimality only shapes performance. To supply the certificates, we develop sequential convex synthesis that monotonically grows the certified tube toward the exact viability kernel. We validate our approach in simulated quadrotor flight through uncertain obstacles, where it outperforms invariance-based safety filters, and in hardware deployments aboard a full-scale IndyNXT autonomous racecar, where it repeatedly recovers the car from an aggressive raceline at the limits of handling in the rain. Recoverability provides a certified exit strategy, extending formal safety guarantees to aggressive, learned, and experimental behaviors without requiring their invariance.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: JEPA Dots: Dual-Latent World Model for Language-Guided Robot Control
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Xianhao Pan, Chi Li, Hanchao Li, Yunxin Liu, Jiankai Sun
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: JEPA Dots introduces a dual-latent framework for language-guided robot control, achieving 84.9% success by separating dynamics and task representations while maintaining invariant world predictions.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Predictive world models for language-guided robot control face a fundamental conditioning challenge: instructions should influence action selection without altering the predicted consequences of fixed actions under identical observations. To address this challenge, we introduce JEPA Dots (Dynamics-Oriented Task Separation), a compact dual-latent framework that jointly learns visual dynamics and language-guided control through separate dynamics and task representations. Language-conditioned task features guide a flow-matching policy, while masked attention restricts world prediction to instruction-independent dynamics history and supplied actions. In closed-loop evaluation on 40 trained LIBERO tasks, JEPA Dots achieves 84.9% overall success with approximately 39.1M parameters, compared with the published 78.7% of NanoVLA-S with 161.0M parameters under a different evaluation protocol. In the reference experiment, JEPA Dots also improves overall success from 76.0% for our task-ID-conditioned adaptation baseline to 84.9%, with LIBERO-Goal success increasing from 67.1% to 88.5%. Instruction-switching experiments further confirm that task representations and policy outputs respond to language changes, while dynamics representations and world predictions remain invariant under fixed observations and supplied actions.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: T-WLA: Bridging Slow Vision and Fast Touch with a World-Language-Action Model
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Kaichen Zhou, Yuzhen Chen, Hannah Yao, Chonghe Jiang, Rao Fu
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: T-WLA integrates visual memory with tactile feedback to enhance contact-rich manipulation, achieving significant improvements in motion prediction and task success rates.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: In contact-rich manipulation, contact conditions can change before a visual policy updates its action plan. Recomputing the plan through the visual policy adds latency, while tactile feedback alone does not specify how the ongoing motion should be revised for the task. We introduce T-WLA, a world-language-action architecture that uses shared visual memory to guide both action generation and tactile correction. At each visual update, the visual branch integrates the current image, task instruction, and retrieved history into a visual memory that conditions base-action generation. The same memory is cached for a lightweight tactile editor, which combines it with the active action chunk and incoming touch to predict residual corrections to unexecuted actions without rerunning the visual branch. Future-image and future-pressure prediction provide training-only supervision, encouraging the visual memory and tactile features to capture interaction dynamics relevant to action generation and correction. We evaluate T-WLA on tactile-conditioned hand-motion prediction using EgoTouch and Tachin, and on four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks. On EgoTouch, T-WLA reduces finger-joint MPJPE by 30% relative to the strongest evaluated baseline. Across four real-robot tasks, T-WLA achieves 51.0% mean success versus 23.0% for the baseline, a gain of 28.0 percentage points. Videos and code are available at https://t-wla.github.io/.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: One Frozen Simulator Is Not Enough: Simulator Collapse in Multi-Agent RL
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Simon Yu, Nicholas Tomlin, Marwa Abdulhai, Ximing Lu, Derek Chong
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: The paper identifies "simulator collapse" in multi-agent reinforcement learning, proposing Verbalized Sampling and Co-Training as solutions to enhance agent generalization and performance with diverse simulators.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) for human-AI interaction usually trains the agent against a single large language model (LLM) that simulates the user. We show that agents trained this way can systematically fail to generalize, and we trace the failure to simulator collapse: the simulator LLM is mode-collapsed, and a policy trained against it learns narrow strategies that exploit the simulator's mode behavior; these strategies transfer poorly to unseen simulators and to real users. We formalize the collapse and propose two solutions. Verbalized Sampling, applied at inference time, samples each simulator reply from a verbalized response distribution. Co-Training, applied during training similar to self-play, co-evolves the simulator as the policy, so the policy cannot exploit the mode behavior. A population variant samples the simulator for each rollout from a pool of recent checkpoints. We validate both solutions on three benchmarks: Persuasion for Good, tau^2-bench, and CooperBench. Verbalized Sampling improves held-out success by up to 9% over single-simulator RL, and Co-Training pushes gains further to 14%; the human study shows similar gain on real users. Both solutions also preserve the policy diversity that collapses under single-simulator RL. Overall, our findings on simulator collapse point to diverse simulators as a requirement for RL agents that serve real users. We release SCOPE, an open-source framework for Population Co-Training in multi-agent RL.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: ALOHA Lightning: Learning Fast and Precise Manipulation
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: John Hua Yao. Qi Wu, Yihuai Gao, Chelsea Finn, Zipeng Fu
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: ALOHA Lightning enables robots to learn and execute fast, precise manipulation tasks at near-human speeds through kinesthetic teaching and a robust learning pipeline.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Learning from human demonstrations has enabled robots to acquire a wide range of manipulation skills, but learned policies typically execute far slower than ordinary humans. This speed gap is mainly due to lack of an interface for collecting demonstration data at high speed, and the difficulty in training policies that can robustly execute high-speed motions. In this paper, we present ALOHA Lightning (Flash ALOHA), a system for learning fast and precise robotic manipulation. Our system uses kinesthetic teaching to intuitively collect near-human-speed demonstrations on a backdrivable bimanual platform, yielding natural and fast trajectories. We also present a learning pipeline that enables smooth high-speed execution through test-time action smoothing and aligns the visual data distribution between data collection and deployment with masking. Given 50 demonstrations for each task, ALOHA Lightning autonomously completes bimanual tasks such as ball tossing and catching, folding shorts, battery insertion, and bussing tables for over 80% success rates while close to human speed. Project website: https://flash-aloha.github.io/

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: VISTAQA: Benchmarking Joint Visual Question Answering and Pixel-Level Evidence
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Mozhgan Nasr Azadani, Yimu Wang, Yongpeng Zhu, Lihong Chen, Milan Ganai
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: VISTAQA is a benchmark for evaluating visual question answering by requiring models to provide correct answers and pixel-level evidence, revealing significant performance gaps in current systems.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Establishing a clear link between model predictions and the visual evidence that supports them is critical for transparency and reliability in multimodal reasoning, yet current multimodal large language model (MLLM) evaluations do not explicitly enforce this alignment. Existing benchmarks assess either textual answer correctness or pixel-level localization in isolation, leaving the coupling of reasoning and grounding an open challenge. We introduce VISTAQA, a comprehensive benchmark for joint evaluation of free-form answer correctness and pixel-level evidence grounding in visual question answering. VISTAQA comprises 1,157 expert-curated samples spanning six task types and six visual domains, ranging from direct perception to compositional and relational reasoning. VISTAQA requires models to not only answer correctly, but to also provide precise segmentation masks that support their answers. It also includes hallucination-aware examples where no valid visual evidence exists. To support this enhanced evaluation, we introduce GROVE, a unified evaluation metric that enforces joint correctness by combining textual accuracy and grounding quality via a per-sample geometric mean, ensuring neither dimension can compensate for deficiencies in the other. Comprehensive experiments across grounding-aware models and hybrid pipelines with general-purpose MLLMs reveal that even the strongest systems achieve limited performance under GROVE, highlighting a substantial gap between answer accuracy and visual evidence alignment. Project page can be found at https://vistaqa.github.io.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: SAGE-VQA: A Training-Free, Self-Evolving Agentic Framework with Grounded Evidence for Knowledge-Based Visual Question Answering
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Ruirui Shen, Jianqi Gao, Xiangfeng Luo, Yonggang Zhang, Muran Yu
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: SAGE-VQA introduces a training-free framework for knowledge-based visual question answering, enhancing reasoning through evidence verification and self-evolving memory without model parameter updates.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Knowledge-based visual question answering (KB-VQA) aims to combine visual information with external knowledge to answer user questions. Existing methods face two main bottlenecks: visual perception errors can propagate into hallucinations, and generalization across scenarios remains limited. To address these issues, we propose SAGE-VQA (Self-evolving Agent framework with Grounded Evidence), a training-free agentic framework that combines evidence verification with experience evolution. Our key insight is to explore an Evidence-Driven Adaptive Reasoning (EDAR) strategy. It accurately acquires and verifies question-relevant fine-grained visual information. It also extracts and refines reusable experience to support robust reasoning across tasks. Specifically, we design a Co-verified Visual Grounding module that verifies question-relevant visual information and provides grounded evidence for subsequent reasoning. We further introduce a Self-evolving Hierarchical Memory (SHM) mechanism. SHM organizes experiences into declarative and procedural memories based on their nature. These memories can be reused in subsequent reasoning and continually refined through feedback, without updating model parameters. Experimental results show that our method outperforms competing methods based on lightweight open-source vision-language models (VLMs) as well as those based on closed-source VLMs. Moreover, our method can serve as a plug-and-play reasoning framework for existing VLMs without modifying their architectures.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: MindTopo: Can Foundation Models Reason in Topological Space?
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Yunfei Ge, Anbang Liu, Qineng Wang, Johnalbert Garnica, Jianwen Lyu
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: MindTopo benchmarks foundation models' topological reasoning and planning abilities across cognitive properties, revealing performance gaps compared to human scores and highlighting areas for improvement.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Spatial reasoning depends not only on metric properties such as distance, angle, and shape, but also on topological relations that remain invariant under continuous deformation. Cognitive science identifies these relations as foundational to spatial understanding, yet foundation-model evaluations largely focus on metric or viewpoint-dependent relations. We introduce MindTopo, a benchmark of topological intuition across five properties grounded in cognitive science and formal topology, namely continuity, separation, order, enclosure, and knots.
