LPAVR transforms Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) from a decoding acceleration mechanism into a lookahead signal for anticipating upcoming reasoning intent. During MTP decoding, the draft head generates multiple future tokens, while the target model verifies them in parallel and retains the longest prefix consistent with its decoding trajectory. This target-verified prefix contains near-future semantics, which LPAVR uses to construct lookahead-guided visual evidence and assess whether history-guided evidence covers the indicated regions. If the coverage is sufficient, the history-guided evidence is retained; otherwise, LPAVR switches to the lookahead-guided evidence. This better aligns the visual context with upcoming reasoning and improves consistency between draft predictions and target-model decoding. Experiments on multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks show that LPAVR improves both reasoning accuracy and the acceptance rates of MTP speculative tokens, jointly enhancing visual reasoning and speculative decoding efficiency.

Multimedia Lab (MMLab).title: CaPtain: A Pipeline for Post-Training Code-as-Policy Robot Agents
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).authors_text: Yijia Fan, Xilin He, Yilei Jiang, Dongming Wu, Jiaxu Wang
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).summary: CaPtain is an open post-training pipeline that transforms small vision-language models into effective code-as-policy robot agents, achieving significant performance improvements without relying on pre-trained models.
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).debug_abstract: Across coding, web, and tool-use tasks, language-model agents are now routinely trained with the same recipe: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to learn the interface, then multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) to master it. Code-as-policy (CaP) casts robot manipulation in the same form, as the policy writes code against robot APIs and reads back the results, so the same recipe should apply. Yet existing CaP agents sidestep training: they either prompt closed frontier models or delegate manipulation to pre-trained vision-language-action models (VLAs) and high-level skills, while small open vision-language models (VLMs) fail outright. We present CaPtain, an open post-training pipeline that turns a small open VLM into a capable CaP agent, with no VLA, frontier model, or privileged state at test time. CaPtain trains and deploys the policy inside CaPtain-Harness, which exposes low-level perception, geometry, and guarded-motion primitives across simulation and real hardware. We first align the base model via SFT on synthetic trajectories generated with GPT-6 Astra, then apply multi-turn RL. Multi-turn RL must credit tens of agent requests, whose physical effects often surface turns later, from a single end-of-episode outcome. We therefore introduce a physical critic that reads privileged simulator state, never seen by the policy, and credits each request by how much it changes the predicted chance of success. Starting from Qwen3.5-4B (0% zero-shot), CaPtain-4B reaches 55.4% held-out LIBERO success after SFT and 73.8% after RL. On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 78.5%, surpassing several frontier-model agents, and its RL gains persist across three perturbation suites (+17.6 to +21.2 points). Without target-domain training, it attains 83.3% on SimplerEnv WidowX, exceeds frontier models on CaP-Bench, and runs on a real robot after simulation-only adaptation. We release all code, data, and model weights.

Multimedia Lab (MMLab).title: FlowMoDE: Coarse-to-fine Flow Matching for Detail-aware Sim-to-Real Monocular Depth Estimation
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).authors_text: Liangjing Shao, Wanhao Liu, Jinsong Lin, Zhiwei Fang, Hongliang Ren
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).summary: FlowMoDE introduces a coarse-to-fine flow-matching framework for efficient, detail-aware monocular depth estimation, outperforming existing methods in sim-to-real applications.
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).debug_abstract: Monocular depth estimation is a fundamental capability for 3D spatial perception in robotic and intelligent systems. While data-driven discriminative methods have achieved compelling performance for monocular depth estimation, generative approaches can reconstruct fine structural details with stronger generalization. However, most existing generative diffusion models suffer from low inference efficiency caused by multi-step sampling, whereas single-step diffusion models struggle to recover high-fidelity depth maps. To mitigate these drawbacks, this paper presents FlowMoDE, a coarse-to-fine flow-matching-based framework for efficient, structure-aware monocular depth estimation supporting sim-to-real and cross-scene generalization. The core architecture first conducts coarse-level decoding conditioned on diffused features extracted from a pre-trained semantic encoder, and subsequently restores fine-grained structural patterns via expanded decoding layers. Trained exclusively on a single synthetic indoor dataset, our proposed method outperforms prior methods across five real-world indoor and outdoor datasets, yielding an average 14.1% reduction in relative error against state-of-the-art works as well as 9.9\% reduction in chamfer distance for point cloud reconstruction. We further validate the generalization capability of FlowMoDE on realistic robotic scenes, with qualitative comparisons against state-of-the-art methods. The project page is https://flowmode-shao.netlify.app/

Multimedia Lab (MMLab).title: HandMimicX: Learning Human-Like Dexterous Manipulation via an Object-Centric Policy from Egocentric Videos
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).authors_text: Zihan Gao, Yufei Liu, Yuhong Zhang, Zhen Yu, Xinhao Huang
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).summary: HandMimicX presents an object-centric framework for learning dexterous manipulation from egocentric videos, enabling generalizable robotic skills through reinforcement learning and natural hand-object interactions.
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).debug_abstract: Learning dexterous manipulation from human videos remains an open challenge, particularly in the context of transferring a single demonstration into a spatially generalizable robotic skill and maintaining physically plausible human-like interactions. Unlike prior works that emphasize hand-motion imitation, we introduce an object-centric framework for acquiring dexterous skills from egocentric human RGB-D videos. Within our framework, we formulate the reinforcement learning (RL) objective in terms of object motion to decouple the underlying skill from the specific hand trajectory and impose constraints on hand-object interaction states to promote more anatomically natural hand configurations. Extensive experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate that our method enables efficient learning from human videos and generalizable skill transfer across novel spatial configurations.

Multimedia Lab (MMLab).title: Parse Before You Execute: Efficient Spatial Reasoning with Executable Primitives
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).authors_text: Xiwei Liu, Yulong Li, Xinling Zhuang, Xuhui Li, Yichen Li
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).summary: The PEPS framework enhances spatial reasoning in Vision-Language Models by committing to executable requirements before execution, improving accuracy and efficiency while reducing costs and latency.
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).debug_abstract: Spatial reasoning in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) has increasingly benefited from tool-integrated pipelines that ground computation in explicit geometry. However, existing systems often compile queries into relatively open-ended artifacts, such as code, task constraints, tool plans, or gathered evidence, leaving what must be resolved before execution under-specified. This can lead to unnecessary tool acquisition and iterative refinement, while still producing plausible reasoning traces from incomplete spatial commitments. We identify this failure mode as under-committed query compilation. To address it, we propose PEPS, a training-free agentic paradigm Parsing Executable Primitives for Spatial reasoning under a typed FESM schema over Frame, Entity, State, and Metric. PEPS follows a parse-before-execute principle: the Parser commits each query to a compact set of executable requirements; the Executor selectively grounds the required primitives through fixed geometric APIs and deterministic computation; and the Verifier checks execution sufficiency, enabling early termination or targeted repair. Extensive experiments across challenging spatial reasoning benchmarks show that PEPS consistently improves reasoning accuracy while substantially reducing refinement rounds, API cost, and end-to-end latency over strong tool-integrated baselines. These results demonstrate that explicit requirement commitment can make tool-integrated spatial reasoning not only more reliable, but also more execution-efficient.

Multimedia Lab (MMLab).title: Decompose and Reorganize: Planning with Primitives and Visuomotor Policies Learned from Demonstrations
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).authors_text: Yizhou Chen, Hang Xu, Dongjie Yu, Yupu Lu, Tengye Xu
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).summary: The DR-LfD framework integrates visuomotor policies into TAMP, enabling efficient skill decomposition and reorganization for dexterous bimanual manipulation with fewer demonstrations.
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).debug_abstract: Successfully automating dexterous, long-horizon bimanual manipulation requires frameworks capable of both high-level reasoning and fine-grained execution. Traditional task and motion planning (TAMP), while excellent at symbolic planning, is often brittle in contact-rich operations. Simultaneously, imitation learning (IL), while effective in manipulation tasks with visual feedback, is limited by its low capability in spatial generalization and multi-stage operation. To reconcile their complementary strengths and limitations, we propose DR-LfD (Decomposed and Reorganized Skills Learned from Demonstrations), a framework that integrates visuomotor policies into a TAMP-gated decision-making system. Based on contact relationships, DR-LfD decomposes human demonstrations into atomic skills, which are reproduced as visuomotor policies or object-centric primitives. The initiation, termination, and constraints of the visuomotor policies are carefully modeled and implemented in a TAMP-compatible form, enabling reorganization of skills learned from different sources. DR-LfD transforms the learning problem from one requiring exponential demonstration data over possible skill sequences to one whose demonstration burden scales with the number of distinct skill types, with limited data for each skill. Real-world and simulation benchmarks demonstrate data-efficient skill composition under unseen setups and physical constraints. On two DexMimicGen tasks, DR-LfD with 100 demonstrations outperforms diffusion-based imitation policies with 1000.

Multimedia Lab (MMLab).title: GPU-accelerated Incremental Euclidean Distance Transform for Online Motion Planning of Mobile Robots
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).authors_text: Yizhou Chen, Shupeng Lai, Jinqiang Cui, Biao Wang, Ben M. Chen
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).summary: This paper presents a GPU-accelerated system for incremental Euclidean Distance Transform and Occupancy Grid Maps, enhancing real-time online motion planning for mobile robots.
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).debug_abstract: In this letter, we present a volumetric mapping system that effectively calculates Occupancy Grid Maps (OGMs) and Euclidean Distance Transforms (EDTs) with parallel computing. Unlike these mappers for high-precision structural reconstruction, our system incrementally constructs global EDT and outputs high-frequency local distance information for online robot motion planning. The proposed system constructs OGM with massive amount of data from multiple types of sensor inputs. Using GPU programming techniques, the system quickly computes EDT in parallel within local volume. The new observation is continuously integrated into the global EDT using the parallel wavefront algorithm while preserving the historical observations. Experiments with datasets have shown that our proposed approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art robot mapping systems and is particularly suitable for mapping unexplored areas. In its actual implementations on aerial and ground vehicles, the proposed system achieves real-time performance with limited onboard computational resources.

Multimedia Lab (MMLab).title: Online Learning of Heterogeneous Locomotion Dynamics under Reinforcement Learning Policies for Precise Loco-Manipulation
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).authors_text: Tianlin Zhang, Weipeng Xia, Lingwei Zhang, Yiyang Shao, Zhongyu Li
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).summary: The paper presents an online learning method using a contaminated Gaussian model to improve loco-manipulation accuracy by addressing heterogeneous locomotion dynamics under a fixed policy.
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).debug_abstract: How to reuse a pretrained locomotion policy for precise loco-manipulation is still an open problem. We propose an online method to learn the closed-loop dynamics under a frozen locomotion policy. The learned model predicts floating-base motion and improves loco-manipulation accuracy. However, unobserved latent conditions of the policy introduce heterogeneous responses, meaning that the same observed state will lead to different motions. Direct learning without accounting for this heterogeneity introduces bias and fluctuations into dynamics estimates, degrading floating-base prediction and end-effector tracking. To address this problem, a contaminated Gaussian model is proposed to approximate the effects of latent conditions. The model uses two Gaussian components to approximate predictable and unpredictable responses under the same observed state. Then, the contaminated Gaussian model is combined with a Gaussian process to construct an online learner using random Fourier features (RFFs). The learner estimates each response's probability of belonging to the predictable component and uses it to weight online updates, capturing predictable responses while reducing bias and fluctuations caused by heterogeneous observations. With consistent and unbiased dynamics estimates, model predictive control (MPC) predicts floating-base motion accurately and enables precise loco-manipulation. A finite-sample error bound is established to ensure uniform convergence in online learning. Simulation and hardware experiments demonstrate consistent end-effector tracking across different manipulator configurations and tasks, with errors of 0.01 m.

Multimedia Lab (MMLab).title: From Events to Enhancement: A Survey on Event-Based Imaging Technologies
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).authors_text: Yunfan Lu, Xiaogang Xu, Pengteng Li, Yusheng Wang, Yi Cui
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).summary: This survey reviews event-based imaging technologies, detailing sensor characteristics, enhancement tasks, advanced applications, and ongoing challenges in the field.
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).debug_abstract: Event cameras offering high dynamic range and low latency have emerged as disruptive technologies in imaging. Despite growing research on leveraging these benefits for different imaging tasks, a comprehensive study of recently advances and challenges are still lacking. This limits the broader understanding of how to utilize events in universal imaging applications. In this survey, we first introduce a physical model and the characteristics of different event sensors as the foundation. Following this, we highlight the advancement and interaction of image/video enhancement tasks with events. Additionally, we explore advanced tasks, which capture richer light information with events, \eg~light field estimation, multi-view generation, and photometric. Finally, we discuss new challenges and open questions offering a perspective for this rapidly evolving field. More continuously updated resources are at this link: https://github.com/yunfanLu/Awesome-Event-Imaging

Multimedia Lab (MMLab).title: Where to Learn and How Far to Roll Out: Efficient Adaptive Training for GUI Agents
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).authors_text: Yuxiang Chai, Quyu Kong, Panrong Tong, Steven Hoi, Yue Wang
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).summary: The paper presents a two-stage adaptive training framework for GUI agents that enhances efficiency by optimizing learning locations and rollout lengths, reducing interactions by 56-61%.
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).debug_abstract: Trajectory-level GRPO is a common approach for training multi-step GUI agents, but repeatedly rolling out complete trajectories from the task root can be inefficient: task-level rewards provide coarse supervision over which intermediate decisions require improvement, while already-mastered prefixes are repeatedly re-executed before reaching difficult states. We introduce a two-stage adaptive training framework that jointly addresses where to learn and how far to roll out. We first construct reusable intermediate checkpoints from successful expert trajectories and select informative pivots using action disagreement, which measures uncertainty directly from sampled GUI actions. Stage I performs one-step RL at these pivots to improve uncertain local decisions. Stage II then progressively expands policy responsibility through adaptive Local, Suffix, and Root training according to task progress. Recoverable checkpoints enable repeated training from intermediate states without replaying the preceding trajectory. Across MobileGym and CUA-Gym-Hub, our method reduces environment interaction by 56-61% relative to Vanilla GRPO while improving task performance, demonstrating that jointly allocating training across states and rollout ranges can substantially improve GUI-agent RL efficiency.

Multimedia Lab (MMLab).title: CuBot-STT: Simultaneously Transport and Tighten for Lattice-type Modular Reconfiguration Robot
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).authors_text: Chongxi Meng, Da Zhao, Yanmin Zhou, Runjie Shen, Zhipeng Wang
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).summary: CuBot-STT is a modular reconfiguration robot that simultaneously transports and locks modules, enhancing efficiency and structural integrity while optimizing planning through advanced learning techniques.
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).debug_abstract: Lattice-type modular reconfigurable robots rearrange standardized modules across tasks. Dedicated transport robots reduce module weight and cost by eliminating module level reconfiguration actuators. But existing systems use low capacity connections or internal fastening robots that occupy space for functional components. This paper presents CuBot-STT, which integrates module transport, interface locking, and release in one external robot. Cubic modules provide structural support and $24\,\mathrm{V}$ power distribution. On each face, a gear transmission converts one external input into motion of four helical locking points, preserving internal space. The robot uses alternating foot support, a gripper for module handling, and a tightening head for interface actuation. The controller coordinates two-foot support and module locking through continuous constraint transfers. The planner decomposes relocation costs into an analytical lower bound and a residual learned through expert-guided, goal conditioned Q-learning. Contact face $A^*$ search expands relocation sequences into robot primitives satisfying connectivity, asymmetric manipulation, and foot stance constraints. Experiments demonstrate normal and tangential interface capacities of $300\,\mathrm{N}$ and $490\,\mathrm{N}$, electrical continuity across six modules, and autonomous reconfiguration of an 11-module lattice. Planning benchmarks show superior search efficiency over analytical guidance and bidirectional heuristic search, with generalization beyond training lattice sizes without fine-tuning.

Multimedia Lab (MMLab).title: YOLOF-MLD: A Multi-Level Distillation Framework for Efficient Object Detection
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).authors_text: Xiaolong Wu, Liming Zheng, Zitong Liu, Yue Zheng
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).summary: YOLOF-MLD introduces a multi-level distillation framework that enhances object detection efficiency on edge devices, achieving significant parameter reduction and competitive accuracy.
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).debug_abstract: Efficient object detection on resource-constrained edge devices is essential for safety-critical applications such as fire-smoke monitoring. However, current lightweight frameworks, such as YOLO26, still rely on the parameter-dense multi-branch Feature Pyramid Network (FPN), preventing full exploitation of their lightweight advantage. Replacing FPN with YOLOF's single-input-single-output (SiSo) neck is a promising solution but causes substantial accuracy loss. To alleviate this, we propose YOLOF-MLD, a CPU-efficient multi-level distillation (MLD) framework that combines a YOLO26n backbone, a SiSo neck, and MLD. It aligns features at the backbone via sliced-semantics matching, neck with receptive-field matching, and response levels. On D-Fire and Annotated Fire-Smoke (AFS) datasets, YOLOF-MLD reduces the parameter count of YOLO26n by 35.7\% and achieves a 62.3\% speedup on Raspberry Pi 5, attaining 71.6% and 59.9% mAP@50, respectively, compared with 75.5% and 60.0% for YOLO26n. These results demonstrate a competitive accuracy--latency trade-off for edge deployment. Our code is available at https://github.com/XiaolongWU111/YOLOF---MLD/blob/main/README.md.

Multimedia Lab (MMLab).title: TaskFrame: Connecting Task-Level Planning with Frame-Level Control for Game Agents
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).authors_text: Guangzhi Wang, Junfu Pu, Yiran Wang, Xingyilang Yin, Honghao Chen
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).summary: TaskFrame integrates task-level planning and frame-level control in game agents, enhancing performance in dynamic environments through a hierarchical planner-controller framework.
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).debug_abstract: Building general game agents requires both high-level task reasoning and low-latency action control in rapidly changing visual environments. These capabilities favor models with substantially different computational profiles, making them difficult to realize within a single model. In this work, we present TaskFrame, a hierarchical planner-controller framework that connects task-level planning with frame-level keyboard-and-mouse control. A vision-language task planner decomposes a high-level goal into an ordered sequence of atomic instructions and is optimized through supervised learning and dependency-aware GRPO. The hidden states of special goal tokens that terminate each atomic instruction provide continuous goal embeddings that are cached and reused across control steps. A causal Transformer controller combines the embedding of the active goal with recent observations to predict discrete keyboard and mouse-button actions and continuous camera motion at every game step. We train the system in three stages: planner training, controller pretraining, and joint alignment. Experiments in Minecraft show that TaskFrame is competitive with general-purpose vision-language models on instruction decomposition, and that in closed-loop evaluation the agent achieves a higher combat success rate than the evaluated baselines.

Multimedia Lab (MMLab).title: Probing Spatial State Representations in Visual Foundation Models
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).authors_text: Baiqiao Yin, Zhongang Cai, Ruisi Wang, Qiwei Liang, Lei Yang
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).summary: This study evaluates visual foundation models' spatial representations, revealing varied capabilities in object persistence, predictive updates, and actionability under dynamic viewing conditions.
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).debug_abstract: An observer sees only part of the surrounding world, yet must keep track of what lies beyond the current view. Spatial perception therefore involves more than recognizing individual images: it calls for a persistent spatial state that is updated under self-motion and used to guide action. Do visual foundation models provide representations that support such a state? We study this question through four levels of spatial capability---spatial structure, object persistence, predictive spatial update, and actionability---using frozen-feature probes on ten representations under streaming egocentric observations of static indoor environments. The resulting capability profiles vary across tasks, network layers, and prefix lengths: strong readout of the visible scene does not ensure accurate object persistence or future-feature retrieval. Matched controls separate readout accuracy from reliance on visual history and motion. Native future prediction retains recoverable spatial structure, but a spatial reader trained on real features does not transfer to predicted features unchanged. Finally, goal-dependent candidate selection does not establish reliable continuous action utility: predicted actions respond to goal changes, yet supplying the correct goal does not reliably improve progress. Across the four levels, object persistence and actionability build on camera-pose readout, whereas feature prediction builds on visible-scene readout. Together, these findings motivate evaluating spatial representations not only by what can be decoded from them, but by whether that information is maintained beyond observation, updated predictively, and used for goal-directed action.

Multimedia Lab (MMLab).title: Kinematic-Tactile Aligned Dexterous Retargeting with Contact Wrench Space Alignment
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).authors_text: Xinyuan He, Ziheng Xu, Yueyuan Chen, Yufan Ye, Yuanshuo Tan
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).summary: This paper presents a hierarchical framework for aligning kinematics and tactile information in dexterous manipulation, achieving high replay success and fidelity in robot hand trajectories.
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).debug_abstract: Human demonstrations provide a natural and scalable source of data for learning dexterous manipulation policies. However, existing retargeting methods primarily transfer human kinematics, while the tactile information underlying physical interaction is rarely preserved across embodiments. To address this limitation, we present a hierarchical three-stage framework for kinematic-tactile aligned dexterous retargeting. We use object-centric contact wrench space as a physical representation for tactile alignment between human and robot hands. The framework first aligns hand kinematics and contact geometry, and then constructs a human wrench support profile from tactile forces and contact geometry. Robot fingertip force targets are subsequently optimized to cover the human wrench support and converted into joint position corrections, yielding directly replayable robot hand trajectories. We evaluate the framework in simulation and real robot experiments across three pouring conditions. In the real robot experiments, our method achieves a 96.7\% replay success rate and higher wrench transfer fidelity than representative retargeting baselines. The framework enables physically grounded transfer of kinematic and tactile information from human demonstrations to robot hands, providing a path toward scalable learning of contact-rich dexterous manipulation.

Multimedia Lab (MMLab).title: WorldProbe: When Video World Models Fall Apart under Long-Horizon Spatial Exploration
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).authors_text: Minqi Wang, Jie Peng, Hejun Dong, Ruchang Yao, Puyi Wang
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).summary: WorldProbe introduces a benchmark revealing that video world models struggle with long-horizon exploration, highlighting inconsistencies in long-range memory despite improved local generation quality.
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).debug_abstract: Video world models generate future visual observations from camera or action inputs, with the goal of synthesizing persistent 3D worlds that can be explored across time and space. Existing benchmarks typically evaluate short interactions or rely on camera trajectories fixed before generation. The performance of video world models under long-horizon exploration with extensive camera motion remains under-explored. We introduce WorldProbe, a diagnostic benchmark that uses a goal-conditioned multimodal agent to adapt camera actions online during generation. WorldProbe comprises 164 test cases across four probing families. Across 10 state-of-the-art models, we generate more than 1,600 rollouts totaling approximately 800 minutes, with horizons up to 180 seconds. Our evaluation across four dimensions reveals both the degradation of local measures and the emergence of long-range inconsistencies. We find that recent models sustain visual and content quality for longer, while long-range memory and evolution remain weak. These results expose a gap between locally stable generation and persistent world consistency that is largely missed by existing benchmarks. Code and benchmark resources are available at https://github.com/Untitled-W/WorldProbe.

Multimedia Lab (MMLab).title: GROME: GROunding Factorized MEmory into Video World Models
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).authors_text: Fang Yu, Xiaoxue Wu, Haiyu Zhang, Yangfu Li, Botong Zhao
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).summary: GROME is a novel memory framework that enhances video world models by decoupling static and dynamic information for improved long-horizon consistency and scene fidelity.
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).debug_abstract: Long-horizon consistency is essential for video world models, yet it becomes difficult to maintain once observed content falls outside the context window. Existing memory mechanisms either retrieve history as implicit context, which remains constrained by context capacity and entangles static and dynamic information or consolidate history into explicit global representations, which struggle to model evolving dynamics and accumulate geometric errors. To overcome these limitations, we introduce \textbf{GROME}, a novel factorized memory framework that augments video world models for long-horizon coherence across both static scenes and dynamic entities. GROME operates via three synergistic components: 1)~\emph{Static-Dynamic Factorization} decouples historical evidence into static and dynamic components, preserving static scene geometry and dynamic entity states separately; 2)~\emph{Local Memory Retrieval} selects spatially aligned static history to eliminate geometric drift alongside the latest dynamic entity states to ensure temporal continuity; 3)~\emph{Training-Free Memory Injection} seamlessly grounds the factorized memory into video world models via their native conditioning pathways. Experiments on long-horizon revisit scenarios demonstrate that GROME substantially enhances scene persistence and dynamic entity fidelity over existing methods, all while preserving the visual quality and controllability of the frozen backbone without additional training. Beyond self-rollouts, GROME readily accommodates external observations as plug-and-play memory, unlocking flexible and controllable video continuation and scene exploration.

Multimedia Lab (MMLab).title: HiFOR: Hierarchical Foresight with Action-Guided World Grounding for Vision-Language-Action Model
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).authors_text: Rongxing Ding, Hongyu Qu, Kehong Wu, Xudong Wang, Fan Zhang
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).summary: HiFOR introduces a hierarchical foresight framework that integrates short-term and long-term predictions with action-guided retrieval to enhance robotic manipulation in Vision-Language-Action models.
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).debug_abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated promising capabilities in robotic manipulation by integrating visual perception, language understanding, and action generation. Recent advances have further incorporated future prediction to enhance the understanding of environmental dynamics and task progression. However, existing methods often model short-term dynamics and long-term task objectives separately, while directly incorporating predicted futures into action policies without sufficiently considering their relevance to current action requirements. To address these limitations, we propose HiFOR, a hierarchical foresight framework with action-guided world retrieval. Specifically, Hierarchical Foresight Prediction jointly predicts short-term state evolution, semantic milestones, and final goal states through a Hierarchical Dependency Mask (HDM), establishing dependencies across temporal horizons. Building upon these predictions, Structure-Aware Latent World Modeling organizes future latent representations along the horizon, view, and spatial dimensions to facilitate fine-grained retrieval. Furthermore, Action-Guided Factorized World Retrieval adaptively retrieves relevant future information from the structured latent world based on evolving action representations during denoising, providing targeted guidance for action generation. Extensive experiments on two simulation benchmarks and six real-world robotic manipulation tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

Multimedia Lab (MMLab).title: SELF: A Robust Singular Value and Eigenvalue Approach for LLM Fingerprinting
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).authors_text: Hanxiu Zhang, Qiang Xu, Yue Zheng
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).summary: SELF is a robust fingerprinting method for LLMs that enhances IP protection by using singular and eigenvalue decomposition to resist false claims and modifications.
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).debug_abstract: Safeguarding the Intellectual Property (IP) of Large Language Models (LLMs) against model theft represents a critical challenge in contemporary AI research. Although fingerprinting is essential for establishing forensic evidence for model derivation, existing methods are susceptible to false claim attacks, weight manipulations, or high false positive rates, undermining their utility. To overcome these limitations, we propose SELF, \rev{a novel intrinsic weight-based fingerprinting scheme tailored for robust IP forensics via adversarial model lineage verification}. SELF eliminates dependency on input and inherently resists false claims, achieving robust \rev{provenance detection} through unique, scalable and transformation-invariant fingerprint extraction via singular value and eigenvalue decomposition of LLM attention weights. Experimental results demonstrate that SELF maintains high IP infringement detection accuracy while significantly outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in reducing false positives and showing strong robustness against various downstream modifications, including quantization, pruning, and fine-tuning attacks. Our code is available at https://github.com/HanxiuZhang/SELF_v4.

Multimedia Lab (MMLab).title: Ego-CEVR: Learning Cross-Embodiment Visual Representations from Human Egocentric Videos
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).authors_text: Keru Zhou, Zhirui Fang, Xinrun Xu, Yaopeng Lou, Zeyuan He
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).summary: Ego-CEVR is a framework that leverages egocentric videos to learn hierarchical visual representations for robot manipulation, enhancing task understanding and action alignment.
Multimedia Lab (MMLab).debug_abstract: As egocentric video becomes increasingly available for embodied learning, an important research question is how to turn this low-cost, scalable source of data into robot manipulation capabilities. Egocentric videos naturally provide rich context for high-level task understanding, while real-robot demonstrations with wrist observations and action annotations provide supervision for fine-grained action alignment. We present Ego-CEVR, a data-native framework for hierarchical visual representation learning that assigns distinct learning objectives to global and interaction representations. The global module learns object relations, task state, and temporal progress through future prediction on egocentric video. The Interaction module interprets wrist observations in global context and learns local alignment and contact cues through robot action supervision. Separate residual paths expose both representations to the action policy, preserving direct access to task context alongside fine-grained execution information. Ego-CEVR supports independent pretraining of its global video module on large-scale human egocentric videos and videos from diverse robot embodiments, without requiring robot action labels or paired wrist observations.

OpenDriveLab.title: GLoTouch: Global-to-Local Haptic Perception Using a Parallel Gripper for Object Search, Recognition, and Grasping Without External Vision
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Zonglin Li, Wanruo Zhang, Yiming Wang, Kun Song, Xinyi Zhou
OpenDriveLab.summary: GLoTouch is a novel haptic perception framework enabling parallel grippers to perform object search, recognition, and grasping in low-light conditions without external vision.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Perceiving objects in the environment is a fundamental capability of autonomous robots. In dark or low-light environments, external cameras often fail to reliably perceive object positions and geometry; when visual sensing is unavailable, completing target search, recognition, and grasping through touch alone becomes a key robot manipulation capability. This task must simultaneously address container-scale spatial exploration and object-scale fine-grained geometric perception, which is particularly challenging for low-degree-of-freedom parallel grippers. However, a unified framework remains lacking for connecting container-scale spatial exploration with object-scale fine-grained geometric perception and grasping. To address this challenge, we present \textbf{GLoTouch}, a global-to-local haptic perception and manipulation framework built on a parallel gripper. In the global stage, the gripper holds a passive long-reach probe, combining force measurements with known tool geometry to localize contacts and actively estimate candidate-object positions, coarse contours, and heights. In the local stage, the robot sets down the probe and uses the bilateral visuotactile sensors on the same gripper to directly acquire local haptic observations, which are matched against a given target 3-D model without object-specific training. We evaluate the framework in both simulation and real-robot experiments. Source code will be open-sourced.

OpenDriveLab.title: CoT-WAM: Collaborative Training of Vision-Language Models and World-Action Models via Plan Latents
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Jinhao Zhang, Yushen Zuo, Ke Rui, Weitao Zhou, Haibao Yu
OpenDriveLab.summary: CoT-WAM is a novel framework that integrates vision-language models and world action models for enhanced semantic competence and predictive capabilities in robot manipulation tasks.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: General robot manipulation requires both semantic competence and physical foresight. World action models (WAMs) acquire an understanding of and predictive capability over the physical world by jointly modeling visual foresight and action distributions. However, existing WAMs still lack semantic competence: they have limited ability to perform open-world scene understanding, semantic reasoning, and long-horizon planning. Although vision-language models (VLMs) provide these capabilities, effectively integrating their semantic priors into WAM prediction and control remains challenging. To address this challenge, we propose CoT-WAM, a jointly trained WAM-VLM framework. CoT-WAM uses a learnable embedding to exchange information between the VLM and the WAM, which is supervised by textual and goal-image signals during training to encode rich intent information. A tailored two-stage training strategy enables joint optimization and more effective collaboration between the VLM and WAM. We evaluate CoT-WAM on six benchmarks covering control performance, zero-shot generalization, and long-horizon planning. CoT-WAM achieves SOTA performance on LIBERO, CALVIN, and RoboCasa-Kitchen, and demonstrates stronger zero-shot generalization on LIBERO-Plus and LIBERO-Pro without fine-tuning. On RoboCasa365, it further improves long-horizon planning over baselines with and without external planners. Real-world experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in practical deployments. Code is available at: https://github.com/jhz1192/CoT-WAM.git

OpenDriveLab.title: EgoPass-Bench: Identifying Objects That May Affect the Wearer's Passage in Egocentric Video
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Hongyu Wang, Chuhan Li, Congjin Xu, Xuandong Zhao, Hua Shen
OpenDriveLab.summary: EgoPass-Bench evaluates observer-relative interactions in egocentric video, revealing significant gaps between motion perception accuracy and relevant-entity identification in multimodal foundation models.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Understanding an egocentric environment requires reasoning about how surrounding entities affect the observer's actions. Existing evaluations of multimodal foundation models (MFMs) examine observer localization, motion trajectories, and action feasibility, but leave the discovery and interpretation of evolving observer-entity interactions insufficiently assessed. We introduce EgoPass-Bench, a benchmark for observer-relative interaction understanding in real-world egocentric video. EgoPass-Bench comprises 284 manually reviewed evaluation clips recorded using Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 2) smart glasses and 2,201 distinct questions across five tasks assessing motion perception, interaction judgments about specified entities, and relevant-entity discovery without target cues. Our evaluation of eight frame-based and six native-video configurations reveals a pronounced discrepancy between motion perception and interaction understanding. The strongest evaluated model, GPT-6 Astra, correctly recognizes object motion in 91.37% of 394 comparisons involving the same targets, but correctly identifies changes in passage constraints in only 66.50%. Across all 574 entity-discovery questions, it trails the two-person human baseline by $23.65 \pm 7.45$ percentage points (paired 95% CI), while exceeding the always-empty baseline (36.76%) by at least 18.9 percentage points. Further analysis reveals frequent inclusion of entities that neither pose a plausible physical conflict nor constrain passage, showing that accurate motion recognition does not ensure reliable relevant-entity discovery.

OpenDriveLab.title: MAWAM: A Multi-Agent World-Action Model for Coordinated Manipulation
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Xianzhe Fan, Chi-Pin Huang, Fu-En Yang, Jing Wang, Yecheng Wu
OpenDriveLab.summary: MAWAM is a multi-agent model that enhances coordinated robot manipulation by predicting joint actions and future states, achieving significant performance improvements in real and simulated tasks.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Every move in a robot team changes the world in which its teammates must act. Coordinated manipulation therefore calls for predicting the team's actions together with the physical future they jointly create. We introduce MAWAM, a multi-agent world-action model that jointly generates each robot's future views and executable action chunks in a single sample. Built from a pretrained single-robot world-action backbone, MAWAM jointly denoises all robots' action and future-view tokens through cross-agent attention, while preserving a separate control interface for each robot. MAWAM achieves the highest success on all three real-robot tasks (laundry-bag collection, bath-towel folding, and umbrella handover), with 67.8% mean success, 18.9 percentage points above MA-VLA trained on the same demonstrations and cameras. In simulation, MAWAM reaches 90.3% mean success on eight tasks with teams of up to four arms. Ablations show that cross-agent attention and team-stage future-video supervision both improve coordinated control: without attention, a four-arm relay falls from 95.0% to 39.0%, and without this supervision, Place Food falls from 78.0% to 47.0%.

OpenDriveLab.title: RefreshGrad: An Online Adaptive Data-sampling Method for Diffusion-based Visuomotor Learning
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Dijia Zhan, Jinyi Li, Xuemiao Xu, Yan Zhou, Yu Liu
OpenDriveLab.summary: RefreshGrad is an adaptive data-sampling method that enhances visuomotor learning by dynamically prioritizing informative trajectory segments during training, improving task success rates significantly.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Training vision-language-action (VLA) policies from demonstrations typically samples trajectory segments uniformly or relies on static offline data curation before training. However, we find that demonstration data vary sharply in supervision value across temporal windows, and that each window's value to the policy evolves substantially during training rather than being fixed or captured by raw loss alone. Motivated by this finding, we propose RefreshGrad, an online adaptive data-sampling framework that periodically scores temporal windows from the evolving policy using five policy-native signals and dynamically adjusts their sampling weights during training. RefreshGrad focuses optimization on informative, learnable windows without altering the policy architecture, training objective, or inference cost. Across ten LIBERO-Plus manipulation tasks, RefreshGrad boosts average success from 60.7% (Uniform) and 68.2% (FAKTUAL) to 76.1% under visual perturbations, and from 57.4% and 73.3% to 81.3% in clean scenes.

OpenDriveLab.title: AeroBelief: Budgeted First-Action Verification for Evidence-Guided Aerial Sensing
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Tianren Li, Dongbo Li, Hongkai Chen, Jie Liu, Guoliang Xing
OpenDriveLab.summary: AeroBelief enhances aerial sensing efficiency by verifying actions against reference scores, achieving higher task completion with significantly fewer evaluations and processed images.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Aerial sensing must combine uncertain overhead context with current observations while budgeting prediction, movement and image processing. AeroBelief uses the next executable action as the unit of verification against reference scores. It groups candidate views by first action, scans them with an inexpensive proposer, and selectively queries a structured world model (WM). Calibrated group bounds support strict commitment; a six-query controller connects selective prediction with belief updates, acceptance checks and scheduled sensing. Across four layout families, 40 worlds and 960 closed-loop executions, the AeroBelief controller completes 75.42% of tasks, compared with 73.33% for exhaustive WM scoring and 65.83% for line-of-sight geometry, using 91.81% fewer reference-candidate evaluations than exhaustive scoring. In fixed-reference replay with a six-query cap, proposer-scaled anchored bounds raised first-action certificate availability from 36.25% to 54.69% and reduced mean queries per state by 13.54% relative to unit-scale anchored bounds. A complete ground-hosted pipeline processes 2,685 self-collected 20-megapixel unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) images from seven DJI Mavic 3M routes. Context-guided admission and feedback retain all eight independently supported target confirmations with 76.05% fewer processed images and 70.02% less accumulated active processing service than uncapped all-frame processing; feedback saves another 5.17% of images relative to static context. The studies connect budgeted action selection with evidence-driven processing of recorded flight imagery.

OpenDriveLab.title: LeCompass: Task-Level Execution through State-Indexed Interfaces
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Kai Shi, Shiqi Zhao, Zimo Li, Hairong Qu, Hongyu Ma
OpenDriveLab.summary: LeCompass is a state-indexed execution framework utilizing predictive architectures to enhance task-level decision-making and spatial feedback, achieving significant improvements in execution success rates across multiple trials.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Action-conditioned joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) offer a foundation for predictive decision-making by modeling the consequences of actions in representation space. Yet evaluating local reachability in latent space does not by itself provide a task-level execution interface: intermediate targets must be generated, local inference has finite budgets, and execution requires spatial feedback and persistent interaction state. We introduce LeCompass, a state-indexed execution framework built around a frozen LeWorldModel (LeWM). A proposer supplies intermediate latent targets, while CompassFlow searches the source space of a learned trajectory prior to obtain effective action candidates under limited predictive-evaluation budgets. Patch-token readouts provide spatial feedback, while observation-based memory supports phase transitions and bounded recovery. State-indexed targets support cross-episode context-goal composition. On 1,000 official TEST full-episode Cube trials, the complete LeCompass execution system achieves 86.9% native 4-cm reach. Separate matched analyses show that predictive ranking raises success from 4.7% to 44.9% on TEST PushT and from 33.8% to 77.7% on TEST TwoRoom. These results demonstrate task-level execution with task-dependent roles for latent target proposal, predictive search, and observation-grounded control.

OpenDriveLab.title: Structured Role-Aware Policy Optimization for Multimodal Reasoning
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Bingqing Jiang, Guoxi Zhang, Jasper Wang, Bingning Wang, Difan Zou
OpenDriveLab.summary: The paper introduces Structured Role-aware Policy Optimization (SRPO) to enhance multimodal reasoning in vision-language models by assigning role-specific credit to perception and reasoning tokens.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR), especially with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), has shown strong potential for improving the reasoning capabilities of large vision-language models (LVLMs). However, in multimodal reasoning, final-answer rewards are typically assigned at the sequence level and do not distinguish the functional roles of different tokens, making it difficult to determine whether a correct answer is supported by task-relevant visual evidence. In this paper, we revisit multimodal RLVR from the perspective of role-aware token-level credit assignment, where structured responses are decomposed into perception tokens for extracting visual evidence and reasoning tokens for deriving answers from that evidence. Based on this perspective, we propose Structured Role-aware Policy Optimization (SRPO), which refines the sequence-level GRPO advantage into role-aware token-level advantages without changing the reward function. Specifically, SRPO assigns role-specific credit by using self-distilled on-policy contrasts: perception tokens are emphasized according to their visual dependency under original versus corrupted visual inputs, while reasoning tokens are emphasized according to their consistency with the generated perception. These role-specific signals are further unified through a shared trajectory-level baseline, yielding positive token weights that adjust relative update magnitudes while preserving the original GRPO reward and advantage signs, without requiring external reward models or separate teachers. Experiments across diverse multimodal reasoning benchmarks show that SRPO improves evidence-grounded reasoning, highlighting the importance of moving beyond uniform sequence-level credit toward role-aware optimization for reliable multimodal reasoning.

OpenDriveLab.title: Mixing Regularization for Average-Reward $Q$-Learning and $Q$-Planning
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Julien Roger, Sam Bodmer, Jian Qian, Benjamin Riviere
OpenDriveLab.summary: This paper introduces a regularization approach for average-reward Q-learning and planning, enhancing convergence and exploration by leveraging mixing properties of a reference policy.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: The average-reward setting for reinforcement learning is challenging because, without discounting, the span-contraction of the Bellman operator depends on the mixing properties of the underlying Markov dynamics. Whereas existing work typically assumes contraction, for instance through environment mixing, we study regularization toward a given reward-agnostic, $m$-step mixing policy to control the mixing properties of the learned policy. Our central mixing lemma quantifies how the reference policy's mixing properties transfer to the resulting learned policies. In particular, a single regularizer-dependent quantity simultaneously controls the contraction of the regularized Bellman operator and the exploration of the resulting policies. A second regularizer-dependent quantity controls the bias introduced by regularization, revealing a trade-off between convergence speed and approximation accuracy. Building on this result, we establish finite-time guarantees for regularized $Q$-iteration, synchronous and single-trajectory $Q$-learning, and $Q$-planning. Under one-step mixing, our bounds for approximating the regularized fixed point match the classical model-query bound for relative value iteration and, up to logarithmic factors, an existing sample-complexity bound for synchronous $Q$-learning. We also establish finite-time guarantees under multi-step mixing. For $Q$-planning, we characterize how the planning horizon trades off boundary bias against sample complexity. Finally, we present numerical studies validating the analysis: (i) knowledge of a strong mixing policy improves convergence and exploration, with larger benefits under more severe bottlenecks; and (ii) the observed rankings of $α$-divergence regularizers by bias and convergence speed are consistent with our theoretical analysis.

OpenDriveLab.title: GroundAnything: Reconciling Parallel Decoding with Precise Visual Grounding at Flash Speed
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Qize Yu, Lianrui Fan, Bowen Ping, Xini Ding, Zetian Song
OpenDriveLab.summary: GroundAnything is a 4B-parameter model that achieves fast, precise visual grounding through parallel decoding and iterative denoising, outperforming existing models on multiple benchmarks.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Autoregressive (AR) grounding models serialize spatial predictions, introducing sequential latency and imposing a causal order on output tokens. We view grounding as visual evidence extraction: objects, locations, and spatial relations are jointly constrained by the image and query, yet their dependencies do not imply an intrinsic left-to-right generation order. This distinction makes bidirectional diffusion a natural fit, allowing spatial hypotheses to emerge in parallel and be jointly refined through iterative denoising. We introduce GroundAnything, a 4B-parameter grounding foundation model that reconciles fast parallel decoding with precise localization through blockwise denoising. Training combines grounding pretraining from public datasets and dedicated data engines, direct AR-to-diffusion conversion with joint AR and diffusion objectives, supervised fine-tuning, and GRPO-based reinforcement post-training. Across 30 grounding benchmarks, our autoregressive variant, GroundAnything-VLM, establishes a new overall state of the art among similarly sized models at 72.42%, remaining competitive with GPT-6 Astra (71.35%). With entropy-guided decoding, GroundAnything also surpasses the prior state of the art at this scale, averaging 61.75% versus 53.32% for the fast MTP-based LocateAnything model. We further explore decoding strategies, showing that an optional self-speculative mode achieves a 4.51$\times$ speedup over the AR counterpart with a 0.74 percentage-point drop in COCO F1mIoU. Infrastructure experiments show that progressive inference optimizations translate parallel decoding into practical speedups. These gains support efficient visual grounding in latency-sensitive real-world systems.

OpenDriveLab.title: GroundingPI: A Grounding Foundation Model towards Physical Intelligence with Visual Primitives
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Qize Yu, Lianrui Fan, Boyu Chen, Jiaqi Liang, Xini Ding
OpenDriveLab.summary: GroundingPI is a state-of-the-art grounding foundation model that enhances physical intelligence in robotics by improving object localization and manipulation through advanced multimodal training techniques.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Precise grounding matters. It specifies which object is the target and where that object is, even in clutter and for tiny objects, and it has to be fast enough for closed-loop control. Yet vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAMs) take perception from general-purpose vision-language and video-generation backbones, which still fail in these settings. We introduce GroundingPI, a 4B grounding foundation model that generates points and boxes as quantized coordinates in a shared vocabulary. Training combines multimodal and spatial pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning with GRPO, using supervision from public datasets and dedicated data engines. Against 44 baselines across 34 grounding benchmarks spanning 11 perceptual capabilities, GroundingPI establishes a new state of the art, averaging 73.68%, above the larger GPT-6 Astra (71.54%). As a downstream visual backbone, GroundingPI improves performance on robotic manipulation and autonomous driving. Across RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboCasa-GR1, it outperforms all evaluated backbones in all four out-of-distribution settings, with relative gains of up to 24.8% over the strongest baseline. On RoboCasa-GR1, GroundingPI trained with 50% of the demonstrations outperforms those baselines trained with 75%. Its mean open-loop L2 error on nuScenes is 0.296 m. We systematically analyze GroundingPI's pretraining in scale and data composition. Grounding quality and downstream manipulation improve with pretraining scale, with generalization tracking perceptual gains most closely. Analyzing the data recipe across these 11 perceptual capabilities shows dense grounding's substantial benefits for both, and OCR's potential as a catalyst for perceptual learning. These results support grounding as a perceptual foundation, and dedicated perceptual pretraining as a promising direction for foundation models of physical intelligence.

OpenDriveLab.title: Composable Driving Style for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Guantian Zheng, Lidong Yu, Tianyu Gao, Jiashu Li, Jiaxing Chen
OpenDriveLab.summary: YOUDrive enables composable control of driving styles in end-to-end autonomous driving through a vision-language-action planner that adjusts behavior via learned task vectors.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: End-to-end driving policies can achieve strong task performance while offering limited control over their driving style. Driving style describes how a vehicle accelerates, brakes, and maintains distance. Policies trained without explicit preference conditioning lack a direct mechanism for adjusting these behaviors at inference. We propose YOUDrive, a vision--language--action planner for continuous and composable driving-style control. Each teacher's behavior is distilled into a task vector, a learned parameter update that induces a style direction in the planner's representation. These directions can be scaled and combined at inference without retraining the backbone. Conditioned on these directions, a flow-matching decoder models a multimodal trajectory distribution and generates kinematically feasible motion alternatives. We introduce the Style Alignment Score (SAS) to describe human-referenced kinematic behavior after safety and task gating. On NAVSIM navtest, a single coefficient monotonically controls assertiveness across six teacher-derived personas, while PDMS remains above 0.90 across the tested individual and blended configurations, reaching 0.954. Further analyses reveal systematic policy-specific kinematics after controlling for scene context, whereas the evaluated discrete style labels provide limited additional explanatory power. Code, checkpoints, and the metric will be released.

OpenDriveLab.title: CP-Guard+: A New Paradigm for Malicious Agent Detection and Defense in Collaborative Perception
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Senkang Hu, Yihang Tao, Zihan Fang, Guowen Xu, Hangcheng Cao
OpenDriveLab.summary: CP-Guard+ introduces a novel malicious agent detection and defense framework for collaborative perception in autonomous driving, enhancing safety through efficient feature-level identification and robust contrastive loss.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Collaborative perception (CP) is a promising method for safe connected and autonomous driving, which enables multiple vehicles to share sensing information to enhance perception performance. However, compared with single-vehicle perception, the openness of a CP system makes it more vulnerable to malicious attacks that can inject malicious information to mislead the perception of an ego vehicle, resulting in severe risks for safe driving. To mitigate such vulnerability, we first propose a new paradigm for malicious agent detection that effectively identifies malicious agents at the feature level without requiring verification of final perception results, significantly reducing computational overhead. Building on this paradigm, we introduce CP-GuardBench, the first comprehensive dataset provided to train and evaluate various malicious agent detection methods for CP systems. Furthermore, we develop a robust defense method called CP-Guard+, which enhances the margin between the representations of benign and malicious features through a carefully designed Dual-Centered Contrastive Loss (DCCLoss). Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on both CP-GuardBench and V2X-Sim, and demonstrate the superiority of CP-Guard+.

OpenDriveLab.title: Dune: A Zeroth-Order Optimizer with Time-Conditioned Historical Error Regression for VLA Test-Time Adaptation
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Chengyang Dong, Ze Chen, Kai Ye, Chutian Wang, Heng Xu
OpenDriveLab.summary: Dune is a novel zeroth-order optimizer that enhances test-time adaptation for VLA models by integrating historical error prediction to reduce estimation variance and improve stability.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) enables Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models to handle distribution shifts during deployment without source-domain retraining. However, backpropagation-based adaptation incurs heavy memory overhead on resource-constrained robots, whereas zeroth-order (ZO) methods suffer from high estimation variance under limited perturbation budgets. We observe that while ZO estimation enables low-memory adaptation with rapid initial gains, it often stalls or degrades over long-horizon updates due to noisy gradient estimates. To address these limitations, we propose Dune, a zeroth-order optimizer that stabilizes long-horizon adaptation by coupling online historical error prediction with current perturbation observations. Specifically, Dune learns a lightweight, time-conditioned error predictor from past optimization dynamics and fuses its predictions with instantaneous ZO estimates, achieving effective variance reduction without backpropagation or extra forward passes. Additionally, we theoretically characterize how estimation variance restricts convergence in high-dimensional, small-population regimes, motivating the use of historical statistics. Extensive experiments on LIBERO and real-world robots demonstrate that Dune achieves superior success rates under a low memory footprint, with ablations confirming improved closed-loop stability and post-disturbance recovery.

OpenDriveLab.title: RemoteVLPG: How to Obtain a Specific VLM for Language-Guided Path Generation on Remote Sensing Images?
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Junzhe Dang, Mengmeng Zhang, Yuxiang Zhang, Wei Li
OpenDriveLab.summary: The paper presents RemoteVLPG, a method for creating a task-specific Vision-Language Model for language-guided path generation on remote sensing images, demonstrating superior zero-shot performance.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: We study how to obtain a task-specific Vision-Language Model (VLM) for language-guided path generation between start and end points on remote sensing images. We explore this question from three aspects. First, we implement three widely used architectural approaches and compare their performance. Second, we design a scalable method for constructing pre-training data and build an effective pre-training dataset with a degree of diversity. Methods trained on this dataset achieve promising zero-shot performance. Third, we construct three benchmarks that support stratified evaluation and design three metrics for path generation. We investigate this problem through extensive experiments. The results show that the zero-shot performance of methods trained on the constructed pre-training dataset can exceed that of some advanced commercial VLMs. Code and Dataset can be available at https://github.com/jzdang/RemoteVLPG

OpenDriveLab.title: WeightCode: Installing New Capabilities into Neural Networks via Weight-Space Programming
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Bo Li, Taoyong Cui, Bob Zhang, Mengran Li, Chengyang Zhang
OpenDriveLab.summary: WeightCode introduces Weight-Space Programming to enhance neural networks' capabilities by directly modifying weights with executable programs, achieving significant performance improvements without retraining.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Neural networks encode learned capabilities in their weights, yet extending those capabilities with explicit task knowledge remains a fundamental challenge. Here we show that Weight-Space Programming (WSP), in which executable programs read, construct or modify a network's weights directly, can install new capabilities within trained neural networks. WeightCode, a WSP framework, uses a frozen language model to write executable weight programs that install new computations into trained neural networks using task knowledge and their existing weights, without gradient-based training. Once installed, the new capabilities run independently of the language model. Given a grammar or eight demonstrations, weight programs enable previously unseen command compositions (0% to 99.8% exact match) and a new pickup action (0% to 98.4% success), while preserving the original command and navigation capabilities. On ImageNet, four weight programs achieve net gains of 8.84-17.62 points while preserving clean accuracy, outperforming the best of eight fine-tuning methods under matched examples, checks, and retention constraints. In a Vision Transformer, causal interventions show that installed noise-correction gates drive robustness gains, while their selective activation preserves clean accuracy. Rerun on five independently trained Vision Transformers without further language model calls, ten weight programs retain 83-110% of their source-network gains on average, whereas copying their fixed weight edits yields negligible gains. Six programs written for an already edited network add 5.23-14.50 points of contrast robustness while retaining the previously installed noise gain. Together, these results establish WSP as a new route to acquiring and accumulating capabilities in trained neural networks through reusable weight programs.

OpenDriveLab.title: MorphTwin: Enriching Deformable Material Responses from Videos for Morphable and Interactive Physical Twins
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Haoqin Hong, Ding Fan, Fubin Dou, Tianyu Huang, Yuzhuo Chen
OpenDriveLab.summary: MorphTwin enhances deformable material simulations from videos by independently controlling deformation responses, achieving significant accuracy improvements over existing methods in real-time applications.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Reconstructing interactive physical twins from video requires accurately capturing how objects deform while maintaining efficient simulation. We observe that reproducing motion in a video does not guarantee correct responses to new forces when the physical representation restricts how an object can deform. In spring-based twins, coupling between volume and shape responses creates such a limitation. We present MorphTwin, which enriches local deformation modes to capture and independently control these responses while retaining standard spring forces and explicit simulation. To support interpretable material editing and transfer, we use offline calibration to map shared relative response changes to stiffness updates on each reconstructed graph. Under identical inverse settings on synthetic scenes, MorphTwin reduces the mean absolute error of Poisson's ratio by 75.8% and the mean relative error of Young's modulus by 22.1% compared to PhysTwin. We introduce an egocentric stereo and RGB-D benchmark covering interactions with objects of varying stiffness. Real-world experiments demonstrate improved reconstruction accuracy and up to 14.4% lower future tracking error than PhysTwin at interactive speeds.

OpenDriveLab.title: PhoneWorld: From Real-App Trajectories to Dynamic and Verifiable Environments for Phone-Use Agents
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Yuxuan Liu, Xin Lai, Junyi Li, Pengyuan Lyu, Chenxin Li
OpenDriveLab.summary: PhoneWorld transforms real app usage data into scalable, verifiable Android environments for training phone-use agents, enhancing performance through a trace-grounded framework.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Real applications provide the training setting closest to phone-agent deployment, but are difficult to reset, scale safely, and verify programmatically. Static screenshots and interaction trajectories preserve realistic evidence but cannot generate new experience. We introduce PhoneWorld, a trace-grounded framework that converts such evidence into runnable, resettable, and verifiable Android environments. PhoneWorld induces a usage-weighted interaction skeleton from observed pages, transitions, and state-changing operations; translates it into a behavior-grounded app specification; realizes the specification through an autonomous build--inspect--repair loop; and synthesizes executable tasks with programmatic verifiers. The resulting suite spans 34 consumer-facing apps across 16 domains and supports an audited online benchmark, verified trajectory generation, and online RL through common reset and verification interfaces. Evaluations with diverse general and open-source GUI agents show that PhoneWorld supports reliable end-to-end online interaction and exposes capabilities complementary to AndroidWorld. Controlled SFT experiments further show that PhoneWorld trajectories complement AndroidWorld supervision, transfer across online and offline benchmarks, and become more effective as data volume and app coverage increase. Under a matched RL budget, combining PhoneWorld mock-app rollouts with real-app rollouts improves performance over real-app RL alone on both real-phone tasks and AndroidWorld. Together, these results demonstrate that trace-grounded executable abstraction can bridge realistic mobile behavior and scalable agent learning, turning limited real-app evidence into a growing supply of controllable and verifiable environments for training and evaluation.

OpenDriveLab.title: Direct3D-V3: Latent-Free Diffusion Transformers in the Native Voxel Domain
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Shuang Wu, Jiachen Qian, Youtian Lin, Feihu Zhang, Philip Torr
OpenDriveLab.summary: Direct3D-V3 introduces a latent-free diffusion transformer for native 3D generation, directly modeling SDF voxel grids and enhancing geometry fidelity through implicit regularization and camera parameter prediction.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Native 3D generation has largely been built around latent diffusion, with recent advances concentrating on stronger variational autoencoders (VAE) and increasingly elaborate latent representations, from vecset and triplanes to structured sparse voxels. Despite their architectural differences, these methods all share the same premise: geometry is first compressed into a latent space and only then modeled by the generator. We take a different route and propose Direct3D-V3, a latent-free diffusion transformer (DiT) framework that discards the VAE altogether and operates in the native voxel domain, directly modeling raw SDF voxel grids during both training and sampling. To make this direct voxel formulation geometrically reliable, we introduce an implicit manifold regularization over neighboring voxels to suppress non-watertight surfaces, and convert predicted SDF grids into meshes via Marching Cubes so that rendered normal losses can supervise the model directly from its predicted SDF. To improve alignment between the conditioning image and generated geometry, Direct3D-V3 also predicts the camera parameters of the conditioning image as an auxiliary task, encouraging the DiT to learn the mapping from image observations to 3D shape. This latent-free design removes the reconstruction bottleneck, brings training under an objective in the native voxel domain, and yields meshes with substantially richer local detail. The predicted camera and native SDF voxel output further make Direct3D-V3 extensible to generative reconstruction, where diffusion is interleaved with normal-guided refinement to improve alignment with the observed view while the generative prior completes unseen regions. Project page: https://dreamtechai.github.io/Direct3D-V3.

OpenDriveLab.title: Video-OPSD: Exploiting Privileged Visual Evidence for On-Policy Self-Distillation in Video Large Language Models
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Ziyue Wang, Shiqi Huang, Weiwen Xu, Bihan Wen, Xudong Jiang
OpenDriveLab.summary: Video-OPSD enhances on-policy self-distillation in Video Large Language Models by leveraging privileged visual evidence from videos for improved reasoning and performance.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) has recently emerged as an effective post-training paradigm that provides dense token-level supervision from a privileged self-teacher, yet it remains underexplored for Video Large Language Models (Video-LLMs). Existing methods typically construct privileged teachers by augmenting their context with additional information while keeping the primary input unchanged for both teacher and student. In video reasoning, however, privileged information can also be found within the primary input itself: videos contain substantial temporal redundancy, and only a few frames carry the evidence needed to answer a question. Building on this observation, we present $\textbf{Video-OPSD}$, an OPSD framework that exploits privileged visual evidence for both self-teacher construction and knowledge transfer. First, our Evidence-Grounded Self-Teacher conditions the teacher exclusively on annotated evidence frames, while the student reasons over a broader set of frames that contains them. This focused visual context enables more targeted supervision without introducing visual content unavailable to the student. Second, our Evidence-Guided Token Optimization adaptively weights token-level distillation according to an estimate of each reasoning token's reliance on privileged visual evidence, thereby emphasizing perceptually grounded reasoning. Across five video benchmarks and three Qwen-VL backbones, $\textbf{Video-OPSD}$ consistently outperforms Standard OPSD by 1.8-2.3 percentage points on average, establishing an effective and efficient post-training approach for Video-LLMs.

OpenDriveLab.title: Learning When to Think: Dual-Reference Offline Optimization for Adaptive VLM Reasoning
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Hongbin Lin, Sizhe Zou, Juangui Xu, Xinyue Xu, Zhuoli Ouyang
OpenDriveLab.summary: The paper introduces DR-BOLT, a dual-reference optimization method that enhances vision-language models by enabling adaptive reasoning, improving efficiency and performance on multimodal tasks.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Reasoning traces improve vision-language models on complex multimodal tasks, but forcing every input to follow a long reasoning process leads to overthinking and unnecessary inference cost. We study adaptive fast/slow thinking for VLMs, where one model answers directly for simple inputs and reasons step by step when needed. Fast answers and slow traces often come from distinct behavior policies, making a single-reference offline objective misweight one mode. We propose DUAL-REFERENCE BOLT (DR-BOLT), which distinguishes the desired fast/slow mixture reference from the sampling distribution and corrects their mismatch in reward-weighted training. Fast/slow partition competition explains routing in the optimal target; an efficient source-wise correction approximates the exact objective when response formats are well separated. Matched Qwen3-VL comparisons use identical candidate banks to isolate the objective from slow-teacher quality. DR-BOLT improves score-length trade-offs over the evaluated offline and online baselines on ScienceQA and three held-out transfer benchmarks, with a 24.1% cross-benchmark slow ratio and a 2.90-fold end-to-end training speedup over reproduced GRPO. These results support adaptive reasoning in the studied two-reference setting, while broader robustness remains open. Our code is available at https://github.com/HongbinLin3589/DR-BOLT.

OpenDriveLab.title: MobileWeave: Program-First Synthesis of Dependency-Linked Tasks for Training Mobile GUI Agents
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Ziyi He, Xian Wu, Qiyuan Chen, Haitao Li, Cehao Yang
OpenDriveLab.summary: MobileWeave synthesizes executable programs for training mobile GUI agents by modeling app functions as dependency-linked tasks, enhancing performance through explicit subgoal dependencies.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: Native mobile GUI agents require large-scale training trajectories covering both individual app functions and multi-goal workflows within and across apps, which makes automatic task synthesis a promising way to scale training data. Existing synthesis pipelines, however, produce each task as free-form text, leaving implicit how its subgoals depend on one another. This matters because composition is a skill in its own right: a policy may complete each subtask of a workflow on its own, yet fail to chain these subtasks into the complete workflow. We present MobileWeave, which instead synthesizes every task as an executable program derived from the app implementations of a controllable simulator. MobileWeave abstracts each app into a typed capability graph with semantic types shared across apps, composes atomic programs into single- and cross-app composite programs through explicit value and object dependencies, and verifies each program by native execution, deriving both its instruction and its completion check from the same program. Trained on teacher trajectories collected for these tasks and on recovery supervision at the policy's own stalls, MobileWeave-8B improves its base model by 26.7 points on MobileGym and by 8.6, 21.3, and 17.6 points on AndroidWorld, AndroidLab, and MobileWorld, with comparable gains at 4B. Beyond these gains, we find that composition is learnable from task structure: explicit dependencies between subgoals act as a training signal that teaches a policy to compose skills it already masters. We release data, model, and code at https://maxxnotmarx.github.io/MobileWeave/ .

OpenDriveLab.title: Choosing Supervised Post-Processing for Frozen Person Detectors: Information, Object Changes, and Complete Cost
OpenDriveLab.authors_text: Tianyi Zhou, Zijun Jia
OpenDriveLab.summary: The paper evaluates various supervised post-processing methods for frozen person detectors, highlighting the importance of informative readouts and optimized meta classification for improved detection performance.
OpenDriveLab.debug_abstract: A frozen detector computes hypotheses that can support better final outputs through supervised post-processing.
