We apply this characterization to a planar two-finger gripper under proportional-derivative control. We show that two grasps of the same object in the same position and with the same contact forces can differ in stiffness by two orders of magnitude. Likewise, two grasps that share the same stiffness can exhibit very different resonances. Nonlinear simulations confirm the effectiveness of our small-signal analysis in capturing the dynamic behavior of grasping.

Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).title: UGG: Unified Generative Geometry Model
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).authors_text: Amani Kiruga, Zhiyi Li, Ruojin Cai, Hansen Lillemark, Xiaoshan Wu
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).summary: UGG is a unified framework for 4D scene understanding that integrates RGB video and geometric representations, enhancing visual generation and geometric prediction through conditional completion.
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).debug_abstract: Understanding 4D scenes is a core challenge in visual intelligence, requiring models to jointly capture scene geometry, appearance, and dynamics from partial observations. However, existing approaches are subdivided into feedforward models for direct geometric prediction, and generative models for visual synthesis. We introduce UGG, a unified framework for 4D scene understanding that jointly models RGB video and geometric representations such as depth and camera pose. By assigning different noise levels across modalities and time, UGG formulates visual generation and geometric prediction as conditional completion within a single generative model. This flexible formulation enables the model to learn from diverse, heterogeneous datasets with different subsets of geometric and visual annotations. Furthermore, our generative formulation enables inference-time search over multiple plausible scene hypotheses, using geometric evidence extracted from observed RGB frames to improve geometric prediction without ground truth geometry. We demonstrate UGG's effectiveness over non-unified baselines across camera-controlled video generation, depth estimation, and camera pose prediction, including in challenging sparse observation settings. Code and visualizations are available at https://ugg-model.github.io/

Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).title: Personalized Affective Perception via Continual Learning in Human-Agent Negotiation
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).authors_text: Mehmet Onur Keskin, Berk Buzcu, Nikhil Churamani, Reyhan Aydogan, Hatice Gunes
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).summary: The paper presents CLIFER, a continual learning approach for personalized affective perception in human-agent negotiation, enhancing agent adaptability and participant engagement through real-time feedback.
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).debug_abstract: Self-interested intelligent agents that negotiate with humans should interpret nonverbal expressions and adapt their behavior accordingly. However, generic facial-affect models degrade across individuals and contexts, creating a generalization gap. We introduce an affect-adaptive negotiation strategy that incorporates Continual Learning with Imagination for Facial Expression Recognition (CLIFER) to personalize valence-arousal perception in real time. Differential feedback converts changes in valence-arousal direction and intensity into adjustments of the agent's target utility. An asynchronous architecture updates CLIFER in the background during live interaction. In a counterbalanced within-subject study in which 66 participants negotiated with a humanoid robot, the CL-enabled agent achieved significantly higher individual utility and elicited higher participant concession rates than the FaceChannel baseline. The CL condition yielded significantly higher mean arousal estimates, alongside a broader output range. Participant utility and Nash distance did not change significantly between conditions. These outcomes support the practical value of coupling continual affective personalization with differential feedback for real-time negotiation.

Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).title: Same Physics, Different Gradients: A State-of-the-Art Report on Differentiable Physics Simulation
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).authors_text: Lei Shu, Zizhou Huang, Yunuo Chen, Yifei Li, Tao Du
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).summary: This report categorizes differentiable physics simulation methods, clarifying their derivatives' referents and implementations, and evaluates their effectiveness in optimization tasks.
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).debug_abstract: Differentiable simulation propagates derivatives through a physics simulator, turning animation, system identification, control, and computational design into gradient-based optimization. Engines differ in the physics they model and, less visibly, in which mathematical object they differentiate. We separate two questions the literature conflates. The referent is which object the returned derivative belongs to: the finite computation that executed, the converged equation it approximates, or the continuous dynamics. The realization describes the organization of the backward pass: automatically generated differentiation, an equation-level adjoint solve, or a custom adjoint. The referent defines the target against which exactness is assessed; the implementation determines how accurately that target is approximated. Cost depends on the realization together with how the states needed by the backward pass are retained or recovered. Crossing the axes places every method and engine we classify in a cell, separates claims the literature merges, and shows that the apparent trade-off between exactness and memory follows from how methods have been built rather than from a constraint. A second, orthogonal taxonomy covers contact, where the map is non-smooth. We then ask whether a correct gradient helps. Four mechanisms by which useful gradients are lost are cataloged and measured on one testbed, where the advantage of the exact derivative over the equation-level adjoint depends on where the fitting target comes from as much as on the solver budget, and we review the evidence that zeroth-order methods can outperform simulator gradients in the regimes where those mechanisms act. The model classes, systems techniques and applications are surveyed through this lens, and we close with a reporting checklist, a released diagnostic that computes it, and a research agenda.

Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).title: Library of Hands: Fix the Hands, Not the World Model
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).authors_text: Hasaan Ahmad, Qizhen Ying, Yuxuan Sun, Tianjin Huang, Guangming Wang
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).summary: The Library of Hands (LoH) method enhances robotic action prediction by correcting command-to-action mappings without retraining the world model, significantly improving task success rates.
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).debug_abstract: A world model predicts how a scene changes after an action, and a planner uses it to search for actions that reach a goal. If the camera moves or the controller changes, the same command moves the robot differently: when its commands are turned by 90 degrees, a frozen planner with the LeWM world model that succeeds in 77.5% of episodes succeeds in only 7.8%. Current fixes retrain the model, need training data, or forget a set-up when it returns. We propose Library of Hands (LoH), a training-free method that keeps the world model frozen and corrects only the map from commands to applied actions, which we call the hand. LoH reads the hand through the frozen model, with no extra sensor: it finds the action that best explains the change between two camera images (a reading). It stores every hand it identifies, so a returning set-up is recognised rather than re-learnt. In closed-loop tests, LoH more than doubles success on three simulated tasks, from 28.6% to 62.3%, and loses only 0.6 percentage points when nothing changes. It also works, unchanged, with two other world models and on two of three models pretrained on real robot data, and its gain grows with the quality of its readings.

Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).title: Leave It Better Than Found: Value-Guided Cooperation in Sequential Tasks
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).authors_text: Mario Gomez Andreu, Michael Amir, Antonio Marino, Tianxu An, Marco Hutter
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).summary: The paper presents a method for ad hoc robot cooperation in sequential tasks by sharing value functions, enhancing coordination without prior joint training, and improving task success rates.
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).debug_abstract: We consider the problem of sequential task continuation, where one robot acts in a workspace that has been affected by a previous robot. Current approaches in multi-robot cooperation rely heavily on co-training or co-optimization, assumingthat the robots have access to collective interaction data during the policy training or planning process. However, as increasingly varied robotic embodiments and policies are deployed and operate in the same real-world environment, learning policies for cooperation becomes infeasible due to the combinatorial explosion of possible robot combinations that need to be accounted for. To address this challenge, this paper considers the problem of ad hoc sequential cooperation between robots that have never before operated together in a shared environment. We demonstrate that robots can explicitly communicate their environmental preferences through sharing their value functions, enabling coordination without the need for prior joint training. To ground this exchange and prevent overconfidence in out-of-distribution states, we further introduce a k-nearest neighbors (KNN)- based uncertainty filter. Our method yields an increase of up to 48.5 pp compared with naive or even selfish agents, in task success rates across simulated and real-world experiments, demonstrating that value function transmission between agents is useful not merely as an internal learning tool, but as an effective basis for ad hoc coordination. Website: https://proroklab.github.io/PAVE/

Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).title: Edge-Assisted Crowdsensing for Explainable Cyclist Safety Perception
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).authors_text: Hongsen Cao, Chia-Yen Chiang, Mona Jaber, Meihui Wang, Yasmin Fathy
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).summary: This paper presents an edge-assisted crowdsensing system that uses handlebar cameras and a vision-language model to predict cyclist safety scores, enhancing infrastructure planning and continuous monitoring.
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).debug_abstract: Cyclist fatality rates remain high despite policy support for active travel, and autonomous vehicles add complexity to mixed traffic. Neither crash statistics nor multi-model detection pipelines scale to continuous monitoring of perceived safety along a route. We present an edge-assisted crowdsensing system: handlebar cameras supply street-level frames, a vision-language model (VLM) turns each frame into structured traffic attributes through a single prompt, and an explainable boosting machine (EBM) combines them with OpenStreetMap road infrastructure and on-bike kinematics to predict a crowdsourced 1-9 safety score. Extraction belongs at the network edge: the fastest self-hosted model needs 2.49 s per frame and scoring takes 0.4 ms on a CPU. On 1,362 annotated frames from two London routes, the EBM regressor reaches 72.2 percent binary accuracy and a mean absolute error of 1.011 under five-fold cross-validation. It is within one accuracy point of black-box ensembles. Its per-feature shape functions give exact attribution: physical lane separation is worth +0.97 rating points, a painted lane +0.70 and a construction site -0.65. Planners can therefore price an infrastructure change in rating points, and the results enter cost-benefit analysis directly. We also report inter-annotator agreement (alpha = 0.4695), an attribute audit, and a sensitivity analysis linking attribute error to accuracy. With re-encoding, a 20 s sampling interval serves 1,000 riders at 54 Mbit/s at a cost of 1.4 accuracy points, making continuous monitoring practical.

Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).title: Concept-Grounded Reasoning with Prompt-Driven Localization for Interpretable Structured Report Generation
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).authors_text: Xinyue Xu, Hongbin Lin, Juangui Xu, Hualiang Wang, Lehan Wang
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).summary: The CORAL framework enhances medical report generation by integrating spatial grounding and concept-level supervision, improving diagnostic accuracy and interpretability in multimodal large language models.
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).debug_abstract: Medical imaging modalities such as ultrasound and X-ray are widely used in clinical practice, where diagnosis follows a structured, evidence-driven workflow aligned with standardized criteria. While multimodal large language models (MLLMs) show promise for automated medical report generation, most existing systems rely on end-to-end multimodal fusion without modeling clinically defined intermediate attributes, leading to limited grounding and interpretability. To address this issue, we propose CORAL (COncept-grounded ReAsoning with Localization), a multimodal framework that integrates spatial grounding and concept-level supervision into a unified reasoning process. CORAL employs a prompt-driven medical segmentation model to localize lesions and predicts multi-class clinical attributes through a Concept Bottleneck module. The resulting textual concept tokens are combined with mask-modulated visual features within an MLLM to enable structured report generation and diagnostic prediction. Experiments on BUS-CoT and IU X-ray datasets demonstrate consistent improvements in diagnostic accuracy, concept consistency, and report quality over strong general-purpose and medical MLLMs, indicating that concept-grounded reasoning better aligns generation with clinical decision processes.

Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).title: DyCraft: An Agentic System for Long-Horizon 4D Scene Generation
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).authors_text: Jeff Tan, Hang Dai, Zeqian Long, Yanzhe Lyu, R. Kenny Jones
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).summary: DyCraft enhances long-horizon 4D scene generation by decomposing animations into manageable steps, improving coherence and reducing physical violations compared to existing coding agents.
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).debug_abstract: While frontier coding agents can generate high-quality 3D scenes and articulated assets, they struggle to create coherent long-horizon animations. When equipped with general-purpose harnesses, they frequently produce physically implausible outputs, generating objects that interpenetrate, lack physical support, or move unnaturally. Such bare agents struggle to repair these errors because they default to scripting the full animation in one pass, making it difficult to verify their work and disentangle complex spatiotemporal constraints. Drawing on the practice of human animators, we introduce DyCraft, a system for animated 3D scene generation that breaks animation into steps that coding agents can more reliably solve. DyCraft first expands the user's prompt into a detailed plan and builds a static scene. It then creates a 3D storyboard of key animation poses, where each frame is a static 3D scene that the agent can build and debug in isolation. Storyboarding decomposes the problem into pairs of verified start and end states, allowing the agent to author local motion between them with a collection of motion authoring tools. We evaluate DyCraft on 24 long-horizon, multi-shot animation tasks covering humanoid robots, human and animal characters, and physical mechanisms. Compared with a native GPT-6 agent in Codex and prior agentic baselines, DyCraft substantially reduces physical violations and generates higher-quality animated 3D scenes that are more often preferred by human raters.

Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).title: EgoContact: Evaluating Physical Intelligence with Egocentric Video
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).authors_text: Adam Deryło, Alexey Gavryushin, Daniel Cremers, Marc Pollefeys, Xi Wang
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).summary: EgoContact is a large-scale egocentric dataset that evaluates manipulation priors by predicting contact points, revealing current methods' limitations and improving grasp success in robotics.
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).debug_abstract: Egocentric video has emerged as one of the most scalable sources of data for learning generalizable manipulation priors. Yet, despite its growing use in pretraining robotic policies, it has been underutilized as a validation tool for physical intelligence, a key component of which is understanding where to make contact with an object to achieve an intended interaction. We present EgoContact, a large-scale egocentric dataset for evaluating the generalizability and precision of learned manipulation priors through future contact-point prediction. EgoContact contains 22.5K manually verified interaction events, each with a pre-contact observation, semantic intent, and pixel-precise contact locations. We find that current methods often struggle to predict precise interaction contacts and sometimes fail to localize the target object in diverse, in-the-wild scenes, even when allowed multiple predictions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the usefulness of EgoContact's annotated interactions for robotic manipulation: simply using EgoContact as the memory bank of an existing affordance-transfer policy improves grasp success from 14.2% to 31.2% in simulation and from 16% to 58% on a real robot.

Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).title: Any3R: Feedforward 3D Reconstruction from Any Camera Type
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).authors_text: Jingong Chen, Qingwen Zhang, Youming Deng, Chulwoo Pack, Olaf Wysocki
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).summary: Any3R is a feed-forward model for 3D reconstruction that operates robustly across various central camera types without lens-specific retraining, achieving high accuracy on diverse datasets.
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).debug_abstract: Geometry foundation models recover camera poses and dense geometry from a set of images with a feed-forward network, but they expect pinhole images. That assumption is inside the backbone too: the positional encoding and the training loss both bind an image position to a direction in space, and both depend on the lens. We condition both on the dense ray field, the unit direction through every pixel, which describes any central camera without a lens type, distortion coefficients or a bound on field of view. Angular coordinates give the rotary encoding the measured ray angle of each patch, evaluated per view, and solid-angle weighting scales the point loss by the area each pixel covers on the sphere, so neither the encoding nor the supervision depends on the lens. Any3R is therefore a feed-forward model that takes any central camera, and is robust to mixing many camera types per scene, with no retraining per lens. On a benchmark of thirteen central cameras across three datasets, where every method reconstructs with its own predicted camera poses, it is the most consistently accurate method. Any3R enables scalable 3D reconstruction from heterogeneous crowdsourced and archival imagery collections sourced across diverse camera types. Project page: https://jingong-chen.github.io/Any3R/

Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).title: Understanding Human-Robot Collaboration through Joint Action
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).authors_text: Chengwen Zhang, Jianyang Wang, Chang Liu, Yukun Wang, Yuan Xu
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).summary: This systematic review synthesizes 83 empirical studies on human-robot collaboration using Joint Action theory, identifying key constructs and gaps for future research.
Bio-Inspired Robotics Laboratory (BIRL).debug_abstract: Human-robot collaboration requires partners to coordinate interdependent contributions toward a shared goal. Joint Action theory provides concepts for understanding this coordination, but how these concepts are instantiated and combined across empirical research remains fragmented. We conducted a systematic review following PRISMA 2020, identifying 83 empirical papers published between 2021 and 2026. Through theory-driven framework analysis, we organized the literature into nine constructs across three capacities: Representation, Prediction, and Integration. We analyze how these constructs are distributed and co-occur across studies, revealing where empirical evidence concentrates and where it is absent. By mapping empirical HRC research onto a unified Joint Action framework, this review offers a coherent overview of HRC studies, identifies gaps in current evidence, and provides guidelines for future research.

Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.title: Infer3D: Inverse Generative Modeling Enables Robust 3D Reconstruction
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.authors_text: Amani Kiruga, Mark Hamilton, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, William T. Freeman, Vincent Sitzmann
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.summary: Infer3D introduces an inverse generative modeling approach for robust 3D reconstruction, enhancing out-of-distribution accuracy by leveraging latent variable recovery and adaptive inference strategies.
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.debug_abstract: Humans can understand the 3D structure of scenes even from highly unfamiliar or extreme viewpoints. Cognitive science suggests this generalization stems from a top-down generative inference strategy. In contrast, state-of-the-art 3D reconstruction neural networks typically rely on amortized, feedforward inference. While fast, this pattern-matching approach degrades when faced with out-of-distribution (OOD) scene conditions unseen during training. Inspired by the generative nature of human vision, we propose Infer3D, an inverse generative modeling framework that recovers the latent variables of a generative model to best match the monocular input. To prevent degenerate flat outputs, we couple the generative image prior with a frozen 3D lifting network that constrains the optimization space to a valid, multi-view-consistent 3D manifold. Across a variety of controlled synthetic and real-world tasks, Infer3D demonstrates superior OOD reconstruction accuracy compared to feedforward networks trained on equal or larger datasets. Furthermore, mirroring how human perception requires more time to process confusing stimuli, we introduce an adaptive inference strategy that expends more test-time compute on ambiguous OOD examples while efficiently routing in-distribution inputs. Project website: https://amanikiruga.github.io/infer3d-site/

Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.title: PhysVAM: Physics-oriented Future Value Action Model for Dynamic Object Manipulation
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.authors_text: Yuxiang Yang, Jingbo Zhang, Jiaru Zhong, Junliang Chen, Yirui Zhou
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.summary: PhysVAM is a novel model that enhances dynamic object manipulation by predicting future task progress through value-based action generation, significantly improving success rates in simulations and real-world applications.
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.debug_abstract: Predicting future scene or object states does not necessarily reveal how robot-object interactions will advance or hinder a task. This challenge is particularly pronounced in dynamic robotic manipulation, where objects continue moving during perception and execution. Effective action generation therefore requires not only modeling object dynamics but also anticipating how future interactions will shape task progress. To this end, we propose \textbf{PhysVAM}, a Physics-oriented Future Value Action Model that represents anticipated interactions through their effects on future task progress. This value-based formulation provides task-directed foresight without reconstructing future visual states. Conditioned on current observations and historical object and robot motion, PhysVAM jointly learns action generation and multi-horizon future-value prediction. The value branch learns horizon-specific latent representations through future task-value prediction from successful and failed trajectories. These future-value representations are integrated into the action policy through gated cross-attention, guiding action generation toward interactions that facilitate task success. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate superior task success, with absolute success-rate improvements of 27.0 and 27.5 percentage points over the strongest baselines in simulation and real-world tasks, respectively. Project page: https://metarobo.github.io/physvam.github.io/.

Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.title: Optimization-like Reasoning in LLMs over Expanding Search Spaces
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.authors_text: Nicolás Astorga, Nabeel Seedat, Mihaela van der Schaar
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.summary: The paper presents OPT*, a scalable framework for training LLMs in step-by-step optimization-like reasoning across expanding search spaces, enhancing decision-making in complex tasks.
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.debug_abstract: Verifiable reward training has improved mathematical and coding reasoning, but these domains capture only part of step-by-step decision making. Many real-world tasks require finding a high-value feasible plan among many valid alternatives. We introduce OPT*, a scalable family of optimization-style tasks for training and evaluating LLM step-by-step optimization-like reasoning along a complexity axis: each task provides a feasibility checker and evaluator, while a complexity parameter expands the search space without requiring new human labels. This motivates studying these tasks in two regimes: (i) solver-guided online policy optimization, which uses a solver as a value oracle for partial states and applies rank-based reward shaping to reinforce better next steps, and (ii) search-based offline RL when such solvers are unavailable. Theoretically, we relate success in large search spaces to the information a reasoner extracts per unit of search budget. Empirically, we ablate the ingredients that make search efficient on OPT* and show that training on OPT* improves step-by-step optimization-like reasoning.

Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.title: Video-as-Experience: Learning Computer Use via Audio-Visual Understanding
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.authors_text: Guangzhi Sun, Zhonghao Zhai, Yixuan Li, Chao Zhang
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.summary: The VEX framework enhances computer-use agents by leveraging audio-visual understanding from tutorial videos for improved task execution and self-verification, achieving significant performance gains.
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.debug_abstract: Multimodal large language models (LLMs) have enabled capable computer-use agents that perceive graphical user interfaces, reason over instructions, and execute actions. However, existing approaches to learning from video demonstrations typically convert videos into screenshot-based action trajectories, rather than directly leveraging their rich audio-visual information. We introduce VEX (Video as EXperience), a framework that uses audio-visual understanding to unify learning from external demonstrations and reflecting on an agent's own behavior. Following a watch-act-rewatch paradigm, the agent extracts procedural guidance from tutorial videos containing visual demonstrations and spoken explanations, executes tasks, and verifies its progress by rewatching its execution as video. We instantiate VEX with video-SALMONN-VEX, a 9B-scale audio-visual computer-use agent built on the video-SALMONN 2 architecture with a Qwen3.5-9B backbone. We further introduce Action-Grounded Guide Optimization (AGGO), a reinforcement learning method that optimizes video-derived guidance for downstream action prediction, and augment AgentNet, OSWorld, and CUA-Gym with over 24K real-world tutorial videos. Experiments on OSWorld and a complementary subset of CUA-Gym demonstrate consistent improvements, with video-SALMONN-VEX achieving a 22% relative increase in task success over its Qwen3.5 backbone on OSWorld. Moreover, its generated guidance improves Gemini-3.5-flash by 10% relatively on OSWorld. These results highlight the potential of audio-visual understanding as a unified interface for procedural learning and self-verification in computer-use agents.

Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.title: Stable Transformer-Actor-Critic Model Predictive Control: A Contraction Analysis Approach
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.authors_text: Antonio Marino, Valerio Modugno, Marco Cognetti
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.summary: This paper presents a robust Transformer-Actor-Critic MPC framework ensuring physical safety and stability through mathematical constraints and novel contraction analysis for complex control tasks.
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.debug_abstract: Hybrid optimization-learning frameworks, such as Actor-Critic Model Predictive Control (MPC), rely on dynamically adjusting cost parameters to manage complex control landscapes. In this paper, we introduce a certifiably robust Transformer-Actor-Critic MPC architecture that leverages history-aware sequence models to shape local optimization while maintaining strict physical safety guarantees. First, we mathematically constrain the Transformer sequence models to satisfy global incremental Input-to-State Stability ($δ$ISS). Second, we integrate these neural Lipschitz bounds with Riemannian contraction theory, deriving a novel coupled small-gain condition that enforces uniform closed-loop contraction stability across the interconnected system. Evaluated on quadrotor control and decentralized multi-agent navigation tasks subjected to severe observation noise and process disturbances, our closed-loop stable formulation successfully translates theoretical bounds into physical safety.

Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.title: UNIVERSE: Unified Video Action Models for Autonomous Driving with Flexible Mask-Modulated Modality Generation
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.authors_text: Mengmeng Liu, Diankun Zhang, Jiuming Liu, Jianfeng Cui, Hongwei Xie
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.summary: UNIVERSE introduces a unified video-action model using a mask-modulated Diffusion Transformer for efficient autonomous driving, enhancing action generalization and enabling flexible inference without costly future-video generation.
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.debug_abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) can improve action generalization in autonomous driving by learning scene dynamics through dense future-video supervision. However, deploying such models often requires costly future-video generation, while architectures that bypass video rollout typically separate video and action parameters or alter their learned dependencies at inference. We introduce UNIVERSE, a unified video-action model built on a single mask-modulated Diffusion Transformer (DiT) that combines shared-parameter learning with modality-independent inference. Its Modality-Decoupling Visibility Mask allows future video and trajectory tokens to attend to a common historical context while blocking mutual attention between the two future modalities. As a result, future-video supervision directly updates the parameters used for trajectory denoising, yet video tokens can be omitted at test time without changing the trajectory branch's training-time attention dependencies. The same model supports trajectory-only, video-only, and joint video-action generation. Trajectory-only inference achieves a 4.3x speedup over coupled video-action rollout with comparable planning accuracy. UNIVERSE achieves 91.0 PDMS on NAVSIM, compared with 89.6 for a Two-DiT variant, and demonstrates strong zero-shot transfer to nuScenes and Bench2Drive without target-domain fine-tuning. Controlled ablations further support the complementary benefits of shared parameters, dense video co-training, and modality-decoupled visibility.

Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.title: MemReg: Streaming Outdoor LiDAR Point Cloud Registration with Hybrid Memory Buffers
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.authors_text: Jiuming Liu, Mengmeng Liu, Guangming Wang, Lihao Liu, Michael Ying Yang
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.summary: MemReg introduces a multi-frame outdoor LiDAR registration network utilizing hybrid memory buffers to enhance performance by leveraging temporal correlations in streaming sequences.
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.debug_abstract: Prior outdoor LiDAR registration works are commonly limited by the pair-wise input paradigm, which neglects temporal correlations inherent within streaming sequences. In this paper, we propose a novel multi-frame outdoor point cloud registration network for streaming LiDAR scans enhanced with pose-related memory buffers. The key observation is that long-term temporal LiDAR sequences can provide rich global contextual information to complete sparse measurements, filter outliers, and address low-overlap problems, thereby boosting registration performance. Specifically, two hybrid memory buffers are designed, including an implicit memory feature buffer and an explicit memory pose buffer, to store and dynamically update pose-related temporal features. Moreover, a novel dynamic history weighting module is developed to adaptively fuse current and history pose-related features. Extensive experiments on three outdoor datasets, including KITTI, nuScenes, and Apollo-Southbay, demonstrate state-of-the-art performance of MemReg, surpassing all previous pair-wise methods and also multi-frame SLAM systems. Our method also generalizes surprisingly well to multiview indoor registration scenarios with rather competitive performance on 3DMatch, 3DLoMatch, and ScanNet. Code will be released at https://github.com/IRMVLab/MemReg.

Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.title: UnderOneFacade: Worldwide Facade Semantic Segmentation Benchmark Dataset
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.authors_text: Yi Wang, Fan Wang, Prabin Gyawali, Ziyang Xu, Anna Klimkowska
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.summary: UnderOneFacade introduces a comprehensive 3D facade segmentation benchmark with 2.7 billion annotated points, addressing cross-domain generalization challenges in architectural recognition.
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.debug_abstract: Globally consistent semantic digital twins require centimeter-accurate and geographically transferable 3D facade segmentation. However, progress in facade parsing is limited by the lack of large-scale, standardized benchmarks for evaluating cross-domain generalization. Existing datasets are geographically narrow, semantically inconsistent, or insufficiently precise. We introduce UnderOneFacade, the largest cross-country and cross-continent 3D facade benchmark to date, comprising centimeter-accurate point clouds with hierarchical, harmonized, and architecturally grounded semantic labels totaling 2.7 billion annotated points. Through a systematic evaluation of representative point-, graph- and transformer-based architectures, we show that current methods struggle to recognize fine-grained architectural elements and degrade significantly across geographic domains, with the best models achieving only up to 33 IoU on the fine-grained LoFG3 benchmark. By combining geometric precision with standardized semantics at unprecedented scale, UnderOneFacade establishes a rigorous benchmark for developing robust and transferable 3D segmentation models. The dataset, evaluation scripts, and pretrained models will be released upon publication.

Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.title: Certified Policy Optimisation for Nested Causal Bandits via PAC-Bayes Risk
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.authors_text: Tim Woydt, Paul-David Zuercher
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.summary: The paper introduces Nested Causal Thompson Sampling for Nested Contextual Causal Bandits, providing a PAC-Bayesian risk certification for safe deployment in hierarchical decision-making contexts.
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.debug_abstract: Critical sequential decisions are rarely single-timescale: a strategic decision causally shapes the context in which every subsequent tactical choice is made; standard bandit and reinforcement-learning theory does not capture this causal coupling between timescales. We formalise the problem class as Nested Contextual Causal Bandits (NCCBs), a hierarchical SCM where each level's action sets the next level's context distribution, and propose Nested Causal Thompson Sampling (NCTS), which draws one mechanism-factorised belief per episode and acts recursively under it. Our main theoretical result is a causal PAC-Bayesian excess-risk bound that certifies any candidate deployment policy from historic data alone, off-policy and anytime, answering the deployment question: can we trust this agent here, and at what risk? Experiments on a hierarchical SCM show that, against a matched RFF-GP joint regression on the same function class, the factorised SCM-mechanism posterior transfers significantly better zero-shot under exogenous distribution shifts, the recursive meta-to-inner commit significantly dominates the joint-commit alternative in distribution, and the certificate significantly contracts as offline data accumulates. Combining these results, we establish progressive certified handover, a safe-deployment method: each timescale flips from a legacy controller to NCTS when gains can be certified, independently of the others.

Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.title: NEXUS: Neural Energy Fields for Physically Consistent Contact-Rich 3D Object Dynamics
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.authors_text: Qizhen Ying, Guangming Wang, Yangchen Pan, Victor Adrian Prisacariu, Brian Sheil
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.summary: NEXUS introduces a neural energy-field framework for modeling physically consistent 3D object dynamics in contact-rich environments, enhancing trajectory accuracy and video generation quality.
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.debug_abstract: Physics-grounded video generation requires controllable 3D object dynamics that remain physically consistent under contact, deformation, and external forcing. Existing trajectory-based methods often model isolated physical effects, making it difficult to compose conservative and non-conservative dynamics in contact-rich 3D scenes. We present NEXUS, a neural energy-field framework for contact-rich 3D object dynamics. NEXUS represents each object as a structural graph and constructs dynamic object-object and object-environment contact graphs. Inspired by Hamiltonian Neural Networks, NEXUS formulates motion through scalar energy and dissipation terms rather than directly predicting states or accelerations. Conservative effects, including gravity and elastic deformation, are composed as additive energy terms, while non-conservative effects such as damping and impact-induced energy loss are modeled with learned Rayleigh-style dissipation. Forces are derived by differentiating the energy and dissipation functions and rolled out with a multi-substep semi-implicit integrator. Across controlled trajectory benchmarks, NEXUS improves long-horizon accuracy over representative learned and physics-structured dynamics baselines under varying mechanical properties and physical-effect compositions. We further show that NEXUS trajectories provide effective guidance for contact-rich video generation, improving physical plausibility while maintaining competitive visual quality.

Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.title: Input-output characterization of robotic grasping: Connecting design parameters to grasp behavior through the admittance
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.authors_text: Julien Vanderheyden, Guillaume Drion, Pierre Sacré, Fulvio Forni
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.summary: This paper introduces a small-signal analysis method to characterize robotic grasping dynamics through admittance, revealing significant variations in stiffness and resonance among similar grasps.
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.debug_abstract: Low-impedance grippers make the dynamics of a grasp matter. Current grasp metrics, however, are static: they describe how a held object resists constant loads, not how it responds to time-varying ones. To quantify this, we rely on small-signal analysis to characterize a grasp by its admittance, the transfer matrix relating load perturbations to object displacements around an equilibrium. This transfer matrix recovers the stiffness and stability of the grasp at zero frequency and captures its natural frequencies and peak gain under time-varying loads. We apply this characterization to a planar two-finger gripper under proportional-derivative control. We show that two grasps of the same object in the same position and with the same contact forces can differ in stiffness by two orders of magnitude. Likewise, two grasps that share the same stiffness can exhibit very different resonances. Nonlinear simulations confirm the effectiveness of our small-signal analysis in capturing the dynamic behavior of grasping.

Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.title: UGG: Unified Generative Geometry Model
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.authors_text: Amani Kiruga, Zhiyi Li, Ruojin Cai, Hansen Lillemark, Xiaoshan Wu
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.summary: UGG is a unified framework for 4D scene understanding that integrates RGB video and geometric representations, enhancing visual generation and geometric prediction through conditional completion.
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.debug_abstract: Understanding 4D scenes is a core challenge in visual intelligence, requiring models to jointly capture scene geometry, appearance, and dynamics from partial observations. However, existing approaches are subdivided into feedforward models for direct geometric prediction, and generative models for visual synthesis. We introduce UGG, a unified framework for 4D scene understanding that jointly models RGB video and geometric representations such as depth and camera pose. By assigning different noise levels across modalities and time, UGG formulates visual generation and geometric prediction as conditional completion within a single generative model. This flexible formulation enables the model to learn from diverse, heterogeneous datasets with different subsets of geometric and visual annotations. Furthermore, our generative formulation enables inference-time search over multiple plausible scene hypotheses, using geometric evidence extracted from observed RGB frames to improve geometric prediction without ground truth geometry. We demonstrate UGG's effectiveness over non-unified baselines across camera-controlled video generation, depth estimation, and camera pose prediction, including in challenging sparse observation settings. Code and visualizations are available at https://ugg-model.github.io/

Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.title: Personalized Affective Perception via Continual Learning in Human-Agent Negotiation
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.authors_text: Mehmet Onur Keskin, Berk Buzcu, Nikhil Churamani, Reyhan Aydogan, Hatice Gunes
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.summary: The paper presents CLIFER, a continual learning approach for personalized affective perception in human-agent negotiation, enhancing agent adaptability and participant engagement through real-time feedback.
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.debug_abstract: Self-interested intelligent agents that negotiate with humans should interpret nonverbal expressions and adapt their behavior accordingly. However, generic facial-affect models degrade across individuals and contexts, creating a generalization gap. We introduce an affect-adaptive negotiation strategy that incorporates Continual Learning with Imagination for Facial Expression Recognition (CLIFER) to personalize valence-arousal perception in real time. Differential feedback converts changes in valence-arousal direction and intensity into adjustments of the agent's target utility. An asynchronous architecture updates CLIFER in the background during live interaction. In a counterbalanced within-subject study in which 66 participants negotiated with a humanoid robot, the CL-enabled agent achieved significantly higher individual utility and elicited higher participant concession rates than the FaceChannel baseline. The CL condition yielded significantly higher mean arousal estimates, alongside a broader output range. Participant utility and Nash distance did not change significantly between conditions. These outcomes support the practical value of coupling continual affective personalization with differential feedback for real-time negotiation.

Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.title: Same Physics, Different Gradients: A State-of-the-Art Report on Differentiable Physics Simulation
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.authors_text: Lei Shu, Zizhou Huang, Yunuo Chen, Yifei Li, Tao Du
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.summary: This report categorizes differentiable physics simulation methods, clarifying their derivatives' referents and implementations, and evaluates their effectiveness in optimization tasks.
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.debug_abstract: Differentiable simulation propagates derivatives through a physics simulator, turning animation, system identification, control, and computational design into gradient-based optimization. Engines differ in the physics they model and, less visibly, in which mathematical object they differentiate. We separate two questions the literature conflates. The referent is which object the returned derivative belongs to: the finite computation that executed, the converged equation it approximates, or the continuous dynamics. The realization describes the organization of the backward pass: automatically generated differentiation, an equation-level adjoint solve, or a custom adjoint. The referent defines the target against which exactness is assessed; the implementation determines how accurately that target is approximated. Cost depends on the realization together with how the states needed by the backward pass are retained or recovered. Crossing the axes places every method and engine we classify in a cell, separates claims the literature merges, and shows that the apparent trade-off between exactness and memory follows from how methods have been built rather than from a constraint. A second, orthogonal taxonomy covers contact, where the map is non-smooth. We then ask whether a correct gradient helps. Four mechanisms by which useful gradients are lost are cataloged and measured on one testbed, where the advantage of the exact derivative over the equation-level adjoint depends on where the fitting target comes from as much as on the solver budget, and we review the evidence that zeroth-order methods can outperform simulator gradients in the regimes where those mechanisms act. The model classes, systems techniques and applications are surveyed through this lens, and we close with a reporting checklist, a released diagnostic that computes it, and a research agenda.

Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.title: Library of Hands: Fix the Hands, Not the World Model
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.authors_text: Hasaan Ahmad, Qizhen Ying, Yuxuan Sun, Tianjin Huang, Guangming Wang
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.summary: The Library of Hands (LoH) method enhances robotic action prediction by correcting command-to-action mappings without retraining the world model, significantly improving task success rates.
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.debug_abstract: A world model predicts how a scene changes after an action, and a planner uses it to search for actions that reach a goal. If the camera moves or the controller changes, the same command moves the robot differently: when its commands are turned by 90 degrees, a frozen planner with the LeWM world model that succeeds in 77.5% of episodes succeeds in only 7.8%. Current fixes retrain the model, need training data, or forget a set-up when it returns. We propose Library of Hands (LoH), a training-free method that keeps the world model frozen and corrects only the map from commands to applied actions, which we call the hand. LoH reads the hand through the frozen model, with no extra sensor: it finds the action that best explains the change between two camera images (a reading). It stores every hand it identifies, so a returning set-up is recognised rather than re-learnt. In closed-loop tests, LoH more than doubles success on three simulated tasks, from 28.6% to 62.3%, and loses only 0.6 percentage points when nothing changes. It also works, unchanged, with two other world models and on two of three models pretrained on real robot data, and its gain grows with the quality of its readings.

Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.title: Leave It Better Than Found: Value-Guided Cooperation in Sequential Tasks
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.authors_text: Mario Gomez Andreu, Michael Amir, Antonio Marino, Tianxu An, Marco Hutter
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.summary: The paper presents a method for ad hoc robot cooperation in sequential tasks by sharing value functions, enhancing coordination without prior joint training, and improving task success rates.
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.debug_abstract: We consider the problem of sequential task continuation, where one robot acts in a workspace that has been affected by a previous robot. Current approaches in multi-robot cooperation rely heavily on co-training or co-optimization, assumingthat the robots have access to collective interaction data during the policy training or planning process. However, as increasingly varied robotic embodiments and policies are deployed and operate in the same real-world environment, learning policies for cooperation becomes infeasible due to the combinatorial explosion of possible robot combinations that need to be accounted for. To address this challenge, this paper considers the problem of ad hoc sequential cooperation between robots that have never before operated together in a shared environment. We demonstrate that robots can explicitly communicate their environmental preferences through sharing their value functions, enabling coordination without the need for prior joint training. To ground this exchange and prevent overconfidence in out-of-distribution states, we further introduce a k-nearest neighbors (KNN)- based uncertainty filter. Our method yields an increase of up to 48.5 pp compared with naive or even selfish agents, in task success rates across simulated and real-world experiments, demonstrating that value function transmission between agents is useful not merely as an internal learning tool, but as an effective basis for ad hoc coordination. Website: https://proroklab.github.io/PAVE/

Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.title: Edge-Assisted Crowdsensing for Explainable Cyclist Safety Perception
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.authors_text: Hongsen Cao, Chia-Yen Chiang, Mona Jaber, Meihui Wang, Yasmin Fathy
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.summary: This paper presents an edge-assisted crowdsensing system that uses handlebar cameras and a vision-language model to predict cyclist safety scores, enhancing infrastructure planning and continuous monitoring.
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.debug_abstract: Cyclist fatality rates remain high despite policy support for active travel, and autonomous vehicles add complexity to mixed traffic. Neither crash statistics nor multi-model detection pipelines scale to continuous monitoring of perceived safety along a route. We present an edge-assisted crowdsensing system: handlebar cameras supply street-level frames, a vision-language model (VLM) turns each frame into structured traffic attributes through a single prompt, and an explainable boosting machine (EBM) combines them with OpenStreetMap road infrastructure and on-bike kinematics to predict a crowdsourced 1-9 safety score. Extraction belongs at the network edge: the fastest self-hosted model needs 2.49 s per frame and scoring takes 0.4 ms on a CPU. On 1,362 annotated frames from two London routes, the EBM regressor reaches 72.2 percent binary accuracy and a mean absolute error of 1.011 under five-fold cross-validation. It is within one accuracy point of black-box ensembles. Its per-feature shape functions give exact attribution: physical lane separation is worth +0.97 rating points, a painted lane +0.70 and a construction site -0.65. Planners can therefore price an infrastructure change in rating points, and the results enter cost-benefit analysis directly. We also report inter-annotator agreement (alpha = 0.4695), an attribute audit, and a sensitivity analysis linking attribute error to accuracy. With re-encoding, a 20 s sampling interval serves 1,000 riders at 54 Mbit/s at a cost of 1.4 accuracy points, making continuous monitoring practical.

Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.title: Concept-Grounded Reasoning with Prompt-Driven Localization for Interpretable Structured Report Generation
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.authors_text: Xinyue Xu, Hongbin Lin, Juangui Xu, Hualiang Wang, Lehan Wang
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.summary: The CORAL framework enhances medical report generation by integrating spatial grounding and concept-level supervision, improving diagnostic accuracy and interpretability in multimodal large language models.
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.debug_abstract: Medical imaging modalities such as ultrasound and X-ray are widely used in clinical practice, where diagnosis follows a structured, evidence-driven workflow aligned with standardized criteria. While multimodal large language models (MLLMs) show promise for automated medical report generation, most existing systems rely on end-to-end multimodal fusion without modeling clinically defined intermediate attributes, leading to limited grounding and interpretability. To address this issue, we propose CORAL (COncept-grounded ReAsoning with Localization), a multimodal framework that integrates spatial grounding and concept-level supervision into a unified reasoning process. CORAL employs a prompt-driven medical segmentation model to localize lesions and predicts multi-class clinical attributes through a Concept Bottleneck module. The resulting textual concept tokens are combined with mask-modulated visual features within an MLLM to enable structured report generation and diagnostic prediction. Experiments on BUS-CoT and IU X-ray datasets demonstrate consistent improvements in diagnostic accuracy, concept consistency, and report quality over strong general-purpose and medical MLLMs, indicating that concept-grounded reasoning better aligns generation with clinical decision processes.

Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.title: DyCraft: An Agentic System for Long-Horizon 4D Scene Generation
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.authors_text: Jeff Tan, Hang Dai, Zeqian Long, Yanzhe Lyu, R. Kenny Jones
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.summary: DyCraft enhances long-horizon 4D scene generation by decomposing animations into manageable steps, improving coherence and reducing physical violations compared to existing coding agents.
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.debug_abstract: While frontier coding agents can generate high-quality 3D scenes and articulated assets, they struggle to create coherent long-horizon animations. When equipped with general-purpose harnesses, they frequently produce physically implausible outputs, generating objects that interpenetrate, lack physical support, or move unnaturally. Such bare agents struggle to repair these errors because they default to scripting the full animation in one pass, making it difficult to verify their work and disentangle complex spatiotemporal constraints. Drawing on the practice of human animators, we introduce DyCraft, a system for animated 3D scene generation that breaks animation into steps that coding agents can more reliably solve. DyCraft first expands the user's prompt into a detailed plan and builds a static scene. It then creates a 3D storyboard of key animation poses, where each frame is a static 3D scene that the agent can build and debug in isolation. Storyboarding decomposes the problem into pairs of verified start and end states, allowing the agent to author local motion between them with a collection of motion authoring tools. We evaluate DyCraft on 24 long-horizon, multi-shot animation tasks covering humanoid robots, human and animal characters, and physical mechanisms. Compared with a native GPT-6 agent in Codex and prior agentic baselines, DyCraft substantially reduces physical violations and generates higher-quality animated 3D scenes that are more often preferred by human raters.

Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.title: EgoContact: Evaluating Physical Intelligence with Egocentric Video
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.authors_text: Adam Deryło, Alexey Gavryushin, Daniel Cremers, Marc Pollefeys, Xi Wang
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.summary: EgoContact is a large-scale egocentric dataset that evaluates manipulation priors by predicting contact points, revealing current methods' limitations and improving grasp success in robotics.
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.debug_abstract: Egocentric video has emerged as one of the most scalable sources of data for learning generalizable manipulation priors. Yet, despite its growing use in pretraining robotic policies, it has been underutilized as a validation tool for physical intelligence, a key component of which is understanding where to make contact with an object to achieve an intended interaction. We present EgoContact, a large-scale egocentric dataset for evaluating the generalizability and precision of learned manipulation priors through future contact-point prediction. EgoContact contains 22.5K manually verified interaction events, each with a pre-contact observation, semantic intent, and pixel-precise contact locations. We find that current methods often struggle to predict precise interaction contacts and sometimes fail to localize the target object in diverse, in-the-wild scenes, even when allowed multiple predictions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the usefulness of EgoContact's annotated interactions for robotic manipulation: simply using EgoContact as the memory bank of an existing affordance-transfer policy improves grasp success from 14.2% to 31.2% in simulation and from 16% to 58% on a real robot.

Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.title: Any3R: Feedforward 3D Reconstruction from Any Camera Type
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.authors_text: Jingong Chen, Qingwen Zhang, Youming Deng, Chulwoo Pack, Olaf Wysocki
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.summary: Any3R is a feed-forward model for 3D reconstruction that operates robustly across various central camera types without lens-specific retraining, achieving high accuracy on diverse datasets.
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.debug_abstract: Geometry foundation models recover camera poses and dense geometry from a set of images with a feed-forward network, but they expect pinhole images. That assumption is inside the backbone too: the positional encoding and the training loss both bind an image position to a direction in space, and both depend on the lens. We condition both on the dense ray field, the unit direction through every pixel, which describes any central camera without a lens type, distortion coefficients or a bound on field of view. Angular coordinates give the rotary encoding the measured ray angle of each patch, evaluated per view, and solid-angle weighting scales the point loss by the area each pixel covers on the sphere, so neither the encoding nor the supervision depends on the lens. Any3R is therefore a feed-forward model that takes any central camera, and is robust to mixing many camera types per scene, with no retraining per lens. On a benchmark of thirteen central cameras across three datasets, where every method reconstructs with its own predicted camera poses, it is the most consistently accurate method. Any3R enables scalable 3D reconstruction from heterogeneous crowdsourced and archival imagery collections sourced across diverse camera types. Project page: https://jingong-chen.github.io/Any3R/

Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.title: Understanding Human-Robot Collaboration through Joint Action
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.authors_text: Chengwen Zhang, Jianyang Wang, Chang Liu, Yukun Wang, Yuan Xu
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.summary: This systematic review synthesizes 83 empirical studies on human-robot collaboration using Joint Action theory, identifying key constructs and gaps for future research.
Affective Intelligence and Robotics Labo.debug_abstract: Human-robot collaboration requires partners to coordinate interdependent contributions toward a shared goal. Joint Action theory provides concepts for understanding this coordination, but how these concepts are instantiated and combined across empirical research remains fragmented. We conducted a systematic review following PRISMA 2020, identifying 83 empirical papers published between 2021 and 2026. Through theory-driven framework analysis, we organized the literature into nine constructs across three capacities: Representation, Prediction, and Integration. We analyze how these constructs are distributed and co-occur across studies, revealing where empirical evidence concentrates and where it is absent. By mapping empirical HRC research onto a unified Joint Action framework, this review offers a coherent overview of HRC studies, identifies gaps in current evidence, and provides guidelines for future research.

人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).title: ReflectScene:MLLM-Guided Closed-Loop Diffusion for 3D Indoor Scene Generation
人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).authors_text: Jiawei Shen, Jie Feng, Junpeng Zhang, Guanbin Li, Wanyi Chen
人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).summary: ReflectScene introduces a closed-loop diffusion framework that integrates MLLM-guided semantic feedback for improved 3D indoor scene generation, enhancing functional consistency and semantic alignment.
人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).debug_abstract: Text-conditioned 3D indoor scene generation requires layouts satisfying geometric, functional, and semantic constraints. However, existing diffusion methods rely primarily on static textual conditions, limiting their ability to assess evolving scenes and translate semantic discrepancies into executable object-level corrections. MLLM-based post-hoc refinement provides semantic feedback but remains decoupled from denoising, potentially disrupting scene coherence. We propose ReflectScene, an MLLM-guided closed-loop diffusion framework. First, we introduce Hierarchical Prior-Grounded Scene Understanding that aligns structured layouts with multi-view visual evidence, to interpret object-specific context and scene global semantics via a frozen multi-modal large language model (MLLM). Second, we propose MLLM-Guided Semantic Reward Evaluation to distill MLLM's diagnoses and assessments on possible candidate corrections into a lightweight Reward Predictor, enabling correction decision making with reduced computation burden. Finally, Decision-Conditioned Trajectory-Consistent Diffusion is proposed to integrate selected corrections through transient conditioning and persistent clean-estimate projection, correcting object layout in the generated scene while preserving non-target arrangements throughout denoising. Experiments on 3D-FRONT demonstrate improved functional consistency and semantic alignment while maintaining competitive generation quality and diversity.

人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).title: PhysScope: Agentic Multimodal Physics Reasoning with Grounded Visual Memory
人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).authors_text: Haoyang Liu, Kecheng Liang, Xinyu Li, Weixing Chen, Yang Liu
人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).summary: PhysScope enhances vision-language models' physics reasoning by enabling self-correction of scope mismatches through explicit constraints and memory management, improving accuracy on benchmarks.
人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).debug_abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can correctly interpret physics diagrams yet apply constraints outside the states or conditions in which they hold, causing premise errors to propagate through subsequent calculations. We introduce PhysScope, an inference-time visual harness that supports self-correction of these scope mismatches without updating model weights. PhysScope enables the model to link physical scopes directly to its visual observations and explicitly constructs derived views to support reasoning. The harness imposes explicit constraints on state distinctions, conditions, and physical scopes during model reasoning, and checks agent-proposed revisions against sources and scopes. Accepted revisions invalidate registered dependents, thereby maintaining scope-aware working memory. On PhysAlign, PhysScope achieves higher solving scores than direct solving across all six evaluated VLMs. With Gemini-3.8-flash, it outperforms Canvas-CoT by 9.34 percentage points and substantially improves solving accuracy on the out-of-distribution (OOD) PhysUniBench benchmark. Ablation studies support explicit scope management and dependency maintenance as design principles for multimodal physics reasoning agents.

人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).title: One View, One Action: Spatially Generalizable VLAs through Observation-Aligned Experts and Cross Graph Consistency
人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).authors_text: Jinxi Liu, Ruifeng Zhai, Hao Liu, Guangrun Wang
人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).summary: The OVOA-VLA model enhances spatial generalization in multi-view VLA systems by enabling view-specific action predictions and improving robustness to viewpoint changes through directed attention graphs.
人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).debug_abstract: Multi-view vision-language-action (VLA) models still face challenges in spatial generalization, particularly under changes in camera viewpoints and robot initial states. These models typically receive action supervision only in the robot base frame, requiring them to implicitly learn the spatial correspondence between observations from each view and base-frame actions. We propose One View, One Action (OVOA-VLA), which learns to predict actions in each view's camera frame, allowing the same physical motion to provide diverse, observation-aligned supervision across views. OVOA-VLA jointly trains a base-frame expert and view-specific action experts, whose robot-state inputs and action targets are expressed in their respective camera frames. Two complementary directed attention graphs model both directions of interaction between the base and view-specific experts, jointly leveraging view-specific action supervision to improve base-frame prediction. Cross Graph Consistency further encourages agreement between the two graphs' base-frame predictions for the same sample. With the same multi-view inputs, the model supports both full and base-only inference. Experiments across multiple simulation benchmarks demonstrate improved manipulation performance and robustness to camera-viewpoint and robot-initialization perturbations. Full and base-only inference achieve average success rates of 88.1% and 85.7% on LIBERO-Plus, respectively. In real-world evaluations, base-only inference raises the average success rates from $π_{0.5}$'s 28.3% to 58.3% across three tasks under spatial distribution shifts.

人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).title: MemFolder: Structure-Guided Memory Folding for Efficient Agent Memory Management
人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).authors_text: Xuyang Liu, Chenwen Lu, Junxi Wang, Siyu Ren, Xinying Lin
人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).summary: MemFolder introduces a structure-guided memory folding framework that efficiently reduces record count and context length in agent memory management, enhancing performance retention while minimizing storage costs.
人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).debug_abstract: Long-term agents accumulate large external memory stores as interactions unfold, increasing the costs of storage, retrieval, and response generation. Efficiency is constrained by two coupled factors: a growing record count increases retrieval overhead, while longer retrieved contexts increase prefill computation and decoding-time attention costs. Existing methods prune or consolidate records, but pruning can discard useful evidence, whereas consolidation may produce fewer yet longer retrieval units. We introduce MemFolder, a structure-guided memory folding framework that sequentially reduces record count and context length. The framework comprises two core components that share memory groups, using cross-record structure to guide both evidence consolidation and compact representation. RecordFolder grounds entity mentions, progressively selects representative yet complementary anchors, and combines semantic and entity affinity with temporal chaining to consolidate compatible records into fewer retrieval units. ContextFolder encodes the original records within these groups into compact text and uses verification feedback to revise encodings when key facts cannot be recovered. Experiments on the three text-based memory benchmarks LoCoMo, PersonaMem, and LongMemEval and the two multimodal benchmarks M3-Bench-web and M3-Bench-robot demonstrate the strong performance of our methods. Notably, on Mem0, RecordFolder retains 99.0% of the original average performance across the three text-based benchmarks with 50% fewer records, exceeding the strongest baseline by 1.9 percentage points in performance retention. Combined with ContextFolder, existing record compression methods further shorten their output records while retaining most of their performance.

人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).title: Dune: A Zeroth-Order Optimizer with Time-Conditioned Historical Error Regression for VLA Test-Time Adaptation
人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).authors_text: Chengyang Dong, Ze Chen, Kai Ye, Chutian Wang, Heng Xu
人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).summary: Dune is a novel zeroth-order optimizer that enhances test-time adaptation for VLA models by integrating historical error prediction to reduce estimation variance and improve stability.
人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).debug_abstract: Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) enables Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models to handle distribution shifts during deployment without source-domain retraining. However, backpropagation-based adaptation incurs heavy memory overhead on resource-constrained robots, whereas zeroth-order (ZO) methods suffer from high estimation variance under limited perturbation budgets. We observe that while ZO estimation enables low-memory adaptation with rapid initial gains, it often stalls or degrades over long-horizon updates due to noisy gradient estimates. To address these limitations, we propose Dune, a zeroth-order optimizer that stabilizes long-horizon adaptation by coupling online historical error prediction with current perturbation observations. Specifically, Dune learns a lightweight, time-conditioned error predictor from past optimization dynamics and fuses its predictions with instantaneous ZO estimates, achieving effective variance reduction without backpropagation or extra forward passes. Additionally, we theoretically characterize how estimation variance restricts convergence in high-dimensional, small-population regimes, motivating the use of historical statistics. Extensive experiments on LIBERO and real-world robots demonstrate that Dune achieves superior success rates under a low memory footprint, with ablations confirming improved closed-loop stability and post-disturbance recovery.

人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).title: WeightCode: Installing New Capabilities into Neural Networks via Weight-Space Programming
人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).authors_text: Bo Li, Taoyong Cui, Bob Zhang, Mengran Li, Chengyang Zhang
人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).summary: WeightCode introduces Weight-Space Programming to enhance neural networks' capabilities by directly modifying weights with executable programs, achieving significant performance improvements without retraining.
人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).debug_abstract: Neural networks encode learned capabilities in their weights, yet extending those capabilities with explicit task knowledge remains a fundamental challenge. Here we show that Weight-Space Programming (WSP), in which executable programs read, construct or modify a network's weights directly, can install new capabilities within trained neural networks. WeightCode, a WSP framework, uses a frozen language model to write executable weight programs that install new computations into trained neural networks using task knowledge and their existing weights, without gradient-based training. Once installed, the new capabilities run independently of the language model. Given a grammar or eight demonstrations, weight programs enable previously unseen command compositions (0% to 99.8% exact match) and a new pickup action (0% to 98.4% success), while preserving the original command and navigation capabilities. On ImageNet, four weight programs achieve net gains of 8.84-17.62 points while preserving clean accuracy, outperforming the best of eight fine-tuning methods under matched examples, checks, and retention constraints. In a Vision Transformer, causal interventions show that installed noise-correction gates drive robustness gains, while their selective activation preserves clean accuracy. Rerun on five independently trained Vision Transformers without further language model calls, ten weight programs retain 83-110% of their source-network gains on average, whereas copying their fixed weight edits yields negligible gains. Six programs written for an already edited network add 5.23-14.50 points of contrast robustness while retaining the previously installed noise gain. Together, these results establish WSP as a new route to acquiring and accumulating capabilities in trained neural networks through reusable weight programs.

人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).title: RoboMorpher: Scaling Robot Morphology Representations for Cross-Embodiment Action Prediction
人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).authors_text: Wenwei Lin, Yan Qin, Weiliang Deng, Zixuan Li, Kaixuan Wang
人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).summary: RoboMorpher enhances cross-embodiment action prediction by integrating morphology-conditioned action tokenization and scalable kinematic supervision, outperforming traditional joint-space control methods.
人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).debug_abstract: Learning shared action representations is central to cross-embodiment manipulation. However, identical joint values can produce different spatial configurations across robots, limiting representations learned from joint values alone. We introduce RoboMorpher, a morphology-conditioned action tokenizer that jointly reconstructs joint angles and link poses to associate control coordinates with their kinematic effects. MorphGen supplies scalable kinematic supervision by generating serial-arm descriptions from survey-derived geometric priors. We pretrain RoboMorpher on 40 million morphology-state pairs and integrate the frozen tokenizer into a vision-language-action policy for discrete prediction and continuous refinement. We also introduce EmbodiBench, a ten-task benchmark with 30 generated URDFs per task. With downstream URDFs excluded from tokenizer pretraining, the policy achieves 56.40% success on RoboTwin 2.0 and 23.27% on EmbodiBench, exceeding continuous joint-space control by 9.73 and 15.34 percentage points. Removing link-pose supervision reduces EmbodiBench success by 17.94 percentage points, supporting morphology-aware geometric supervision for joint-action representation learning.

人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).title: When Semantics Matter: Reliability-Aware Semantic-Rhythm Control for Co-Speech Gesture Generation
人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).authors_text: Zhirui Xing, Ming Meng, Kaige Li, Ziyi Xu, Zhaoxin Fan
人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).summary: The paper presents a reliability-aware framework for co-speech gesture generation that enhances semantic expressiveness while maintaining rhythmic synchronization and robustness against acoustic noise.
人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).debug_abstract: Co-speech gesture generation aims to synthesize natural gestures that are both temporally synchronized with speech and semantically consistent with the spoken content. Although recent methods can generate rhythmically plausible motions, they often rely heavily on acoustic prosody while underutilizing textual semantics, especially when semantic annotations are incomplete, noisy, or unavailable. Consequently, the generated gestures may follow speech rhythm while failing to express the intended semantics. To address this problem, we propose a reliability-aware semantic-rhythm control framework for co-speech gesture generation. We first learn a discrete motion prior that represents continuous gestures in a compact and structured motion-code space. We then introduce a dual-branch semantic contribution estimation mechanism consisting of a full multimodal branch and an audio-only branch. Their distributional discrepancy provides a model-based proxy for text-induced predictive influence, which is interpreted jointly with segment-level semantic relevance. Based on this estimate, a controllable semantic-rhythm objective selectively strengthens semantic guidance in content-relevant segments while limiting unnecessary semantic intervention in rhythm-dominant segments. Furthermore, we treat background noise as an acoustic reliability condition and introduce noise-conditioned feature modulation together with benefit-regularized latent perturbation to improve generation robustness under realistic acoustic environments. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves a favorable balance among semantic expressiveness, rhythmic synchronization, motion diversity, and robustness, enabling reliable and controllable co-speech gesture generation.

人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).title: Let the Mind Conceive, Let the Hand Achieve: Coupling Grounded Action and Progress Evaluation for Long-Horizon Manipulation
人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).authors_text: Youpeng Wen, Gang Wang, Tianyu Huang, Weiwei Zhang, Zhijian Huang
人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).summary: Orchestra enhances robot manipulation by effectively managing task planning, execution, and progress evaluation, achieving significant improvements in multi-step instruction execution success rates.
人机物智能融合实验室 (HCP).debug_abstract: A robot following a multi-step instruction needs to act on the right objects in the right order, even as the scene changes. It must also maintain awareness of task progress and determine when to advance. To address these challenges, we introduce Orchestra, an agent harness that separates task planning and execution management from action generation.
