机器人系统实验室 (RSL).debug_abstract: This paper presents a novel autonomous robotic assembly framework for constructing stable structures without relying on predefined architectural blueprints. Instead of following fixed plans, construction tasks are defined through targets and obstacles, allowing the system to adapt more flexibly to environmental uncertainty and variations during the building process. A reinforcement learning (RL) policy, trained using deep Q-learning with successor features, serves as the decision-making component. As a proof of concept, we evaluate the approach on a benchmark of 15 2D robotic assembly tasks of discrete block construction. Experiments using a real-world closed-loop robotic setup demonstrate the feasibility of the method and its ability to handle construction noise. The results suggest that our framework offers a promising direction for more adaptable and robust robotic construction in real-world environments.

机器人系统实验室 (RSL).title: ART of PIV: Agentic Real-Time Particle Image Velocimetry for Active Flow Control
机器人系统实验室 (RSL).authors_text: Antonio Terpin, Francesco Banelli, Alan Bonomi, Raffaello D'Andrea
机器人系统实验室 (RSL).summary: The ART of PIV automates the particle image velocimetry pipeline selection, enhancing accuracy and speed for real-time flow control by reducing errors and improving performance.
机器人系统实验室 (RSL).debug_abstract: Particle image velocimetry (PIV) measures fluid motion from images of tracer particles, but its accuracy depends on choices throughout the estimation pipeline, including image preprocessing, flow estimation, and postprocessing. These choices are typically left to expert tuning, and a fixed configuration can become less accurate as conditions change. This matters especially when PIV supplies feedback for real-time control, where measurements must be both accurate and fast, and flow conditions vary. We introduce ART of PIV -- short for Agentic Real-Time and also a nod to the art of tuning a PIV pipeline -- which automates pipeline choice for each image pair. A learned agent selects a configuration according to a chosen measurement objective from a library assembled for a specified speed budget. Across cross-correlation, classical optical-flow, and learning-based estimators, ART of PIV reduces average end-point error (AEPE) by 12.2-22.4 % relative to the best single estimator at matched speed, with gains extending to 1000-4000 image pair/s. In a simulated local velocity regulation task, it reduces mean normalized closed-loop cost by 13.24-13.59 percentage points relative to a tuned fixed estimator, with the same classical controller in both cases. In a tabletop water channel, we illustrate two ways to tune ART of PIV for a fluidic pinball of three rotating cylinders: selecting between complementary optical-flow tunings for accuracy, and selecting regions of interest with coherent rotation or shear using a common flow estimator. For the first variant, we train a DreamerV3 reinforcement learning controller directly in the physical world and demonstrate tracking of a prescribed flow field in the wake of a fluidic pinball.

机器人系统实验室 (RSL).title: Contact-based optimization for collision-free motion planning for a million robots
机器人系统实验室 (RSL).authors_text: Jan Kamm, Antonio Terpin, Raffaello D'Andrea
机器人系统实验室 (RSL).summary: The paper presents a contact-based optimization algorithm, SCI, enabling efficient collision-free motion planning for up to one million robots by leveraging contact dynamics.
机器人系统实验室 (RSL).debug_abstract: Multi-agent robotic systems have attracted growing interest in recent years, with applications ranging from coordinated drone shows to autonomous operations on land, in the air, and on water. At the planning level, robot motion is often modeled using double-integrator dynamics (with low-level controllers handling the physical dynamics during execution) with a minimum-energy objective subject to collision-avoidance constraints and limits on position, velocity, and acceleration. The complexity of the problem resides in the constraints, which couple the trajectories and make the optimization problem nonconvex. Existing numerical approaches typically discretize and optimize entire trajectories, which becomes expensive for large fleets. We exploit the structure of optimal trajectories by organizing optimization around contacts, at which robots reach the minimum allowed separation. We formulate a coupled algebraic system in contact variables and reconstruct trajectories analytically between contacts. Our algorithm, sequential contact insertion (SCI), starts from unconstrained trajectories, inserts contacts at separation violations, and jointly adjusts their times and states. Numerical experiments demonstrate planning for one million robots in minutes and thousands of robots in fractions of a second. On problems feasible for a fixed-grid sequential convex programming baseline, SCI achieves median speedups of several orders of magnitude at matching solution accuracy.

机器人系统实验室 (RSL).title: Rethinking Asymmetry in Self-Supervised 3D Geometry Learning
机器人系统实验室 (RSL).authors_text: Gyeongjin Kang, Freeman Cheng, Botao Ye, Weijie Lyu, Ming-Hsuan Yang
机器人系统实验室 (RSL).summary: This paper proposes a novel self-supervised 3D geometry learning approach that enhances depth and pose estimation by imposing asymmetry in the 3D representation space rather than the input space.
机器人系统实验室 (RSL).debug_abstract: Self-supervised learning relies on asymmetry between what a model observes and what it must explain. Recent methods learn 3D geometry from unposed images by predicting cameras and scene structure, then rendering held-out views. To avoid trivial solutions, they impose this asymmetry in the input space, restricting how views interact through separate branches or masked attention. We revisit this design with geometric accuracy, rather than rendering quality, as the main objective. When a held-out view lies between context views, the context already constrains the geometry it observes. We therefore impose the asymmetry in the 3D representation space, excluding held-out views only from the reconstructed scene while a shared backbone uses all views for correspondence. This improves depth and pose estimation over input-space designs. We further exploit view density: sparse and dense observations depict the same scene but provide different amounts of correspondence. Aligning sparse-context features with dense-context features supplies a geometric training signal alongside rendering, without a pretrained geometric teacher. We additionally align features with a frozen vision foundation model, which brings further gains. None of these signals requires geometric annotation, and the resulting model improves geometry estimation over prior self-supervised methods. Controlled experiments isolate the contribution of each component, and self-supervised pretraining also improves subsequent supervised training.

机器人系统实验室 (RSL).title: Rapid co-design of Buoyancy-assisted robots for Challenging Locomotion using Gaussian Evolutionary Specialists
机器人系统实验室 (RSL).authors_text: Ankit Sinha, Nitish Sontakke, Dennis Hong, Yusuke Tanaka, Sehoon Ha
机器人系统实验室 (RSL).summary: The paper presents Gaussian Evolutionary Specialists (GES), a framework that optimizes buoyancy-assisted robot designs and control, significantly improving performance and reducing co-design time.
机器人系统实验室 (RSL).debug_abstract: Designing high-performance legged robots requires jointly optimizing morphology and control. Model-free reinforcement learning (RL) enables learning complex controllers during co-design, but repeatedly training policies across candidate morphologies makes design optimization computationally expensive. Existing approaches can amortize policy learning across morphologies, but a single shared policy tends to converge toward one control strategy regardless of morphology, which we refer to as behavioral diversity collapse. We introduce Gaussian Evolutionary Specialists (GES), an RL-based co-design framework that maintains a population of specialist policies whose design-space territories evolve according to their relative control performance. We evaluate GES on the Buoyancy-Assisted Light Legged Unit (BALLU) robot for obstacle traversal and ramp walking over design spaces of up to four dimensions. GES achieves higher best design performance than Monolithic and Mixture-of-Experts baselines, with gains of 5.0-9.0 cm in obstacle height and 10.0-12.7 points in ramp grade. For the same 200 design-optimization evaluations, GES reduces wall-clock co-design time by 67.4% compared with retraining a policy for every candidate. Finally, teleoperated hardware experiments evaluate the optimized BALLU morphology, which traverses obstacles of up to 24 cm, compared with 8 cm on the original design.

机器人系统实验室 (RSL).title: EgoContact: Evaluating Physical Intelligence with Egocentric Video
机器人系统实验室 (RSL).authors_text: Adam Deryło, Alexey Gavryushin, Daniel Cremers, Marc Pollefeys, Xi Wang
机器人系统实验室 (RSL).summary: EgoContact is a large-scale egocentric dataset that evaluates manipulation priors by predicting contact points, revealing current methods' limitations and improving grasp success in robotics.
机器人系统实验室 (RSL).debug_abstract: Egocentric video has emerged as one of the most scalable sources of data for learning generalizable manipulation priors. Yet, despite its growing use in pretraining robotic policies, it has been underutilized as a validation tool for physical intelligence, a key component of which is understanding where to make contact with an object to achieve an intended interaction. We present EgoContact, a large-scale egocentric dataset for evaluating the generalizability and precision of learned manipulation priors through future contact-point prediction. EgoContact contains 22.5K manually verified interaction events, each with a pre-contact observation, semantic intent, and pixel-precise contact locations. We find that current methods often struggle to predict precise interaction contacts and sometimes fail to localize the target object in diverse, in-the-wild scenes, even when allowed multiple predictions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the usefulness of EgoContact's annotated interactions for robotic manipulation: simply using EgoContact as the memory bank of an existing affordance-transfer policy improves grasp success from 14.2% to 31.2% in simulation and from 16% to 58% on a real robot.

机器人系统实验室 (RSL).title: EgoHTR: Egocentric 4D Demonstrations of Human Terrain Traversal
机器人系统实验室 (RSL).authors_text: Alex Brandes, Haig Conti Georges Sajelian, Manthan Patel, Dominik Hollidt, Chenhao Li
机器人系统实验室 (RSL).summary: The EgoHTR dataset enhances humanoid robot training by providing 4D human motion sequences in complex terrains, enabling improved locomotion policies and context-aware navigation.
机器人系统实验室 (RSL).debug_abstract: Deploying humanoid robots in unstructured terrain remains an open problem. While classic reinforcement learning struggles with the sheer complexity of real-world interactions, more promising methods leveraging human priors remain limited to models lacking contextual awareness. The restricted motion synthesis is a direct consequence of existing dataset pipelines failing to capture human-scene sequences in challenging environments. To bridge this gap between humanoid learning and scene reconstruction, we introduce the Egocentric Human-Terrain Reconstruction (EgoHTR) dataset. We develop and open-source a reconstruction pipeline capturing 55 scene-aligned 4D human motion sequences in diverse, complex environments using a multi-sensor setup of egocentric wearables and a portable 3D scanner. The resulting dataset comprises over 150k frames, which we evaluate against motion-capture ground truth, demonstrating state-of-the-art accuracy and establishing a rigorous benchmark for human motion analysis and synthesis. Further, we leverage this data to train perceptive locomotion policies, demonstrating hardware deployment on a Unitree G1 for reconstructed reference motions. Our pipeline enables community-driven dataset extensions and factors the problem to help researchers build foundational, context-aware robots that reliably traverse uneven terrain.

机器人系统实验室 (RSL).title: Learning Multi-Phase Robot Loco-Manipulation via Phase-Conditioned Policy Optimization
机器人系统实验室 (RSL).authors_text: Simone Manni, Annika Wollschläger, Dario Bellicoso, Abel Gawel, Marco Hutter
机器人系统实验室 (RSL).summary: This paper presents a phase-conditioned policy optimization method for training robots in complex loco-manipulation tasks across diverse hardware, enhancing efficiency and adaptability.
机器人系统实验室 (RSL).debug_abstract: Complex whole-body loco-manipulation requires executing diverse maneuvers, such as crouching, grasping, and locomotion, within a single long-horizon task. While performing simple pick-and-place behaviors is well-established, scaling to complex, long-horizon tasks remains difficult. Currently, this challenge is addressed by relying on human motion data and correspondingly humanoid platforms, which limits platform independence and introduces substantial data processing overhead. Instead, we extend proximal policy optimization (PPO) to train a single policy for multi-phase tasks across diverse robotic hardware, leveraging prior task structure to shape behavior. Our method adapts PPO using a phase-conditioned critic, phase-gated reward functions, and a multi-phase reset curriculum to guide exploration. To support varied hardware, we employ a decoupled hierarchical control architecture that separates lower-level balancing dynamics from high-level phase execution. We demonstrate multi-stage loco-manipulation skills on hardware on both the Unitree G1 and a Boston Dynamics Spot equipped with a manipulator arm, and validate our design choices through ablations. Our approach enables the acquisition of complex loco-manipulation behaviors purely through environment interaction while directly incorporating high-level task structure into policy learning.

机器人系统实验室 (RSL).title: Compatibility and future-proof testing for multi-agent systems
机器人系统实验室 (RSL).authors_text: Yueshan Li, Lorenzo Fiaschi, Andrea Censi, Emilio Frazzoli
机器人系统实验室 (RSL).summary: The paper proposes a bi-level structure for ensuring compatibility and future-proofness in independently developed autonomous agents through seed agents and independent testing, avoiding centralized design constraints.
机器人系统实验室 (RSL).debug_abstract: Independently developed autonomous agents, such as autonomous vehicles, must guarantee joint compatibility, such as safety and task-completion requirements, when they operate in a shared environment. Existing methods require a centrally designed specification, or interaction mechanism before any agent is deployed. However, such centralized design is unrealistic when agent designs are confidential to their developers, and it is not flexible enough to accommodate future agent designs. We study a bi-level structure in which a regulator coordinates developers by publishing seed agents, and each developer independently tests its agent to ensure that it is compatible with every seed-compatible agent, a property we call future-proofness. Under this structure, joint compatibility is guaranteed for any agents that are designed and tested independently, without any coordination with each other. In this work, we first formulate compatibility for general multi-agent systems and show why it is not trivially implied by seed-compatibility. We then characterize the future-proof agents as the closure of the seed and show that this closure is monotone in the seed. Finally, we study a class of executable tests that involve interaction with the seed alone, and we ask to what extent such tests can distinguish the future-proof agents.

机器人系统实验室 (RSL).title: FTP-1: A Generalist Foundation Tactile Policy Across Tactile Sensors for Contact-Rich Manipulation
机器人系统实验室 (RSL).authors_text: Chengbo Yuan, Zicheng Zhang, Mingjie Zhou, Wendi Chen, Yi Wang
机器人系统实验室 (RSL).summary: FTP-1 is a pioneering generalist tactile policy that enables transferable manipulation skills across diverse sensors, improving performance in contact-rich tasks by significant margins.
机器人系统实验室 (RSL).debug_abstract: Despite the success of vision-based generalist robotic policies, existing tactile-based policies remain tied to fixed embodiments and sensor setups. This is because tactile signals are highly heterogeneous across hardware, making cross-sensor generalization difficult. We present FTP-1,the first generalist foundation tactile policy pretrained to acquire transferable tactile manipulation abilities across diverse sensors and embodiments. FTP-1 supports varied tactile inputs, including image-, array-, and state-based signals, by using heterogeneous encoders to project them into unified morphology-aware latent tokens that are jointly modeled by a shared tactile Transformer expert. Pretrained on around 3,000 hours of tactile manipulation data aggregated from 26 data sources, spanning human and robot demonstrations across 21 sensors, FTP-1 learns tactile skills that transfer beyond the sensors seen during pretraining. Across downstream finetuning experiments spanning 5 hardware configurations, FTP-1 improves contact-rich manipulation on seen sensor setups by +17.2% and, surprisingly, transfers to two previously unseen tactile-sensor setups, achieving a +31% gain in success rate. FTP-1 establishes the first unified foundation baseline for tactile manipulation, providing future tactile policies with a shared model-level starting point. Pretrained models, datasets, training code and more visualization at https://ftp1-policy.github.io.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: MIR-Depth: Multi-Range Refinement for Single-View RGB-D Depth Completion of Transparent Objects
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Xinzhe Fu, Qi Shao, Yuanfei Xie, Taoyu Wu, Zhihao Cao
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: MIR-Depth enhances single-view RGB-D depth completion for transparent objects by integrating multi-range hypotheses and selective refinement, achieving superior accuracy in robotic grasping tasks.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Recovering accurate visible-surface depth from a single RGB-D image and an object mask is essential for robotic grasping and manipulation of transparent objects. Specular reflections cause missing depth, while refraction corrupts nonzero returns with background depth, making raw measurements unreliable as surface anchors. Under a fixed sampling budget, refining an initial single-view prediction within a single search interval either misses large refraction offsets or sacrifices fine local resolution. To resolve this single-view trade-off, MIR-Depth constructs Coordinate-Aware Multi-Range Hypotheses: a 3D-aggregated global inverse-depth volume and depth-axis-filtered pixel-wise local volumes around a prior-guided initial depth. Selective Recurrent Refinement then introduces out-of-bounds lookup masking and validity-masked softmax fusion to iteratively update inverse depth from these volumes using a multi-scale ConvGRU. Finally, Spatially Gated Correction applies a learned per-pixel spatial gate to the full-resolution residual, preserving accurate initial geometry without imposing raw sensor readings as hard constraints. Experiments on TransCG, TODD, TRansPose, ClearPose, and HouseCat6D show that MIR-Depth achieves lower error than ReMake, DFNet, BP-Net, and PSD. Real-robot evaluations confirm accurate surface geometry for 6-DoF grasp pose prediction. Code and pretrained models will be publicly available.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Bridging vision-language reasoning and learned control for legged navigation in the wild
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Takahiro Miki, Robin Schmid, Manthan Patel, Turcan Tuna, Julia Richter
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: ROAM integrates vision-language reasoning with learned control for legged robots, enabling autonomous kilometer-scale navigation in complex environments while highlighting ongoing challenges in VLM reliability.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Autonomous navigation in diverse real-world environments remains one of the greatest challenges in robotics. It demands both robust low-level motion control to handle diverse terrain and high-level reasoning to interpret environmental cues. We present ROAM (Robust Open-world Autonomous Mobility), a system that enables legged robots to perform kilometer-scale navigation in complex alpine and urban settings. ROAM combines the world knowledge of a Vision-Language Model (VLM), pre-trained on internet-scale data, with robust locomotion and local planning policies learned in simulation via reinforcement learning (RL). The VLM provides common-sense reasoning and semantic interpretation of the scene, assessing risks, interpreting signs, and producing semantic labels with associated navigation costs. An open-vocabulary segmentation module converts these labels into a dense, real-time risk map, which conditions two pre-trained RL policies responsible for agile locomotion and local navigation, effectively coupling high-level VLM reasoning with low-level physical control. Real-world experiments showed the system's ability to autonomously navigate a wide range of complex real-world environments. The robot completes kilometer-long hikes with minimal intervention, interprets signs to avoid danger, and evaluates its environment to identify safe areas on which to step. This work represents a step toward the reliable deployment of systems in unstructured environments. However, it also underscores the challenges that remain in VLM reliability and spatial reasoning, indicating that foundational models are a crucial component but not yet a complete solution for navigation in the wild.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: MARBLE: An Agentic Benchmark for Spatial Reasoning and Visual Abstraction
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Yulun Jiang, Naël Ouerghemi, Yekun Chai, Maria Brbić, Michael Moor
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: MARBLE is a benchmark exposing multimodal language models' struggles with visual-to-spatial abstraction and long-horizon reasoning in complex spatial environments.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: A central challenge for multimodal language models (MLLMs) in real-world tasks is to abstract visual observations into structured spatial states and reason over how those states change under actions over long horizons. Existing multimodal benchmarks often focus on static question answering, where answers can be directly extracted from images, or assume symbolic states are available and bypass the visual-to-spatial abstraction process. We present MARBLE, a diagnostic benchmark for spatially grounded multimodal reasoning and planning across three agent environments: CUBE, MAZE, and BLOX. MARBLE spans 2D and 3D spatial puzzles under geometric constraints, dynamic layouts, and spatial transformations, with difficulty systematically controlled along two axes: observation format and planning horizon. Extensive evaluations show that frontier MLLMs struggle on MARBLE, with the strongest model GPT-5.4 achieving only a 7.3% average success rate across the three environments in the hardest setting. Pairwise ablations on the open-weight models identify visual-to-spatial abstraction as the major bottleneck: when models must infer spatial states from images instead of receiving human-annotated states, success drops from 50.7% to 3.7% for Gemma-4-31B and from 87.9% to 6.5% for Kimi-K2.6. The results indicate that models often fail to construct precise spatial states from visual observations before planning, a task that is straightforward for humans. Overall, MARBLE reveals the gap in reliable visual-to-spatial abstraction for frontier MLLMs and provides a controlled testbed for measuring progress in spatially grounded multimodal reasoning and planning.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Learning Generalizable Hand-Object Tracking from Synthetic Demonstrations
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Runyi Yu, Xiaoyi Lin, Hok Wai Tsui, Yinhuai Wang, Zhijie Peng
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: The paper introduces a system for hand-object tracking using synthetic data, featuring a data generator and a tracker that enables effective transfer to physical environments.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: We present a system for learning generalizable hand-object tracking controllers purely from synthetic data, without requiring any human demonstrations. Our approach makes two key contributions: (1) HOG, a highly efficient Hand-Object data generator that rapidly synthesizes diverse, large-scale, and uniformly distributed trajectories; and (2) HOT, a Hand-Object Tracker that bridges synthetic-to-physical transfer through reinforcement learning and interaction imitation learning. Our method extends to diverse object shapes and hand morphologies. HOT also enables cross-simulator transfer. Through extensive evaluations, we show that our approach enables dexterous hands to track challenging, long-horizon sequences including object re-arrangement and agile in-hand reorientation. These results represent a significant step toward scalable foundation controllers for manipulation that can learn entirely from simple, scalable synthetic data, breaking the data bottleneck that has long constrained progress in dexterous manipulation.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: WATERFALL: Workflow for Adaptive Training with Evolutionary Reward Formulation and Automated Learning Loops
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Eleftherios Triantafyllidis, Filippos Christianos, Zhibin Li, Bernd Bickel
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: WATERFALL introduces an automated, iterative workflow for discovering rewards in partially observable environments, outperforming traditional methods by leveraging visual evidence and evolutionary selection.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Reward design remains a central bottleneck in reinforcement learning (RL), particularly in sparse-reward, long-horizon and partially observable settings requiring dependency chaining, memory, and deceptive affordance disambiguation. While recent foundation-model approaches reduce manual reward engineering, most assume goal-conditioning, task descriptions, expert demonstrations, or ground-truth metrics. These assumptions are problematic in partially observable environments, where task-relevant objectives, affordances, and dynamics must be discovered through interaction rather than disclosed a priori. We formalise this problem setting by introducing WATERFALL, an iterative population-based workflow for automated reward discovery under the strict observability constraints inherent in POMDP environments. WATERFALL achieves this by (i) synthesising diverse programmatic reward candidates via persona-conditioned generation, (ii) evaluating candidate behaviour from raw visual rollouts utilising a Swiss-system evolutionary tournament judged by vision-language models to identify elites, and (iii) leveraging longitudinal assessment histories to iteratively mutate, escalate, or prune candidates. We evaluate WATERFALL across fully observable and reveal-gated partially observable environments ranging from discrete to continuous, comparing against sparse-reward RL, intrinsic-motivation and foundation-model reward-synthesis baselines. Our results indicate that WATERFALL discovers and refines reward programs without access to privileged information, outperforming baselines that retain their native information advantages, most clearly in the POMDP regime. Extensive ablations substantiate that visual evidence, tournament-based selection, and iterative refinement are jointly important. Enforcing this contract is what separates autonomous reward discovery from benchmark-privileged reward shaping.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: CoSphere-SLAM: Multi-Agent Panoramic Gaussian Splatting SLAM with Spherical Loop Closure
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Qi Shao, Zhihao Cao, Shuhao Zhai, Taoyu Wu, Zhuoxiao Li
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: CoSphere-SLAM introduces a multi-agent Gaussian splatting framework for panoramic SLAM that effectively addresses loop closure and scale drift challenges, achieving superior mapping accuracy.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Dense collaborative mapping is essential for search and rescue, building inspection, and warehouse automation, where panoramic cameras capture the entire surroundings in a single frame. Unlike pinhole agents that share views only at similar headings, panoramic agents observe overlapping scenes at any 3D orientation, yet searching full rotations also produces mutually consistent false loop closures across distinct symmetric rooms. Moreover, continuous monocular scale drift splits rigidly merged maps at revisited surfaces, while depth noise at short baselines distorts loop translation directions. To address these challenges, we propose CoSphere-SLAM, the first multi-agent Gaussian splatting SLAM framework for panoramic cameras, whose spherical loop closure aligns spherical features over $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ via fast Fourier correlation across arbitrary orientations and rejects symmetric false closures through global $\mathrm{Sim}(3)$ consensus. Building on these closures, directional global optimization solves a per-keyframe $\mathrm{Sim}(3)$ pose graph with log-scale regularization to correct scale drift while separating optical-flow translation directions from depth-based magnitudes. Finally, omnidirectional Gaussian fusion transforms each Gaussian with its keyframe similarity and renders Gaussians at their maximum ray response to jointly refine poses and maps. Experiments on indoor and cross-session multi-agent panoramic benchmarks demonstrate that CoSphere-SLAM achieves state-of-the-art trajectory accuracy and rendering quality among single-agent and multi-agent methods. Project website: https://cosphere-slam.github.io.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: PhyVGGT: Feed-Forward Articulated Object Reconstruction from Monocular Videos
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Qi Shao, Zhihao Cao, Shuhao Zhai, Anh Nguyen, Hong Liang
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: PhyVGGT is a rapid, single-pass framework for 3D articulated object reconstruction from monocular videos, outperforming existing methods in accuracy and efficiency.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Reconstructing an articulated object with its 3D movable parts, joint parameters and unseen articulation states from an uncalibrated monocular video is essential for robot manipulation and interactive digital twins. Existing per-scene optimisation methods require minutes to hours and external depth or camera poses, whereas feed-forward 3D foundation models reconstruct dense point maps in one pass without segmenting movable parts or inferring joints. Even on these monocular point maps, regressing or fitting continuous joints directly fails on casual videos, since cross-frame attention blurs moving part boundaries in deep layers, underestimates motion along the viewing ray and leaves continuous axes ill-conditioned under small opening angles. To address these challenges, we propose PhyVGGT, a single-pass framework on a frozen 3D foundation model that anchors moving-part matching and closed-form joint estimation to the undistorted geometry of the stationary base. First, our Part and Motion Decoder fuses intermediate per-frame tokens with global tokens and references part queries to a static-base query to segment 3D parts, align point maps on the static base and predict learned Bingham priors. Second, our Kinematic Inference Layer fits an orthogonal Manhattan frame to static surface normals, selects the joint axis in closed form under a Bingham posterior combining pairwise motion scatter with the learned priors, and solves a linear system for the hinge pivot to drive unseen states. Trained solely on synthetic data, PhyVGGT achieves state-of-the-art monocular performance across five benchmarks, outperforming FAMOS and monocular ArtiPoint, surpassing posed RGB-D ArtiPoint in median error, and running in 6.8 s per 48-frame video against hours of per-scene optimisation in Articulat3D. Project page: https://phyvggt.github.io.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Polygraph: Large-Scale Multi-Session Trajectory Optimization using Pose Graphs
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Petar Lukovic, Tian Yi Lim, Marc Pollefeys, Pablo Speciale, Hermann Blum
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: Polygraph introduces an online multi-session trajectory optimization method that efficiently integrates independent trajectories into a globally consistent pose graph without building a 3D map.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Robots, vehicles, and wearable devices often traverse the same environment many times. Each pass produces its own trajectory from onboard visual or visual-inertial odometry. These trajectories are locally accurate but drift over time and live in unrelated coordinate frames. Turning many such independent trajectories into one globally consistent set is the large-scale multi-session trajectory optimization problem. Existing solutions largely work offline. All sessions must be available up front, one session is fixed as the reference frame, and a single fused map is then optimized. This paper presents Polygraph, a multi-session trajectory optimization pipeline that processes sessions online, one keyframe and one spatial cluster at a time, and never builds a 3D map. Keyframes are grouped into local clusters. When a cluster closes, it is matched against every other session through learned image retrieval. Candidate pairs are verified with sparse feature matching, monocular metric depth, and robust pose estimation. A two-tier consensus gate admits a cross-session edge into the shared pose graph only once independent evidence corroborates it. A cheap incremental solve keeps the graph current, and a periodic robust batch solve prunes outliers. We evaluate Polygraph on stereo outdoor driving, HoloLens and iPad indoor traversals, legged indoor locomotion with a Boston Dynamics Spot, and large-scale outdoor vehicle and handheld routes. Against the closest prior work on the same GPU model, using its reported timings, Polygraph runs faster, commits fewer loop-closure edges, and matches or improves on accuracy.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: PoliMop: Policy-in-the-Loop Motion Planning in 3D Spaces for Mobile Robots
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Yael Fassbind, Valentin N. Hartmann, Huang Su, Yijiang Huang, Stelian Coros
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: PoliMop introduces a kinodynamic RRT planner that integrates control policies and physics simulation for efficient 3D motion planning in complex environments, enhancing robot adaptability.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Reaching a goal state in a complex environment often requires a robot to overcome challenging terrain and obstacles. Which routes are accessible depends on the robot's physical design, the control policy it uses, and how it modifies its surroundings. We present a kinodynamic rapidly-exploring random tree (RRT) planner that uses physics simulation to exploit skills encoded in the control policy, which allows it to find a path in the scene with respect to the robot's capabilities. The planner samples states from a reduced state space in 3D around the scene and expands the RRT toward each sample using policy rollouts. We guide sampling with a preplanned path for a simple mass-point model to focus exploration on promising regions leading toward the goal state, reducing planning time by up to 63%. Simulation experiments with quadrupeds, humanoids, and wheeled robots demonstrate that our approach supports drop-in integration of various robots and control policies, exploiting their physical and policy capabilities without modifying the underlying planning algorithm. Predefined environmental modifications, such as placing a plank across a gap to build a bridge, will automatically be picked up by the planner as the robot's reachable space expands.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: SAVE: Less is More in Agentic Video Reasoning
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Tymoteusz Wilk, Sergey Prokudin, Xi Wang
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: The paper evaluates agentic video reasoning frameworks, finding that simpler models like SAVE outperform complex ones, especially in long videos with concentrated evidence.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Agentic video-reasoning frameworks iteratively explore a video, choosing what to observe based on the query and evidence gathered so far. Existing methods are typically evaluated with different backbones, preprocessing pipelines, and computational budgets, making it difficult to determine which components actually drive performance, how much they cost, and whether agentic inference is preferable to native video reasoning in the first place. We conduct a controlled evaluation of a diverse set of recent agentic video-reasoning systems across two strong contemporary backbones, with explicit token and monetary-cost accounting. Across Gemini 3 Flash and Gemma 4, most existing agentic frameworks fail to consistently improve over native video inference and often increase computational cost. We investigate two primary questions: (1) How much agentic framework complexity is necessary for effective video reasoning? (2) When, if at all, is agentic video reasoning preferable to just using the backbone directly? To answer the first question, we introduce a deliberately minimal Active Exploration Baseline and show that it remains competitive with substantially more elaborate agents. We then propose targeted extensions to this baseline, yielding SAVE (Simple Agentic Video Explorer). SAVE outperforms all evaluated prior agentic methods in five of six backbone-benchmark settings. Turning to the second question, our results indicate that the advantage of agentic exploration grows when dense processing would otherwise represent answer-relevant events too sparsely, particularly for long videos and temporally concentrated evidence. Overall, our results suggest that agentic video reasoning should favor simple frameworks over increasingly elaborate pipelines and focus primarily on long-form video, where selective evidence acquisition offers the clearest advantage over native inference.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Task-Driven Closed-Loop Design Optimization of Passively Morphing Quadrotors for Contact-Mediated Narrow Gap Traversal
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Etor Arza, Luca Girardi, Gabriel Maquignaz, Javier Paez, Stefan Leutenegger
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: This paper presents a closed-loop design optimization method for passively morphing quadrotors, enhancing their traversal through narrow gaps while maintaining flight efficiency and control performance.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Aerial robots operating in cluttered environments may encounter openings narrower than their nominal width. Existing passively morphing drones reduce their width upon traversal, but they typically involve human-made designs, which can struggle to find the right balance among folding ratio, flight efficiency, and control tracking performance. We introduce a closed-loop design method that jointly optimizes quadrotor geometry and the torque-deflection response of two passively folding arms driven by the success rate in simulation for contact-mediated gap traversal. An optimization algorithm samples candidate designs that are evaluated in a contact-based simulation of the traversal task, where the task success rate is used as a feedback signal to sample progressively better designs over time. The resulting prototype passively reduces its width from 31.3 to 14.1 cm and traverses a 15 cm wide opening at a 2 m/s reference speed. It also tolerates gap approach-angle errors of up to 30 degrees and folds through a 40 cm long confined passage. Compared to a rigid twin, the soft configuration adds only 2 mm of position RMSE and less than 1% electrical power during contact-free flight. These results show that task-driven closed-loop design optimization can produce passively morphing airframes that are compact under contact, tolerant to approach error, and effectively rigid during nominal flight.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: I See What You Want: Decoding Hierarchical Operator Intent from Visual Teleoperation History
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Xiangyi Jia, Kaixian Qu, Shengzhi Wang, Chenyu Yang, Robert Katzschmann
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: The paper introduces VI AMO, a dataset for hierarchical intent prediction in teleoperation, and demonstrates that fine-tuning a vision-language model significantly improves action and mission decoding, enhancing robotic autonomy.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have become a powerful foundation for robotic scene understanding, task planning, and language-conditioned control. A natural question follows: can these models also decode what a human operator intends while teleoperating a robot, without any explicit instruction? We formulate this as hierarchical intent prediction, jointly inferring the ongoing atomic action and the broader mission it serves from a short visual teleoperation history. To study this, we introduce VI AMO (Vision Intention Action and Mission Ongoing), a dataset of 6,600 episodes from eleven robot sources with 13,653 temporally aligned action annotations and 9,702 mission annotations. Large proprietary models struggle with this problem: on held-out episodes, GPT-4o reaches Sentence-BERT similarities of only 0.563 and 0.470 for action and mission, and GPT-5.6 Luna achieves only 0.581 and 0.554. Fine-tuning a VLM on VI AMO yields our Vision-Intention Model (VIM), which raises these scores to 0.825 and 0.821 and still reaches 0.726 and 0.717 on the 35.4% of test actions with both labels absent from training. Finally, as a downstream application, VIM's predicted mission enables a vision-language-action (VLA) policy to take over from the operator mid-task in a real-world environment unseen during VIM fine-tuning, reducing human teleoperation time by 34.6% relative to GPT-4o and 39.8% relative to GPT-5.6 Luna, while cutting intent-prediction latency by roughly 70% on average.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Reactive Task-Oriented Robot-Human Handovers via Generative Hypothesis Selection
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Carmen Scheidemann, Andreea Tulbure, Pascal Burkhard, Marco Hutter
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: The GENESIS-Handover approach enhances robot-human object handovers by generating task-specific hand poses using VLMs, improving task understanding in user studies.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: When humans hand each other objects, they incorporate both geometric and semantic information into this process. For example, passing a knife with the handle towards the recipient, rather than the blade, is both more ergonomic and safer. Recent state-of-the-art methods for task-oriented robot-human handovers have progressed from modeling object geometry to incorporating object affordances. However, they often forgo predicting the explicit, task-specific hand poses a human selects to utilize an object. Since many objects support multiple interaction modalities, e.g., a claw hammer used to strike or pull nails, this variability must be modeled to achieve robust task-oriented handovers. To tackle this, we propose a novel approach, GENESIS-Handover (GENErative HypotheSIS), which leverages VLM image generation to produce a variety of task-specific hand-object interaction hypotheses. These hypotheses are matched in real time to the observed human hand pose, enabling inference of the most suitable handover configuration. By leveraging VLMs as priors of plausible hand-object interactions, the method produces task-conditioned handover strategies for previously unseen object-task pairs. We evaluate the standalone interaction proposal module before deploying the full system on a mobile manipulator. In a user study with 12 participants across five task-object pairs, 83.3% perceived our method to have better task understanding than the previous state of the art.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Autonomous Trail Racing with a Bicycle Robot
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Fabian Jenelten, Deepana Ishtaweera, Pablo Garcia, Liana Margolese, Igor Bogoslavskyi
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: This paper presents a unified learning framework enabling a bicycle robot to autonomously navigate off-road trails at high speeds by encoding terrain semantics for perception and control.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Navigating off-road trails on a mountain bike requires diverse locomotion skills, including aerial maneuvers, cornering, and slip recovery, paired with sophisticated perception for scene understanding. Translating these capabilities to autonomous, two-wheeled robots remains a formidable challenge. We show that autonomous, high-speed trail navigation can be achieved through a single idea: encoding the trail as a semantic layer of the terrain. In simulation, this layer embeds the navigation task into the training environment; during deployment, it is reconstructed onboard from camera and LiDAR data. First, we introduce a unified learning framework that treats local navigation and locomotion as a joint optimization problem, bypassing the twist or pose command interface of classical control hierarchies. With fixed reward weights, the same framework produces both trail racing and agile parkour, shaped only through terrain semantics and episode length. Second, our perception pipeline combines a frozen vision foundation model with a lightweight dual-head decoder that predicts per-pixel terrain semantics and confidence scores, which are fused with LiDAR range measurements into an egocentric semantic elevation map at 30 Hz onboard an NVIDIA AGX Orin. We validate our framework on the Ultra Mobility Vehicle (UMV), a bicycle robot that autonomously raced across all sections of a kilometer-long, unstructured mountain bike trail at speeds exceeding 5 m/s and averaging 3.26 m/s. In simulation, our policy fails up to an order of magnitude less often than hierarchical baselines while driving faster.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Learn-To-Propagate: Distributionally Robust Motion Planning for Nonlinear Uncertain Systems
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Eduardo Figueiredo, Adrien Banse, Qi Heng Ho, Raphael Jungers, Morteza Lahijanian
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: The paper introduces L2P-DR-Forest, a distributionally-robust motion planning algorithm for nonlinear stochastic systems that ensures safety and correctness despite uncertain distributions.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Motion planning for stochastic systems aims to find a sequence of control inputs that drives a system to a goal set while avoiding unsafe states with high probability. Existing approaches, however, are either restricted to linear dynamics with perfect knowledge of the underlying distributions or lack formal correctness guarantees. To address these limitations, we propose \emph{Learn-To-Propagate Distributionally-Robust Forest (L2P-DR-Forest)}, a distributionally-robust sampling-based planning algorithm for \emph{nonlinear} stochastic systems with \emph{unknown} initial state and process noise distributions. Our approach leverages recent advances in optimal transport to learn ambiguity sets that contain the true system distributions with high confidence. We develop an efficient method for propagating these sets through the system dynamics and for verifying their safety. We then integrate these techniques into a novel sampling-based planning algorithm to grow a forest of search trees in the system's state space while accounting for and mitigating the growth of ambiguity-sets radii. We prove that the algorithm is correct, i.e., every returned plan satisfies the specifications with the prescribed confidence, and, under some feasibility and distributional assumptions, is probabilistically complete. Evaluations on several robotic benchmarks demonstrate that our algorithm significantly outperforms existing methods while providing formal guarantees with high confidence.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Swim2Real: Vision-Language Models for Simulator Calibration of a Soft Robotic Fish
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Kevin Qiu, Kyle Liam Walker, Mike Yan Michelis, Marek Cygan, Josie Hughes
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: Swim2Real employs a vision-language model to effectively calibrate a soft robotic fish simulator, significantly reducing error in swimming simulations compared to random and permuted directions.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Calibrating a soft aquatic robot simulator requires matching coupled deformation and propulsion from limited pool recordings. Swim2Real uses a vision-language model (VLM) to compare real and simulated swimming videos and propose updates to 16 simulator parameters. A backtracking line search tests each direction and accepts updates that reduce marker error. To test whether the proposals carry useful directions, we compare them with random and signed-permuted directions under the same line search and simulator budget. In an independent, preregistered fifty-seed replication, Swim2Real reduces the mean best-so-far error over 40 simulator evaluations by 63.4 mm against random directions and 53.2 mm against permuted directions. Both paired comparisons pass Holm correction ($p<10^{-5}$), conditional on run completion. A 24-seed experiment with a second VLM supports the same direction effect. Backtracking averages 16.1 VLM proposals per run versus 39 for Vid2Sid, which attains lower error at the same simulator budget. Ten hardware trials demonstrate open-loop execution of simulator-generated motor commands. Project page and videos: https://swim2real.github.io.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Benchmarking Real-World Robotic Manipulation through Stochastic Challenges
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Elias Gläßer, Gülhan Şikaroğlu, Pavlo Kupyn, Marc Pollefeys, Zuria Bauer
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: This paper introduces stochastic challenges for benchmarking robotic manipulation, enabling reproducible comparisons across platforms in real-world environments through randomized task samples.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: A challenging bottleneck in manipulation research is reproducibility and comparability of methods in real-world environments. Since manipulation is an interactive task, it cannot be evaluated on a static dataset of observations. Benchmarking in simulation is a common remedy, but cannot cover the whole complexity of real-world tests. This paper proposes a new paradigm of stochastic challenges. Like the well-known YCB objects, it is based on reproducible real-world scenes and therefore allows system-level innovation and comparability between different platforms. Due to their stochastic nature, our challenges however, mimic the rigor and surprise of hidden test sets. To this end, we show how different robots in different labs can be compared based on their success rate over different random task samples, if these samples come from the same distribution. We propose stochastic challenges as a general paradigm for robot benchmarking and implement this paradigm in a novel benchmark for mobile manipulation, on which we compare two robots tested in two different labs.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Learning Soft Robotic Dynamics with Active Exploration
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Hehui Zheng, Bhavya Sukhija, Chenhao Li, Klemens Iten, Andreas Krause
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: The paper presents an uncertainty-aware active exploration framework that enhances dynamics modeling of soft robots, achieving superior performance in diverse tasks and conditions.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Soft robots offer adaptability and safety in unstructured environments, yet their compliant, high-dimensional, and nonlinear dynamics make modeling for control difficult. Existing data-driven approaches often fail to generalize, constrained by narrowly focused task demonstrations or inefficient random exploration. We introduce an uncertainty-aware active exploration framework that autonomously learns task-agnostic and generalizable dynamics models of soft robotic systems. We evaluate this framework on three simulated platforms---a continuum arm, an articulated fish in fluid, and a musculoskeletal leg---and on a real-world pneumatically actuated continuum arm. Compared with random exploration and task-specific baseline, our method achieves higher modeling accuracy by actively collecting informative data. This improved model quality yields higher returns in zero-shot control on unseen tasks and robust performance under sensing noise, actuation delays, and material nonlinearities. These results demonstrate that uncertainty-driven active exploration enables data-efficient dynamics learning across soft robotic morphologies, supporting autonomous and adaptable control for compliant robots.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Dynamic Shape Control of Soft Trunk Robots
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Hehui Zheng, Marc Stampanoni, Roshan S. Kaundinya, Ronan Hinchet, George Haller
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: This paper presents an aSSM-based model predictive control method for dynamic shape regulation in soft trunk robots, significantly outperforming linear approaches in practical tasks.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Controlling the shape profile of soft trunk robots extends their reach into complex regions of the workspace and enhances their use in practical applications. Recent advances in soft robot design have enabled soft trunk robots to achieve greater flexibility in conforming to complex shapes. Specifically, trunk robots whose geometries are designed as helicoids have been shown to enable extreme shape-changing capabilities. Their compliance makes them highly nonlinear, which in turn makes shape control difficult. On similar tendon-driven trunk robots, model-based controllers based on the theory of adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs) have achieved high accuracy in closed-loop end-effector tracking. We extend this approach by learning an aSSM model of the full body of a trimmed-helicoid soft trunk robot from data and use this in a model predictive control (MPC) scheme to demonstrate a range of shape control tasks on hardware. On closed-loop dynamic shape regulation, our method outperforms the available linear baselines by a factor of 10. In human-in-the-loop interactive demos, our method completes section-by-section shaping and balances a tennis ball for over 25 seconds, while the linear baselines fall short. A model-free reinforcement learning policy trained for 12 hours on hardware fails on the same balancing task. These results establish aSSM-based MPC as a practical route to full-body shape control on real soft hardware.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Michal Korniak, Marco Bagatella, Ralf Römer, Michal Nauman, Yarden As
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: This study demonstrates that reinforcement learning can enhance generalist robot policies for simultaneous multi-task performance, improving adaptability and generalization beyond initial training tasks.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: The introduction of generalist robot policies has enabled a single, large model to learn to perform a variety of tasks from a vast pre-training corpus. While these models often exhibit powerful zero-shot generalization capabilities, they typically require an adaptation phase to achieve sufficient performance in deployment. Iterated self-improvement via reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated promise in enabling this adaptation, yet such approaches have been largely explored in single-task settings - where the goal is to simply improve on a narrow deployment task - which lies in stark contrast to the multi-task capabilities of the base policy. In this work we ask whether generalist robot policies are capable of multi-task, generalist improvement in deployment - targeting many diverse tasks simultaneously - and what algorithmic recipe enables this. To answer this question, we first develop a set of structured evaluations to test generalist improvement capabilities, and systematically evaluate algorithmic and practical design choices regarding value estimation, policy extraction and resource allocation. We show that not only can generalist policies be improved online across diverse tasks, but that the right recipe can enable generalization and increase performance on tasks not considered during online training. We characterize when this generalization occurs and show that both the training task distribution and the use of value-based RL are critical. To the best of our knowledge, this is among the first evidence for online generalist improvement for robot foundation models.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: SNAP: Semantic Navigation Among Pedestrians
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Jakob Wolfram, Pascal Roth, Fan Yang, Cesar Cadena, Marco Hutter
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: The paper presents an RL navigation policy that integrates semantic terrain and dynamic obstacle avoidance for robots in crowded urban settings, outperforming existing methods.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Navigating crowded urban environments requires robots to avoid pedestrians while adhering to social norms such as remaining on sidewalks. Existing approaches typically address either crowd avoidance or semantic path planning in isolation. We propose a reinforcement learning (RL) navigation policy that jointly reasons about semantic terrain and dynamic obstacles from a single semantically annotated bird's-eye-view (BEV) map, without relying on explicit human-state estimation. Our policy outperforms established crowd-navigation and semantic-aware baselines and transfers zero-shot to a legged robot, demonstrating socially compliant navigation in highly dynamic real-world scenarios.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Sparse Anchors for Visual Multi-Session Registration in Changing Environments
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Yunus Talha Erzurumlu, Niklas Trekel, Saurabh Gupta, Nico Koltermann, Olga Vysotska
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: This paper presents a method for visual multi-session registration using sparse absolute pose anchors to achieve accurate trajectory alignment in changing environments.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Repeated robotic monitoring requires localization across visits to the same environment, even if the environment changes. Such changes can substantially reduce persistent visual content, and repetitive structures can lead to incorrect cross-session correspondences. In this paper, we address visual multi-session registration of a new data recording (the query session) to a previously reconstructed reference map. Under substantial visual and structural changes, cross-session localization may be possible only for parts of the trajectory. In our approach, we therefore rely on a sparse set of reliable absolute pose constraints and combine them with within-session relative-pose information to register the complete trajectory to the reference map. We first estimate absolute alignment hypotheses through visual place recognition, local feature matching, and geometric verification. We then use sequence consensus to reject hypotheses that are inconsistent with a common query-to-reference alignment and retain the remaining poses as absolute anchors. These anchors are refined through featuremetric alignment against a Gaussian feature field and combined with within-session relative-pose constraints in a robust pose-graph optimization. We evaluate our approach on 15 cross-session experiments from the challenging HILTI26 construction-site dataset, covering substantial scene changes and difficult-to-match environments. Our method achieves 94.4% recall within 1m and 100.0% within 5m, outperforming independent image localization, which peaks at 65.3% and 70.7%, respectively, as well as direct registration of independently reconstructed Structure-from-Motion geometry. Our results show that sparse, reliable absolute anchors can provide accurate and complete trajectory registration even when reliable cross-session correspondences are available only for part of the query session.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: WayTrace: A Map-to-Language-to-Trace Hierarchy for Embodied Urban Navigation
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Manthan Patel, Jonas Frey, Pascal Roth, Marco Hutter, Cesar Cadena
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: WayTrace is a hierarchical navigation system that translates web-map directions into actionable commands for robots, enabling robust urban navigation despite GNSS inaccuracies.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Web services provide walking directions for nearly every city, but following them reliably over long routes remains challenging for autonomous robots. Point-goal navigation policies rely heavily on accurate GNSS, while most vision-language navigation models struggle to execute even short instructions outdoors. We present WayTrace, a hierarchical system that connects web-map directions to robot motion through language. An off-the-shelf orchestrator vision-language model reads the turn-by-turn directions, a satellite map and recent camera images, and issues one atomic language command at a time, such as "cross the road to the left". An onboard trace predictor, trained on over one million automatically labelled samples from street-level images, draws the path for this command in the image, and a reinforcement learning policy tracks it. In long-range simulated missions, WayTrace remains robust to GNSS noise and rarely leaves crosswalks or sidewalks, while point-goal baselines degrade sharply with about ten times more violations. Deployed on a wheeled-legged robot, WayTrace completes real-world missions of up to 1.37 km at about 1.1 m/s through a busy city centre, rural trails and a university campus, handling crosswalks, staircases and construction sites. Project page: https://way-trace.github.io

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: LocalNav: Distilling Frontier VLMs and Embodied RL for On-Device Object Goal Navigation
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Nicolas Baumann, Liam Boyle, Pu Deng, Edoardo Ghignone, Boyang Sun
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: LocalNav introduces a distillation strategy for lightweight Vision Language Models, enhancing on-device object goal navigation while significantly reducing latency and maintaining performance.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) have emerged in the robotic domain as a powerful tool that enables environmental perception with language context, serving as a catalyst for open- vocabulary tasks like Object Goal Navigation (ObjectNav). Yet, their computational footprint typically confines them to cloud execution, hindering low-latency inference with local deployment on resource-constrained robots. To address this challenge, we present a distillation strategy that aligns a lightweight, 4B- parameter local VLM to our spatial-semantic navigation interface via frontier model traces for edge execution on embedded GPU devices (e.g., Jetson Orin). While cloud models establish a baseline achieving 41.61% Success Rate (SR) on the HM3D OVON benchmark, zero-shot deployment of our proposed architecture with Qwen3.5-4B reaches only 25.97% SR. We demonstrate that distilling frontier reasoning traces and subsequent finetuning with Embodied Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (E- RLVR) obtains a 37.36% SR, substantially narrowing the gap to large cloud models. However, while deployable on memory- constrained devices, the model cannot compete with round-trip cloud inference time: we identify Token Generation (TG) as the main driver of latency and reduce it with Token Generation (TG)- regularized E-RLVR. The combined method reduces latency by 69.29% and retains a SR of 35.53%. Combined with quantization, this joint strategy yields a cumulative 80.21% reduction in overall inference latency without significantly sacrificing performance, presenting a viable paradigm for local, low-latency VLM execu- tion on mobile robots.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Learning Agile Humanoid Dodgeball with Onboard Monocular Vision
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Feng Tian, Yulin An, Chenhao Li, Matthias Heyrman, Marco Hutter
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: This paper presents an integrated system for humanoid robots to effectively dodge balls using onboard monocular vision, achieving high success rates in dynamic environments.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Humanoid robots operating in shared, dynamic environments must respond to rapidly approaching objects while maintaining balance. We study dodgeball as a controlled test of this capability, coupling visual threat assessment with whole-body evasion, recovery, and target reacquisition. We develop a system that integrates onboard monocular perception, temporal ball-state and threat-flag estimation, and learned whole-body control. A ball detector supplies bounding-box histories, and a temporal estimator predicts relative ball position and a binary threat flag. Separate dodge/recovery and search/track policies share this interface and are composed to support repeated encounters. A three-stage curriculum first trains control with privileged ball states, then starts estimator supervision from stable policy rollouts, and finally replaces the actor's privileged inputs with estimator outputs. Analytic projection and perception randomization provide detector-like training observations without image rendering. Across approach-angle bins in controlled simulation, dodge success ranges from 97.8--100.0% for 5.0 m launches at 6 m/s to 33.2--40.8% for 2.5 m launches at 10 m/s, with 1000 throws per speed--distance condition. On a physical Unitree G1, controlled single-throw success exceeds 85% over more than 15 trials. A hardware sequence demonstrates full-azimuth target reacquisition followed by another dodge. These results demonstrate an integrated onboard-monocular-vision system under highly dynamic motions.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: GoalDex: Learning Image-Goal-Conditioned Policies for Dexterous In-Hand Manipulation
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Arjun Bhardwaj, Mayank Mittal, Maximum Wilder-Smith, Vaishakh Patil, Marco Hutter
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: GoalDex introduces an end-to-end framework for dexterous in-hand manipulation that learns policies from RGB inputs without pose estimation, outperforming traditional methods.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Dexterous in-hand manipulation is commonly formulated around explicit object pose estimation, yet reliable pose tracking is challenging under severe hand-object occlusions and often requires object-specific supervision. This dependence creates a bottleneck between perception and control that can limit robustness and scalability. We present an end-to-end visuomotor framework for dexterous in-hand reorientation that operates on RGB observations and proprioception without intermediate pose estimation. Our approach jointly learns visual representations and control policies through behavior distillation from privileged state teachers and auxiliary reconstruction objectives. Furthermore, we introduce image-goal-conditioned reorientation, allowing desired object configurations to be specified directly through images rather than canonical pose representations. We evaluate our approach across a diverse set of object geometries and instances in simulation, where it consistently outperforms pose-based methods and policies built on pretrained visual encoders. Finally, we demonstrate direct sim-to-real transfer of a single image-goal-conditioned policy across five real-world objects, showing that accurate dexterous reorientation can be achieved without explicit pose estimation. For videos and code release, please refer to the project website: https://rffr.leggedrobotics.com/works/goaldex/

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Closing the Dynamics Gap through Self-Directed Robotic Interaction
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Xilun Zhang, Liam Achenbach, Luis Pabon, Matthew Foutter, Marco Pavone
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: CUE is an agentic system that autonomously interacts with its environment to accurately identify physical parameters, significantly reducing simulation errors in contact-rich dynamics.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Agentic Real2Sim2Real systems can reconstruct a scene in simulation from camera observations, but contact-rich dynamics such as friction and restitution cannot be observed without interaction. We call this the dynamics gap and present CUE, an agentic system that closes it by interacting with the environment itself. Given only a high-level instruction and no resets, the agent builds its own perception, identifies physical parameters, and targets interactions where its simulation is least accurate. On billiards, CUE reduces held-out ball-position error by 72% relative to the strongest baseline across 25 hidden-physics conditions in simulation, and we further deploy it on a real pool table. More details can be found on the project website: https://cue-dynamics.github.io/

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: AgenticMobility: An Open-Source Platform for Multi-AI-Agent Mobility Dynamics
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Jiaheng Xiao, Jiangtao Han, Jiachen Wang, Honghai Li, Lijun Sun
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: AgenticMobility is an open-source platform enabling the study of multi-AI-agent interactions in urban mobility dynamics, facilitating experiments on adaptation and policy impacts.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Understanding mobility dynamics and the effects of urban transportation management policies requires examining how individual travel decisions, traffic conditions, and policy interventions influence one another over time. We present AgenticMobility, an open-source experimental platform for studying how mobility AI agents and other AI agents interact, adapt through repeated experience, and collectively shape mobility outcomes. Persistent agents retain identities and relevant states across rounds, with explicit interfaces defining information access, admissible actions, and decision schedules; linked records trace decisions, execution, and feedback. In the current implementation, large language model (LLM) agents act as travelers choosing routes and departure times and as a manager periodically adjusting link charges within MATSim. A preliminary demonstration spans 100 simulated days in each of five configurations, with one run per configuration and a shared simulation seed. In the joint traveler--manager run, all 1,179,300 finalized target decisions satisfied action constraints; execution checks verified implementation of accepted choices and preservation of personal memories across days. Trajectories show stable route choices alongside departure-time adjustments and differences between controlled-trip and population-wide outcomes. The platform supports experiments on individual adaptation, collective outcomes, and management interventions by varying information access, retained experience, and management feedback. Source code is available at https://github.com/Agentic-City-Research/Agentic-Mobility

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Learning to Build: Autonomous Robotic Assembly of Stable Structures Without Predefined Plans
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Jingwen Wang, Johannes Kirschner, Paul Rolland, Luis Salamanca, Stefana Parascho
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: This paper introduces a reinforcement learning framework enabling autonomous robots to construct stable structures adaptively, without predefined plans, using targets and obstacles.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: This paper presents a novel autonomous robotic assembly framework for constructing stable structures without relying on predefined architectural blueprints. Instead of following fixed plans, construction tasks are defined through targets and obstacles, allowing the system to adapt more flexibly to environmental uncertainty and variations during the building process. A reinforcement learning (RL) policy, trained using deep Q-learning with successor features, serves as the decision-making component. As a proof of concept, we evaluate the approach on a benchmark of 15 2D robotic assembly tasks of discrete block construction. Experiments using a real-world closed-loop robotic setup demonstrate the feasibility of the method and its ability to handle construction noise. The results suggest that our framework offers a promising direction for more adaptable and robust robotic construction in real-world environments.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: ART of PIV: Agentic Real-Time Particle Image Velocimetry for Active Flow Control
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Antonio Terpin, Francesco Banelli, Alan Bonomi, Raffaello D'Andrea
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: The ART of PIV automates the particle image velocimetry pipeline selection, enhancing accuracy and speed for real-time flow control by reducing errors and improving performance.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Particle image velocimetry (PIV) measures fluid motion from images of tracer particles, but its accuracy depends on choices throughout the estimation pipeline, including image preprocessing, flow estimation, and postprocessing. These choices are typically left to expert tuning, and a fixed configuration can become less accurate as conditions change. This matters especially when PIV supplies feedback for real-time control, where measurements must be both accurate and fast, and flow conditions vary. We introduce ART of PIV -- short for Agentic Real-Time and also a nod to the art of tuning a PIV pipeline -- which automates pipeline choice for each image pair. A learned agent selects a configuration according to a chosen measurement objective from a library assembled for a specified speed budget. Across cross-correlation, classical optical-flow, and learning-based estimators, ART of PIV reduces average end-point error (AEPE) by 12.2-22.4 % relative to the best single estimator at matched speed, with gains extending to 1000-4000 image pair/s. In a simulated local velocity regulation task, it reduces mean normalized closed-loop cost by 13.24-13.59 percentage points relative to a tuned fixed estimator, with the same classical controller in both cases. In a tabletop water channel, we illustrate two ways to tune ART of PIV for a fluidic pinball of three rotating cylinders: selecting between complementary optical-flow tunings for accuracy, and selecting regions of interest with coherent rotation or shear using a common flow estimator. For the first variant, we train a DreamerV3 reinforcement learning controller directly in the physical world and demonstrate tracking of a prescribed flow field in the wake of a fluidic pinball.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Contact-based optimization for collision-free motion planning for a million robots
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Jan Kamm, Antonio Terpin, Raffaello D'Andrea
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: The paper presents a contact-based optimization algorithm, SCI, enabling efficient collision-free motion planning for up to one million robots by leveraging contact dynamics.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Multi-agent robotic systems have attracted growing interest in recent years, with applications ranging from coordinated drone shows to autonomous operations on land, in the air, and on water. At the planning level, robot motion is often modeled using double-integrator dynamics (with low-level controllers handling the physical dynamics during execution) with a minimum-energy objective subject to collision-avoidance constraints and limits on position, velocity, and acceleration. The complexity of the problem resides in the constraints, which couple the trajectories and make the optimization problem nonconvex. Existing numerical approaches typically discretize and optimize entire trajectories, which becomes expensive for large fleets. We exploit the structure of optimal trajectories by organizing optimization around contacts, at which robots reach the minimum allowed separation. We formulate a coupled algebraic system in contact variables and reconstruct trajectories analytically between contacts. Our algorithm, sequential contact insertion (SCI), starts from unconstrained trajectories, inserts contacts at separation violations, and jointly adjusts their times and states. Numerical experiments demonstrate planning for one million robots in minutes and thousands of robots in fractions of a second. On problems feasible for a fixed-grid sequential convex programming baseline, SCI achieves median speedups of several orders of magnitude at matching solution accuracy.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Rethinking Asymmetry in Self-Supervised 3D Geometry Learning
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Gyeongjin Kang, Freeman Cheng, Botao Ye, Weijie Lyu, Ming-Hsuan Yang
