Yet real- world robot datasets that capture error recovery and provide frame-level error annotations remain scarce. To address this gap, we introduce and open-source ReSTEP, a dataset of 3,156 episodes across two manipulation tasks with semantic stage labels and frame-level er- ror annotations. ReSTEP supports training and benchmarking progress monitors through successful execution, mistakes, and recovery. Existing progress estimators can struggle to distinguish visually similar task stages and maintain temporally consistent predictions while responding to genuine setbacks. We therefore propose REMORA, an online progress esti- mator that combines recurrent visual memory, distributional prediction, and causal peak selection. Memory retains execution history to help resolve visual ambiguity, while distribu- tional prediction represents alternative progress hypotheses and causal peak selection tracks a supported hypothesis over time. Together, these components enable consistent progress tracking that remains responsive to errors and recovery. Experiments on both ReSTEP tasks demonstrate that REMORA outperforms the state-of-the-art SARM baseline in progress ac- curacy and temporal consistency.

ReThinkLab.title: Aligning Medical Vision Language Models at the Capability Boundary with Entropy Adaptive Rubric Grounding
ReThinkLab.authors_text: Hongyu Bai, Jiaqi Zeng, Chunzheng Zhu
ReThinkLab.summary: The paper presents MedCBR, a two-stage framework enhancing medical vision language models by optimizing diagnostic reasoning through boundary-aware preferences and rubric-grounded reinforcement learning, achieving significant accuracy improvements.
ReThinkLab.debug_abstract: Medical diagnostic reasoning requires verifiable links between visual evidence and clinical knowledge, yet current medical vision language models are aligned with objectives that reward the wrong behavior. Uniform supervised fine tuning lets easy cases dominate updates while clinically critical boundary cases saturate prematurely. Sparse rewards based only on final-answer correctness cannot assess anatomical grounding or clinical logic, inviting reward hacking through answer shortcuts. We propose MedCBR, a two-stage alignment framework coupling boundary-aware preference optimization with rubric-grounded reinforcement learning. First, we construct counterfactual boundary preferences at the model's capability frontier using empirical pass rates and preference pairs that share reasoning prefixes but diverge at decisive diagnostic branches. Difficulty Weighted Boundary Preference Optimization (DBPO) concentrates learning on this calibrated boundary region. Second, we distill reusable clinical rubrics from boundary trajectories and activate them according to prediction entropy. Entropy Gated Grounded Policy Optimization (EGPO) rewards answer correctness, anatomical grounding, and reasoning fidelity while suppressing rubric noise on reliable samples. A reference policy anchored to the boundary-aligned model couples population-level boundary priors with instance-level uncertainty, making diagnostic reasoning more accurate and clinically grounded. Experiments on six medical benchmarks show consistent improvements over strong general, specialized, and reinforcement learning baselines, reaching 61.2% average accuracy with the largest gains on challenging differential diagnosis tasks. Ablations show super-additive gains: combining the two stages exceeds the sum of their individual improvements.

ReThinkLab.title: Learning Safe Flow Matching Robot Policies from Binary Feasibility Oracles
ReThinkLab.authors_text: Jianming Ma, Rongjun Jin, Yizhi Chen, Yue Gao
ReThinkLab.summary: The paper presents an oracle-guided safeguard for safe flow-matching robot policies, ensuring 100% constraint satisfaction during manipulation tasks without explicit constraint models.
ReThinkLab.debug_abstract: Robot foundation models increasingly rely on flow-based action generation for general-purpose manipulation, yet the generated actions are not guaranteed to satisfy physical constraints such as joint limits and collision avoidance. This problem is especially challenging when the feasible set cannot be described analytically and is accessible only through black-box feasibility oracles. We study this practical oracle-only setting and propose an oracle-guided differentiable safeguard for safe flow-matching robot policies. The safeguard uses binary feasibility queries to correct unsafe updates in the forward pass, while extracting local boundary information to provide constraint-aware learning signals in the backward pass. Combined with discrete-time flow matching, the same safeguard is used during training and inference, enabling forward--backward aligned policy learning without explicit or differentiable constraint models. Experiments on obstacle-aware robotic manipulation demonstrate 100% constraint satisfaction while preserving task performance.

ReThinkLab.title: RoboAtom: Large-scale Atomic-Action Supervision for Robot Learning
ReThinkLab.authors_text: Xueyuan Wei, Xuanxu Wang, Xudong Li, Yuping He, Wanshui Gan
ReThinkLab.summary: RoboAtom introduces a large-scale dataset with unified atomic-action annotations, enhancing robot learning through improved skill recognition and task success in various benchmarks.
ReThinkLab.debug_abstract: Fine-grained action annotations can support skill reuse and compositional generalization in robot policies. However, robot datasets typically provide task-level instructions without subtask annotations. Although some include subtask labels, inconsistent formats and conventions hinder cross-source joint training. We propose RoboAtom-Data, which adds unified, time-aligned atomic-action annotations to existing data from multiple sources, covering 1.45 million trajectories, 6.88 million skill-labeled segments, and 16,882.1 hours. Our pipeline combines a unified protocol, large-scale manual annotation, propagation across repeated executions with the same ordered skill sequence, and multi-stage quality control. We evaluate the dataset through automatic atomic-action annotation and robot control. We construct RoboAtom-Bench to standardize evaluation of skill recognition and temporal boundary localization. Trained on the annotated data, RoboAtom-Anno achieves better automatic annotation performance than all evaluated open- and closed-source models on both RoboAtom-Bench and the external WGO-Bench. For robot control, atomic-action supervision paired with hierarchical execution improves task success over task-level baselines on LIBERO-Long, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin. We will release the data, benchmark, model, and construction pipeline to support further research on skill-level robot learning.

ReThinkLab.title: What Should a Navigator Remember? Spatiotemporal Memory for Zero-Shot Vision-Language Navigation
ReThinkLab.authors_text: Yuhang Peng, Zhikai Wang, Ziyi Wang, Jiaru Zhong, Xiaoji Zheng
ReThinkLab.summary: This paper presents a zero-shot vision-language navigation system that optimally organizes spatiotemporal memory to enhance navigation performance without specific training, achieving superior real-world success rates.
ReThinkLab.debug_abstract: Zero-shot vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires an agent to use past observations without navigation-specific training. We study what information an 8B-scale navigation system should retain and how it should be organized for subsequent decisions. Our agent combines instruction progress, hierarchically compressed observation history anchored to poses, and accumulated geometry in complementary task, temporal, and spatial memories. An 8B observer summarizes observations, and an 8B reasoner uses the memories to select waypoint intents or request additional views, a geometric controller executes the selected targets. A semantic information perspective motivates the distinction between retaining evidence, making it accessible to the reasoner, and acquiring further observations. On R2R-CE val-unseen, the complete system achieves the highest among the evaluated Qwen3-based zero-shot baselines. Removing temporal memory reduces SR and sharply increases average path length from 16.9 to 39.1m, removing the spatial-map and planning component reduces SR as well. Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 show that our zero-shot method achieves higher success rates than the post-trained baseline in both corridor and office environments, suggesting better transfer to the evaluated real-world settings. As a complementary evaluation, LAW2 uses paired instruction interventions to examine behavioral responses, instruction following ability beyond endpoint success. These results support preserving task progress, observation history, and geometry in structured memory for zero-shot navigation with smaller open models.

ReThinkLab.title: Test-time Correction: An Online 3D Detection System via Visual Prompting
ReThinkLab.authors_text: Hanxue Zhang, Zetong Yang, Yanan Sun, Li Chen, Fatma Güney
ReThinkLab.summary: The paper presents Test-time Correction (TTC), an online 3D detection system that uses visual prompting for real-time error correction in autonomous driving, enhancing safety and adaptability.
ReThinkLab.debug_abstract: This paper introduces Test-time Correction (TTC), an online 3D detection system designed to rectify test-time errors using various auxiliary feedback, aiming to enhance the safety of deployed autonomous driving systems. Unlike conventional offline 3D detectors that remain fixed during inference, TTC enables immediate online error correction without retraining, allowing autonomous vehicles to adapt to new scenarios and reduce deployment risks. To achieve this, we equip existing 3D detectors with an Online Adapter (OA) module -- a prompt-driven query generator for real-time correction. At the core of OA module are visual prompts: image-based descriptions of objects of interest derived from auxiliary feedback such as mismatches with 2D detections, road descriptions, or user clicks. These visual prompts, collected from risky objects during inference, are maintained in a visual prompt buffer to enable continuous correction in future frames. By leveraging this mechanism, TTC consistently detects risky objects, achieving reliable, adaptive, and versatile driving autonomy. Extensive experiments show that TTC significantly improves instant error rectification over frozen 3D detectors, even under limited labels, zero-shot settings, and adverse conditions. We hope this work inspires future research on post-deployment online rectification systems for autonomous driving.

ReThinkLab.title: WNM-3D: A World Navigation Model with 3D Scene Conditioning for Closed-Loop VLN
ReThinkLab.authors_text: Yuehao Huang, Yunzi Wu, Xiaotao Zhang, Xinhai Li, Jiankun Dong
ReThinkLab.summary: WNM-3D enhances vision-language navigation by integrating 3D scene conditioning into generative world-action models, outperforming previous methods in diverse environments and physical robot deployment.
ReThinkLab.debug_abstract: Recent vision-language navigation (VLN) systems increasingly adapt pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) into vision-language-action (VLA) policies that map egocentric observations and language instructions directly to navigation actions. Although semantically capable, such action-centric training does not explicitly model how the agent's visual observations evolve under its predicted motion. Generative world-action models (WAMs) jointly predict future observations and actions, yet existing WAMs for continuous VLN do not condition joint future-view and action generation on geometry-aware representations inferred from the observation history. We present WNM-3D, a generative World Navigation Model with 3D scene conditioning for continuous VLN. A frozen feed-forward geometry encoder extracts cross-view representations from monocular RGB history, and a trainable 3D Scene-to-Token Adapter converts them into a fixed-length scene prefix for the world-action Diffusion Transformer. Through block-causal attention, this prefix remains visible to every future video-action block throughout joint denoising, providing persistent geometric context. We train WNM-3D with supervised world-action learning, DAgger-style adaptation on policy-visited states, and Counterfactual DanceGRPO refinement. Across GN-Bench and VLN-CE, WNM-3D consistently outperforms the backbone-matched WNM-2D counterpart, demonstrating gains from 3D scene conditioning across distinct visual domains. WNM-3D further outperforms strong VLN baselines on GN-Bench and demonstrates closed-loop deployment on a physical robot. Component and stage-wise ablations support the Adapter design and the complementary roles of DAgger-SFT and subsequent reward-guided refinement.

ReThinkLab.title: OpenFlyV2: An onboard vision-language-action model for aerial perception and navigation
ReThinkLab.authors_text: Junli Liu, Zhongrui You, Chenhui Li, Zhen Li, Yuyang Tian
ReThinkLab.summary: OpenFlyV2 is a unified onboard vision-language-action model enabling aerial robots to perform semantic understanding, spatial reasoning, and navigation efficiently on resource-constrained platforms.
ReThinkLab.debug_abstract: Human cognition flexibly draws on a shared perceptual foundation to understand environments, attend to referenced entities, reason about spatial relationships, and act. Endowing aerial robots with an analogous functional organization remains challenging, as existing systems are often specialized for individual capabilities, dependent on offboard computation, or unable to sustain closed-loop operation on resource-constrained platforms. We present OpenFlyV2, a unified onboard vision-language-action architecture that uses a shared vision-language representation to support semantic understanding, language-grounded perception, spatial reasoning, and continuous aerial control within a single model. A compact action expert converts the shared multimodal context into short-horizon flight waypoints, while motion-aware temporal memory and action priors reduce the computational cost of closed-loop execution. We construct \dataset{}, a simulation-based dataset comprising approximately 70,000 navigation trajectories and 60,000 vision-language instruction--response pairs. OpenFlyV2 generates action chunks, each comprising 12 waypoints, entirely onboard at 10 Hz using an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX. It transfers zero-shot from simulation to physical quadrotor flight, achieving a 48\% navigation success rate across four real-world environments without real-world aerial training data. Extensive results demonstrate that broad vision-language competence and continuous closed-loop flight can coexist within a single model on a resource-constrained aerial platform. Code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/Ideal-ljl/AeroBrain.

ReThinkLab.title: Kinematic-Tactile Aligned Dexterous Retargeting with Contact Wrench Space Alignment
ReThinkLab.authors_text: Xinyuan He, Ziheng Xu, Yueyuan Chen, Yufan Ye, Yuanshuo Tan
ReThinkLab.summary: This paper presents a hierarchical framework for aligning kinematics and tactile information in dexterous manipulation, achieving high replay success and fidelity in robot hand trajectories.
ReThinkLab.debug_abstract: Human demonstrations provide a natural and scalable source of data for learning dexterous manipulation policies. However, existing retargeting methods primarily transfer human kinematics, while the tactile information underlying physical interaction is rarely preserved across embodiments. To address this limitation, we present a hierarchical three-stage framework for kinematic-tactile aligned dexterous retargeting. We use object-centric contact wrench space as a physical representation for tactile alignment between human and robot hands. The framework first aligns hand kinematics and contact geometry, and then constructs a human wrench support profile from tactile forces and contact geometry. Robot fingertip force targets are subsequently optimized to cover the human wrench support and converted into joint position corrections, yielding directly replayable robot hand trajectories. We evaluate the framework in simulation and real robot experiments across three pouring conditions. In the real robot experiments, our method achieves a 96.7\% replay success rate and higher wrench transfer fidelity than representative retargeting baselines. The framework enables physically grounded transfer of kinematic and tactile information from human demonstrations to robot hands, providing a path toward scalable learning of contact-rich dexterous manipulation.

ReThinkLab.title: WorkFactory: Turning Professional Intents into Executable Work for Scalable Agent Training
ReThinkLab.authors_text: Ziyang Zeng, Tingyang Chen, Jia Deng, Qiyao Wang, Shuo Tang
ReThinkLab.summary: WorkFactory is a scalable framework that transforms professional intents into executable tasks, enhancing agent training through structured planning and repair, demonstrated across 112,686 tasks and improved model performance.
ReThinkLab.debug_abstract: Scaling supervised training for working agents requires diverse professional tasks that yield reliable expert demonstrations. However, missing or inconsistent task information can obstruct teacher execution and weaken the resulting supervision. We propose WorkFactory, a scalable framework for constructing coherent and executable professional tasks. Starting from professional intents, information-level planning builds an information support graph to guide task instantiation, explicitly representing the dependencies and locations of information required for the intended outputs. Probe executions then identify support failures and guide repairs while preserving the intended work. We construct 112,686 tasks spanning 612 occupations and use the collected teacher trajectories to fine-tune Qwen models at 4B, 27B, and 35B-A3B scales, yielding the WorkPilot family. All three models improve over their respective base models across four professional-work benchmarks, with WorkPilot-35B-A3B improving from 879 to 1565 Elo on GDPval-AA v2.1. Scaling analyses reveal model-dependent diminishing returns, with execution length first increasing and then decreasing. Controlled component analyses show that planning and repair reduce probe-diagnosed task environment defects and improve downstream performance. The data and models are available at https://github.com/IQuestLab/WorkFactory.

ReThinkLab.title: RPT*: Global Planning with Probabilistic Terminals for Target Search in Complex Environments
ReThinkLab.authors_text: Yunpeng Lyu, Chao Cao, Ji Zhang, Howie Choset, Zhongqiang Ren
ReThinkLab.summary: The paper presents RPT*, a novel approach for solving the HPP-PT problem, optimizing target search paths in complex environments by incorporating probabilistic terminal locations and dynamic programming.
ReThinkLab.debug_abstract: Routing problems such as Hamiltonian Path Problem (HPP), seek a path to visit all the vertices in a graph while minimizing the path cost. This paper studies a variant, HPP with Probabilistic Terminals (HPP-PT), where each vertex has a probability representing the likelihood that the robot's path terminates there, and the objective is to minimize the expected path cost. HPP-PT arises in target object search, where a mobile robot must visit all candidate locations to find an object, and prior knowledge of the object's location is expressed as vertex probabilities. While routing problems have been studied for decades, few of them consider uncertainty as required in this work. The challenge lies not only in optimality ordering the vertices, as in standard HPP, but also in handling history dependency: the expected path cost depends on the order in which vertices were previously visited. This makes many existing methods inefficient or inapplicable. To address the challenge, we propose a search-based approach RPT* with solution optimality guarantees, which leverages dynamic programming in a new state space to bypass the history dependency and novel heuristics to speed up the computation. Building on RPT*, we design a Hierarchical Autonomous Target Search (HATS) system that combines RPT* with either Bayesian filtering for lifelong target search with noisy sensors, or autonomous exploration to find targets in unknown environments. Experiments in both simulation and real robot show that our approach can naturally balance between exploitation and exploration, thereby finding targets more quickly on average than baseline methods.

ReThinkLab.title: FAWAM: Force-Aware World Action Models for Closed-Loop Contact-Rich Manipulation
ReThinkLab.authors_text: Haotian He, Zeyu Yan, Qipeng Liu, Ning Guo, Wenzhao Lian
ReThinkLab.summary: FAWAM enhances contact-rich robotic manipulation by integrating force signals into perception, prediction, and execution, improving success rates significantly over existing methods.
ReThinkLab.debug_abstract: Force signals provide critical interaction cues for contact-rich robotic manipulation. However, existing methods mostly use force as an additional observation modality, without fully exploiting its role in modeling future interaction dynamics or guiding execution-time feedback correction. In this paper, we propose FAWAM, a force-aware world action model that incorporates force information at three levels: perception, prediction, and closed-loop execution. FAWAM first encodes historical 6-axis force/torque signals to modulate action generation, then jointly predicts future actions and end-effector wrenches to explicitly model contact evolution. It further introduces a residual correction module that uses the predicted wrench trajectory as an execution-time reference to refine actions online based on real-time force feedback. Real-world experiments across multiple contact-rich tasks show that FAWAM improves the average success rate by 36.25% over vision-only baselines and 21.25% over existing force-aware baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of our force-aware framework for robust contact-rich manipulation.

ReThinkLab.title: Making Self-Driving Laboratories Auditable:A Unified Framework for Hybrid Actions,Measurements, and Safe Execution
ReThinkLab.authors_text: Zihan Zhang, Zeyu Wu, Xin Zhang, Mingyu Luo, Haohui Que
ReThinkLab.summary: The paper presents a unified framework for self-driving laboratories that integrates hybrid actions, measurements, and safety protocols to enhance execution coordination and traceability.
ReThinkLab.debug_abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) are laboratory systems that couple experimental planning, automated execution, and measurement feedback in a closed loop. Integrating flexible robot control with the typed application programming interfaces (APIs) and continuous measurements exposed by laboratory instruments remains an execution-interface challenge. To address this challenge, we propose a traceable framework comprising four components: LAM (Lab Action Model), OpenSDL, Safe-SDL, and L3-Bench. LAM is a proposed measurement-conditioned policy architecture that extends vision-language-action paradigms to generate both continuous robot trajectories and typed instrument API calls. OpenSDL is an execution substrate with an initial control implementation, designed to map role-level operations to heterogeneous devices, coordinate execution, and record timestamped causal events. The proposed Safe-SDL runtime gate combines pre-dispatch schema and resource checks with signal temporal logic monitoring during execution, including extended waiting periods. L3-Bench (Level-3 Laboratory Benchmark) specifies an episode-level evaluation protocol covering physical outcomes, timing, reproducibility, safety violations, and fault recovery. Together, these components provide an end-to-end design for linking hybrid action generation, monitored device execution, measurement feedback, and experimental evaluation, addressing coordination and traceability challenges in SDL workflows.

ReThinkLab.title: GUI-JEPA: Candidate-Conditioned JEPA Latents as a Fast Action Policy for Mobile GUI Agents
ReThinkLab.authors_text: Bingchao Wang, Yongcheng Jing, Shunyu Liu, Chengyu Wang, Jun Huang
ReThinkLab.summary: GUI-JEPA introduces a novel decoder-free policy for mobile GUI agents, significantly improving action selection speed and efficiency using a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture.
ReThinkLab.debug_abstract: Mobile GUI agents are typically fine-tuned 7B-scale vision-language models (VLMs) that generate each action as text. However, these VLMs decode every action token by token, and even agents that score candidate actions keep a large language model or VLM in the loop, making them slow and memory-hungry. To address these issues, we propose GUI-JEPA, to our knowledge the first decoder-free GUI agent policy built on a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), which selects actions in the latent space of a JEPA encoder pretrained on unlabelled GUI screenshots. Its action- and region-conditioned latent predictor turns the screen latent into one latent per candidate action, letting lightweight heads score all candidates against the instruction in a single batched pass, without decoding a token. We further show that the scorer relies on this latent pathway and that the predictor is trained for the decision itself: a randomly initialised predictor does just as well as one pretrained on screen dynamics. On AndroidControl, GUI-JEPA is 2.8-4.0x faster on the same GPU than a Qwen2.5-VL-7B agent we fine-tune with the same inputs, while reaching 86-92% of its in-distribution accuracy with 6% of its parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/bcwang-sjtu/GUI-JEPA

ReThinkLab.title: Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception
ReThinkLab.authors_text: Lai Wei, Yatai Li, Liangbo He, Jun Lan, Renjie Gu
ReThinkLab.summary: The paper introduces EvidenceConnect, a data synthesis framework enhancing multimodal perception by generating targeted training data that improves spatial reasoning and generalizable evidence connection.
ReThinkLab.debug_abstract: Multimodal perception forms the foundation of multimodal intelligence. In particular, spatial perception and multimodal long-context understanding are two pivotal tasks that underpin embodied AI and multimodal agents. However, synthesizing targeted, high-quality training data for these tasks remains difficult and costly. Our key insight is that these tasks share an underlying capability, which we call connecting evidence: identifying relevant visual facts, binding them to the correct entities, recovering their relations, and composing them into an answer. Crucially, targeted training data are far easier to synthesize for this capability than for these tasks themselves. To strengthen this capability, we propose EvidenceConnect, an easy-to-implement data synthesis framework that uses zoomed views of related regions within a single image to generate questions requiring comparison, aggregation, or chaining of visual evidence. To ensure quality, a reference answer is retained only when independent VLMs agree on it, and region-ablation tests discard questions whose answer survives the removal of selected regions. We then train base VLMs on the resulting data with RLVR, obtaining Zooming without Zooming v2 (ZwZ2). Although the synthesized data are not tailored to any downstream benchmark, ZwZ2 improves fine-grained and spatial perception, with further gains on embodied spatial reasoning, multimodal long-context understanding, multimodal agent tasks, and general visual reasoning. These results establish EvidenceConnect as an effective framework for supervising evidence connection and suggest that strengthening this shared capability leads to more generalizable multimodal perception.

ReThinkLab.title: Does Your Generalist Skill Optimizer Really Incentivize Agentic Tasks? Rethinking Skill Optimization via Bipartite Attribution
ReThinkLab.authors_text: Jiawei Zhou, Bo Peng, Yuxuan Huang, Ming Zhang, Youbang Sun
ReThinkLab.summary: The paper critiques existing skill optimizers, introducing BiPA to evaluate their effectiveness and revealing that learned skills show minimal improvement over hand-written seeds.
ReThinkLab.debug_abstract: Skill optimizers adapt an agent to long-horizon tasks, such as repairing a terminal environment, by rewriting its skill, a natural-language procedure in its context, and keeping the edits that raise success on a small dev set. On such tasks success is noisy, so a gain on a small dev set does not show that an edit helps, and a success score does not show what the edit costs. We introduce BiPA, which replays an optimizer's acceptance rule on candidates identical to its seed to measure what selection alone reports, and records each episode as a bipartite graph of turns and the text they read to trace extra input tokens to the behavior behind them. Across three optimizers, three agentic benchmarks and two models, the learned skills succeed about as often as their hand-written seed, 0.1 points higher on average. Their dev gains vanish on test: keeping the best of several candidates on at most 30 tasks reports gains this large even when none changed. They read about 16% more input tokens: the optimizers almost always add rules, half to re-check work and some to act one call at a time, and the agent follows them as extra turns, each re-sending the whole conversation. Four principles follow: accept an edit only if its gain exceeds what selection alone reports; charge it for the turns it adds, not for its length; let the editor delete and merge rules; show it what earlier rules cost. Code is available at https://github.com/valleysprings/BiPA.git.

ReThinkLab.title: ShredBench: Evaluating the Semantic Reasoning Capabilities of Multimodal LLMs in Document Reconstruction
ReThinkLab.authors_text: Zichun Guo, Yuling Shi, Wenhao Zeng, Chao Hu, Haotian Lin
ReThinkLab.summary: ShredBench evaluates multimodal large language models' semantic reasoning in reconstructing shredded documents, revealing significant performance gaps due to visual discontinuities.
ReThinkLab.debug_abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved remarkable performance in Visually Rich Document Understanding (VRDU) tasks, but their capabilities are mainly evaluated on pristine, well-structured document images. We consider content restoration from shredded fragments, a challenging VRDU setting that requires integrating visual pattern recognition with semantic reasoning under significant content discontinuities. To facilitate systematic evaluation of complex VRDU tasks, we introduce ShredBench, a benchmark supported by an automated generation pipeline that renders fragmented documents directly from Markdown. The proposed pipeline ensures evaluation validity by allowing the flexible integration of latest or unseen textual sources to prevent training data contamination. ShredBench assesses four scenarios (English, Chinese, Code, Table) with three fragmentation granularities (8, 12, 16 pieces). Empirical evaluations on state-of-the-art MLLMs reveal a significant performance gap: The method is effective on intact documents; however, once the document is shredded, restoration becomes a significant challenge, with NED dropping sharply as fragmentation increases. Our findings highlight that current MLLMs lack the fine-grained cross-modal reasoning required to bridge visual discontinuities, identifying a critical gap in robust VRDU research.

ReThinkLab.title: PerceptRL: Making Visual Perception Rewardable in MLLMs from Answers to Interactions
ReThinkLab.authors_text: Tongkun Guan, Zhibo Yang, Mingkun Yang, Haocheng Wang, Wei Shen
ReThinkLab.summary: PerceptRL enhances visual perception in multimodal large language models by utilizing reinforcement learning to verify errors and improve accuracy through structured QA interactions.
ReThinkLab.debug_abstract: Fine-grained visual perception remains a bottleneck during post-training of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), as perceptual errors can constrain gains from reasoning-focused optimization. Although image-caption pre-training improves perception, its influence can weaken as subsequent stages change data mixtures and objectives. Continuing caption supervision during post-training is challenging because subjective, information-dense descriptions complicate verifiable reward design. We present PerceptRL, which strengthens perception at two complementary levels. Perception RL uses a multi-agent pipeline to extract verified errors from dense image captions and convert the corresponding visual facts into QA pairs with fixed answer labels and rule-based rewards. Chain QA links correlated errors, while multiple-choice QA combines unrelated errors. A specialized route targets high-error domains with tailored verification, and a domain-agnostic general route covers errors beyond these domains. Perception Agentic RL addresses fine-grained and dense cases unresolved by single-turn Perception RL through multi-turn inspection with visual tools. We observe coordinate drift even in models trained to use tools, where incorrect crops or annotations distort evidence and propagate errors. Coordinate Injection corrects spatial operations in cold-start trajectories, while a grounding-aware process reward supervises intermediate spatial fidelity alongside final-answer correctness. Training proceeds through shared cold-start SFT, single-turn Perception RL, and multi-turn Perception Agentic RL. Across seven benchmarks under a shared tool-use protocol, PerceptRL achieves 71.6% average accuracy, surpassing the base model with the same tools and the strongest evaluated frontier VLM by 15.7 and 5.2 percentage points, respectively.

ReThinkLab.title: AWARE: Action-Entropy-Weighted and Attention-Guided Retrieval of Observation Evidence for Vision-Language-Action Models
ReThinkLab.authors_text: Jiabing Yang, Yixiang Chen, Yuan Xu, Peiyan Li, Zichen Wen
ReThinkLab.summary: The AWARE module enhances Vision-Language-Action models by efficiently retrieving task-relevant observation evidence using action entropy and attention, improving performance without additional training.
ReThinkLab.debug_abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models combine multimodal perception with robotic control, demonstrating remarkable potential for generalizable manipulation. Yet, enhancing their execution typically relies on auxiliary sensory inputs (e.g., depth, 3D point clouds) or costly fine-tuning. Inspired by the insight that Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) act as key-value memory, we propose Action-Entropy-Weighted and Attention-Guided Retrieval of Observation Evidence (AWARE), an effective, training-free, and plug-and-play module for VLAs. Specifically, AWARE tracks layer-wise uncertainty via an element-wise Action Entropy metric, and retrieves observation evidence into the element's FFN through associative memory lookup. Crucially, the retrieved features are weighted by instruction-guided cross-modal attention to isolate task-relevant observation cues, while injection strength is adaptively scaled by the element's entropy and relative network depth. This selectively channels observation evidence to high-entropy action dimensions and deep layers where grounding decays, while leaving converged representations intact. Across LIBERO, SIMPLER, CALVIN, and real-world robot manipulation, AWARE consistently improves diverse VLA architectures with minimal computational overhead, achieving the largest gains on long-horizon tasks without architectural changes or additional training. Project page: https://jiabingyang01.github.io/AWARE/.

ReThinkLab.title: FTP-1: A Generalist Foundation Tactile Policy Across Tactile Sensors for Contact-Rich Manipulation
ReThinkLab.authors_text: Chengbo Yuan, Zicheng Zhang, Mingjie Zhou, Wendi Chen, Yi Wang
ReThinkLab.summary: FTP-1 is a pioneering generalist tactile policy that enables transferable manipulation skills across diverse sensors, improving performance in contact-rich tasks by significant margins.
ReThinkLab.debug_abstract: Despite the success of vision-based generalist robotic policies, existing tactile-based policies remain tied to fixed embodiments and sensor setups. This is because tactile signals are highly heterogeneous across hardware, making cross-sensor generalization difficult. We present FTP-1,the first generalist foundation tactile policy pretrained to acquire transferable tactile manipulation abilities across diverse sensors and embodiments. FTP-1 supports varied tactile inputs, including image-, array-, and state-based signals, by using heterogeneous encoders to project them into unified morphology-aware latent tokens that are jointly modeled by a shared tactile Transformer expert. Pretrained on around 3,000 hours of tactile manipulation data aggregated from 26 data sources, spanning human and robot demonstrations across 21 sensors, FTP-1 learns tactile skills that transfer beyond the sensors seen during pretraining. Across downstream finetuning experiments spanning 5 hardware configurations, FTP-1 improves contact-rich manipulation on seen sensor setups by +17.2% and, surprisingly, transfers to two previously unseen tactile-sensor setups, achieving a +31% gain in success rate. FTP-1 establishes the first unified foundation baseline for tactile manipulation, providing future tactile policies with a shared model-level starting point. Pretrained models, datasets, training code and more visualization at https://ftp1-policy.github.io.

ReThinkLab.title: Understanding Human-Robot Collaboration through Joint Action
ReThinkLab.authors_text: Chengwen Zhang, Jianyang Wang, Chang Liu, Yukun Wang, Yuan Xu
ReThinkLab.summary: This systematic review synthesizes 83 empirical studies on human-robot collaboration using Joint Action theory, identifying key constructs and gaps for future research.
ReThinkLab.debug_abstract: Human-robot collaboration requires partners to coordinate interdependent contributions toward a shared goal. Joint Action theory provides concepts for understanding this coordination, but how these concepts are instantiated and combined across empirical research remains fragmented. We conducted a systematic review following PRISMA 2020, identifying 83 empirical papers published between 2021 and 2026. Through theory-driven framework analysis, we organized the literature into nine constructs across three capacities: Representation, Prediction, and Integration. We analyze how these constructs are distributed and co-occur across studies, revealing where empirical evidence concentrates and where it is absent. By mapping empirical HRC research onto a unified Joint Action framework, this review offers a coherent overview of HRC studies, identifies gaps in current evidence, and provides guidelines for future research.

赵波老师实验室.title: GLoTouch: Global-to-Local Haptic Perception Using a Parallel Gripper for Object Search, Recognition, and Grasping Without External Vision
赵波老师实验室.authors_text: Zonglin Li, Wanruo Zhang, Yiming Wang, Kun Song, Xinyi Zhou
赵波老师实验室.summary: GLoTouch is a novel haptic perception framework enabling parallel grippers to perform object search, recognition, and grasping in low-light conditions without external vision.
赵波老师实验室.debug_abstract: Perceiving objects in the environment is a fundamental capability of autonomous robots. In dark or low-light environments, external cameras often fail to reliably perceive object positions and geometry; when visual sensing is unavailable, completing target search, recognition, and grasping through touch alone becomes a key robot manipulation capability. This task must simultaneously address container-scale spatial exploration and object-scale fine-grained geometric perception, which is particularly challenging for low-degree-of-freedom parallel grippers. However, a unified framework remains lacking for connecting container-scale spatial exploration with object-scale fine-grained geometric perception and grasping. To address this challenge, we present \textbf{GLoTouch}, a global-to-local haptic perception and manipulation framework built on a parallel gripper. In the global stage, the gripper holds a passive long-reach probe, combining force measurements with known tool geometry to localize contacts and actively estimate candidate-object positions, coarse contours, and heights. In the local stage, the robot sets down the probe and uses the bilateral visuotactile sensors on the same gripper to directly acquire local haptic observations, which are matched against a given target 3-D model without object-specific training. We evaluate the framework in both simulation and real-robot experiments. Source code will be open-sourced.

赵波老师实验室.title: SynthDCB: World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking
赵波老师实验室.authors_text: Zichen Zhu, Dingye Liu, Nan Jiang, Danyang Zhang, Hang Zheng
赵波老师实验室.summary: SynthDCB is a scalable benchmark for device control and environment awareness, utilizing world distillation to evaluate agent performance across diverse tasks and devices.
赵波老师实验室.debug_abstract: Scaling device-control evaluation requires scaling both interactive worlds and the tasks agents must solve. We introduce SynthDCB, a benchmark for environment awareness and device control built through world distillation (WD). World distillation transforms knowledge of device behaviors, constraints, and environmental effects into modular executable components. A unified capability representation connects tool discovery, world execution, and task synthesis. SynthDCB instantiates Home, Car, and Phone with 114 device classes, 1,166 functions, and 95 events, supporting five task families with 32 subtypes. Explicit states and tool-call traces support task validation and agent evaluation. We evaluate 22 models on 2,560 test tasks; the best achieves 88.8% mean Pass@1. Construction experiments demonstrate token efficiency and expansion of task coverage. At the richest knowledge level, WD fully covers 22/23 properties, 19/29 functionalities, and 30/39 event requirements specified in a real RobotVacuum protocol. Furthermore, the 1,000 sampled tasks semantically cover 81.6% of the 854 reference instructions in the real-world corpus. SynthDCB connects an expanding space of real-to-sim executable capabilities to verifiable agent evaluation.

赵波老师实验室.title: DACA: Dual-Anchor Collaborative Agent for Zero-Shot 3D Visual Grounding
赵波老师实验室.authors_text: Jiaming Liu, Linghe Kong, Guixu Zhang, Huaxi Huang
赵波老师实验室.summary: The Dual-Anchor Collaborative Agent (DACA) enhances zero-shot 3D visual grounding by integrating semantic and geometric reasoning for improved accuracy and autonomous decision-making.
赵波老师实验室.debug_abstract: 3D visual grounding (3D-VG) is a task that bridges the natural language and 3D space, serving as a foundational capability for embodied intelligence and human-computer interaction. Although recent 3D-VG agents overcome the reliance on pre-processed 3D point clouds, they essentially employ a unidirectional, pipeline-style tool-calling architecture. This architecture separates semantic understanding from geometric reconstruction, leading to error accumulation and an inability to autonomously recover from failures. To address this flaw, this paper proposes the Dual-Anchor Collaborative Agent (DACA), which reinterprets 3D-VG as a semantic-geometric dual-anchor collaborative reasoning paradigm. DACA comprises two complementary specialized tools: the semantic anchor tool holds the visual semantic features of the target and achieves efficient target tracking via optical flow and VLM local verification; the geometric anchor tool holds the 3D spatial geometric features of the target and performs global spatial reasoning via voxelization and multi-keypoint projection. The two components exchange information bidirectionally via a standardized tool call protocol, autonomously deciding on the next perception-action step to form a closed-loop optimization. Experiments on the ScanRefer and Nr3D benchmarks demonstrate that zero-shot DACA achieves an overall Acc@0.25 of 73.6\% on ScanRefer and 70.4\% overall accuracy on Nr3D, far surpassing the latest zero-shot 3D-VG methods. The code and models are available at https://github.com/liujia99/DACA

赵波老师实验室.title: ECHO: In-Context Behavior foundation model for Humanoid Whole-Body Control
赵波老师实验室.authors_text: Xingyi Wang, Bin Li, Jiyuan Shi, Chenyun Zhang, Weiji Xie
赵波老师实验室.summary: ECHO is an in-context behavior foundation model that enhances humanoid control by adapting general skills to specific environments through structured dynamics representation and residual corrections.
赵波老师实验室.debug_abstract: Humanoid behavior foundation models (BFMs) acquire diverse skills through large-scale motion imitation and massively parallel reinforcement learning, yet broad behavioral capability does not ensure precise execution across physical conditions. Without distinguishing the underlying dynamics, policies may favor conservative compromises over environment-specific precision. We introduce ECHO, an in-context BFM that turns interaction experience into environment-specific control, separating general behavioral capability from dynamics-specific execution. Mixed and Annealed Sampling first establishes a behavior prior in a single pretraining stage by balancing targeted practice with broad motion coverage. Building on this prior, Context Representation and Residual Adaptation learns structured dynamics representations from interaction histories to guide residual corrections to the frozen prior, enabling adaptation without test-time parameter updates. Extensive experiments show that ECHO outperforms all baseline methods across diverse motions and physical conditions. Moreover, deployment on the Unitree G1 demonstrates whole-body teleoperation spanning extreme acrobatics and terrain interaction, alongside payload adaptation in manipulation and whole-body control. Page is available at https://mwondering.github.io/echo-bfm/

赵波老师实验室.title: MemFolder: Structure-Guided Memory Folding for Efficient Agent Memory Management
赵波老师实验室.authors_text: Xuyang Liu, Chenwen Lu, Junxi Wang, Siyu Ren, Xinying Lin
赵波老师实验室.summary: MemFolder introduces a structure-guided memory folding framework that efficiently reduces record count and context length in agent memory management, enhancing performance retention while minimizing storage costs.
赵波老师实验室.debug_abstract: Long-term agents accumulate large external memory stores as interactions unfold, increasing the costs of storage, retrieval, and response generation. Efficiency is constrained by two coupled factors: a growing record count increases retrieval overhead, while longer retrieved contexts increase prefill computation and decoding-time attention costs. Existing methods prune or consolidate records, but pruning can discard useful evidence, whereas consolidation may produce fewer yet longer retrieval units. We introduce MemFolder, a structure-guided memory folding framework that sequentially reduces record count and context length. The framework comprises two core components that share memory groups, using cross-record structure to guide both evidence consolidation and compact representation. RecordFolder grounds entity mentions, progressively selects representative yet complementary anchors, and combines semantic and entity affinity with temporal chaining to consolidate compatible records into fewer retrieval units. ContextFolder encodes the original records within these groups into compact text and uses verification feedback to revise encodings when key facts cannot be recovered. Experiments on the three text-based memory benchmarks LoCoMo, PersonaMem, and LongMemEval and the two multimodal benchmarks M3-Bench-web and M3-Bench-robot demonstrate the strong performance of our methods. Notably, on Mem0, RecordFolder retains 99.0% of the original average performance across the three text-based benchmarks with 50% fewer records, exceeding the strongest baseline by 1.9 percentage points in performance retention. Combined with ContextFolder, existing record compression methods further shorten their output records while retaining most of their performance.

赵波老师实验室.title: Bridging Time and Space: Decoupled Spatio-Temporal Alignment for Video Grounding
赵波老师实验室.authors_text: Xuezhen Tu, Jingyu Wu, Fangyu Kang, Qingpeng Nong, Kaijin Zhang
赵波老师实验室.summary: The paper presents Bridge-STG, an innovative framework that decouples spatio-temporal alignment for video grounding, enhancing performance by addressing token redundancy and semantic coherence.
赵波老师实验室.debug_abstract: Spatio-Temporal Video Grounding requires jointly localizing target objects across both temporal and spatial dimensions based on natural language queries, posing fundamental challenges for existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). We identify two core challenges: \textit{entangled spatio-temporal alignment}, arising from coupling two heterogeneous sub-tasks within the same autoregressive output space, and \textit{dual-domain visual token redundancy}, where target objects exhibit simultaneous temporal and spatial sparsity, rendering the overwhelming majority of visual tokens irrelevant to the grounding query. To address these, we propose \textbf{Bridge-STG}, an end-to-end framework that decouples temporal and spatial localization while maintaining semantic coherence. While decoupling is the natural solution to this entanglement, it risks creating a semantic gap between the temporal MLLM and the spatial decoder. Bridge-STG resolves this through two pivotal designs: the \textbf{Spatio-Temporal Semantic Bridging (STSB)} mechanism with Explicit Temporal Alignment (ETA) distills the MLLM's temporal reasoning context into enriched bridging queries as a robust semantic interface; and the \textbf{Query-Guided Spatial Localization (QGSL)} module leverages these queries to drive a purpose-built spatial decoder with multi-layer interactive queries and positive/negative frame sampling, jointly eliminating dual-domain visual token redundancy. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that Bridge-STG achieves state-of-the-art performance among MLLM-based methods. Bridge-STG improves average m\_vIoU from $26.4$ to $34.3$ on VidSTG and demonstrates strong cross-task transfer across various fine-grained video understanding tasks under a unified multi-task training regime.

赵波老师实验室.title: Evo-DexBench: Benchmarking Generalization across Related Tasks for Dexterous Manipulation
赵波老师实验室.authors_text: Bing Cheng, Yiran Mao, Zewei Ye, Yifan Jin, Xinyi Chen
赵波老师实验室.summary: Evo-DexBench introduces a controlled benchmark for evaluating dexterous manipulation policies' ability to generalize knowledge transfer across related tasks with limited demonstrations.
赵波老师实验室.debug_abstract: General-purpose dexterous manipulation requires policies to transfer knowledge from related tasks to new tasks with only a few target demonstrations. Existing benchmarks often provide too many target demonstrations and leave the differences between source and target tasks uncontrolled. As a result, they cannot clearly distinguish knowledge transfer from task memorization. Our key insight is the Core-Gen principle. Core tasks are related tasks that share a functional interaction and provide source knowledge, while a Gen task is a novel target within the same functional family that has only a few demonstrations. This setup tests whether a policy can reuse functional interaction knowledge. Based on this principle, we propose Evo-DexBench, which controls both source-task relatedness and target-task exposure. It comprises 30 tasks in six functional families, three everyday layouts per task, and 1,248 multimodal demonstrations collected via VR teleoperation with simulated Shadow Hands equipped with 123 taxels. We first compare few-shot adaptation strategies and find that joint Core + Gen training makes the most effective use of Core knowledge. Under this setting, we evaluate six representative policies. The best-performing policy, $π_{0.5}$, achieves a mean success rate of only 24.4%, revealing the limitations of existing methods in transferring functional interaction knowledge. Further analysis shows that on the tested Gen targets, functionally matched Core data yields larger success-rate gains than mismatched data, and that with matched Core data, 8 Gen demonstrations reach the performance of training on 16--32 Gen demonstrations alone. These results indicate that Evo-DexBench separates knowledge transfer from task memorization under controlled conditions and effectively evaluates the generalization of dexterous manipulation policies across related tasks.

赵波老师实验室.title: Dune: A Zeroth-Order Optimizer with Time-Conditioned Historical Error Regression for VLA Test-Time Adaptation
赵波老师实验室.authors_text: Chengyang Dong, Ze Chen, Kai Ye, Chutian Wang, Heng Xu
赵波老师实验室.summary: Dune is a novel zeroth-order optimizer that enhances test-time adaptation for VLA models by integrating historical error prediction to reduce estimation variance and improve stability.
赵波老师实验室.debug_abstract: Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) enables Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models to handle distribution shifts during deployment without source-domain retraining. However, backpropagation-based adaptation incurs heavy memory overhead on resource-constrained robots, whereas zeroth-order (ZO) methods suffer from high estimation variance under limited perturbation budgets. We observe that while ZO estimation enables low-memory adaptation with rapid initial gains, it often stalls or degrades over long-horizon updates due to noisy gradient estimates. To address these limitations, we propose Dune, a zeroth-order optimizer that stabilizes long-horizon adaptation by coupling online historical error prediction with current perturbation observations. Specifically, Dune learns a lightweight, time-conditioned error predictor from past optimization dynamics and fuses its predictions with instantaneous ZO estimates, achieving effective variance reduction without backpropagation or extra forward passes. Additionally, we theoretically characterize how estimation variance restricts convergence in high-dimensional, small-population regimes, motivating the use of historical statistics. Extensive experiments on LIBERO and real-world robots demonstrate that Dune achieves superior success rates under a low memory footprint, with ablations confirming improved closed-loop stability and post-disturbance recovery.

赵波老师实验室.title: Think Before You Distill: Generalization Recovery in Quantized VLAs via Selective Policy Distillation
赵波老师实验室.authors_text: Shen Ruan, Wenchang Gao, Jin Wang, Siao Liu, Zhaxizhuoma
赵波老师实验室.summary: The paper introduces PIVOT-Q, a selective policy distillation framework that enhances robustness in quantized variable-length action policies by targeting vulnerable states during environmental disturbances.
赵波老师实验室.debug_abstract: Post-training quantization has been shown to preserve VLA performance under standard evaluation conditions, but whether it preserves the full-precision model's robustness and generalization remains underexplored. In this study, we systematically study the robustness and generalization of post-quantized VLA policies under environmental disturbances. Empirical results show that quantized policies can become fragile to subtle environmental variations despite retaining comparable in-distribution performance. We further observe that action discrepancies are concentrated in a small subset of the rollout states, while teacher guidance has opposite effects depending on discrepancy: it improves performance at high-discrepancy states but can degrade it at low-discrepancy states. These findings reveal that effective post-quantization recovery requires selective intervention on vulnerable states rather than globally distilling the student. We therefore propose Policy-Induced Vulnerability-Oriented Tuning (PIVOT-Q), a vulnerability-aware On-Policy Distillation (OPD) framework that selectively corrects vulnerable states encountered during quantized-student rollouts using the frozen full-precision policy as a teacher. PIVOT-Q identifies vulnerable states using discounted accumulated discrepancies over a short horizon, applies phase-balanced sparse supervision, and uses a Behavioral Anchor to prevent unintended changes. Experiments under seven LIBERO-Plus environmental variations demonstrate consistent recovery across multiple VLA backbones and quantization methods. Notably, PIVOT-Q outperforms full-state distillation with smaller variance across evaluated settings while using only 20\% of its state-level distillation budget. Our code is available at https://github.com/ruanruan-andy/PIVOT-Q.

赵波老师实验室.title: GTI: Grounding Task Intent Throughout Long-Horizon VLA Manipulation
赵波老师实验室.authors_text: Tianqi Gong, Haochen Niu, Yusheng Zhao, Lantao Zhang, Haoyu Liu
赵波老师实验室.summary: GTI enhances long-horizon VLA manipulation by grounding task intent through phase-specific visual targets and local recovery mechanisms, significantly improving execution success rates.
赵波老师实验室.debug_abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models generate local actions from visual observations, language, and robot state, but long-horizon manipulation requires the global task intent to remain grounded in the currently executable context. We propose GTI (Grounding Task Intent), which uses the current observation and execution history to localize the active subtask and its execution phase. For the same local subtask, GTI generates two phase-dependent visual targets: an interaction/contact state and a local completion state. The local language instruction and the corresponding phase-specific visual target jointly condition the VLA, specifying both what to do now and what state should be reached at the current phase. During execution, anomaly monitoring and local recovery re-establish an intent-consistent execution context through rollback, re-observation, and phase re-evaluation after persistent deviation. We evaluate GTI on RoboCasa365, VLA-Arena Horizon-Long, and real-world PiPER tasks. Relative to matched Global-FT baselines, GR00T success on seen composite RoboCasa365 tasks increases from 14.6%/12.1% to 31.8%/20.4% under ID/OOD evaluation. On VLA-Arena, GTI+$π_{0.5}$ reaches 47.6% overall success versus 45.2% for an adapted ForeAct baseline, with gains of 5.2/6.0 percentage points on the harder L1/L2 tasks. In the three real-robot task experiments, mean full-task success increases from 21.7% to 59.2%. The results indicate that persistent semantic intent localization and phase-conditioned visual grounding improve multi-stage execution, while failure-triggered local recovery provides additional deployment-time support.

赵波老师实验室.title: 3D GameDev Arena: Benchmarking Coding Agents That Plan, Build, and Playtest extreme Long-Horizon Browser Games
赵波老师实验室.authors_text: Bizhe Bai, Jiliang Jian, Yuqing Yan, Tao Chen, Ying Wen
赵波老师实验室.summary: The 3D GameDev Arena introduces a benchmark for coding agents to develop complex 3D games from scratch, highlighting challenges in player enjoyment and game quality assessment.
赵波老师实验室.debug_abstract: Coding agents now resolve repository issues and generate compact playable games, but whether they can build a large 3D game from scratch remains open. Such games tightly couple mechanics, scenes, assets, and interaction logic, and their quality rests on player enjoyment, which existing benchmarks rarely assess. Thus, we introduce 3D GameDev Arena, a first extreme long-horizon benchmark of 108 from-scratch game-development tasks across 14 genres. Given only a text specification and UI/UX reference images, a fully automated plan--implement--test--repair pipeline builds each task into a self-contained browser game. Runs average $\sim$1,000 LLM calls ; the longest uses 14,407 calls, 2.13B tokens, and 608 assets. Evaluation spans (1) objective code-level functional acceptance against the game specification, (2) agent-based QA and playtesting of 3D presentation and playability, and (3) blind pairwise Bradley-Terry human preference in a public arena. The preliminary findings indicate that long-horizon 3D game development remains far from solved, and code-level correctness alone does not dictate player preference. The public arena is hosted online.

赵波老师实验室.title: CoNav-UAV: Cooperative Dual-Altitude Aerial Navigation via Stackelberg Learning
赵波老师实验室.authors_text: Junru Song, Wenhao Zhang, Yang Yang, Xuekai Qiu, Feifei Wang
赵波老师实验室.summary: CoNav-UAV introduces a Stackelberg game framework for cooperative dual-altitude UAV navigation, enhancing target-oriented aerial VLN through mutual adaptation and onboard sensing, significantly improving performance.
赵波老师实验室.debug_abstract: Aerial search missions often require an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) to locate a target from only a brief description of its appearance and surroundings, a task known as target-oriented aerial vision-and-language navigation (VLN). The task demands city-scale exploration and grounding as well as collision-free close-range approach, two interleaved processes that are difficult to reconcile within a single agent. Most existing methods adapt the ground VLN paradigm to a single UAV and rely on external assistance to compensate for its inefficiency. A recent attempt deploys two UAVs at complementary altitudes but still depends on privileged sensing and trains the two agents independently, precluding any mutual adaptation. We propose CoNav-UAV, which models the task as a Stackelberg game between a high-altitude leader and a low-altitude follower to capture their sequential decisions and asymmetric observations and utilities, with both agents using only onboard sensing. We introduce Iterative Stackelberg Learning, which tailors optimization to each agent's role: the leader's high-level vision-language reasoning builds on pretrained capabilities and is refined through memory-based in-context learning, while the follower's precise motion control is fine-tuned through DAgger-style expert distillation. Alternating the two updates lets each agent continually adapt to the other's evolving behavior. CoNav-UAV outperforms single- and dual-agent baselines across three high-fidelity urban scenes from the AerialVLN benchmark. It improves success rate by up to 30.8 points on the learning scene and by up to 9.0 points under cross-scene transfer, where the leader reuses its learned memory and the follower is adapted with 2.6-3.7 times less target-scene data. Extensive ablations confirm the contributions of key components and the benefit of mutual adaptation, with consistent gains across VLM backbones.

赵波老师实验室.title: RoboMorpher: Scaling Robot Morphology Representations for Cross-Embodiment Action Prediction
赵波老师实验室.authors_text: Wenwei Lin, Yan Qin, Weiliang Deng, Zixuan Li, Kaixuan Wang
赵波老师实验室.summary: RoboMorpher enhances cross-embodiment action prediction by integrating morphology-conditioned action tokenization and scalable kinematic supervision, outperforming traditional joint-space control methods.
赵波老师实验室.debug_abstract: Learning shared action representations is central to cross-embodiment manipulation. However, identical joint values can produce different spatial configurations across robots, limiting representations learned from joint values alone. We introduce RoboMorpher, a morphology-conditioned action tokenizer that jointly reconstructs joint angles and link poses to associate control coordinates with their kinematic effects. MorphGen supplies scalable kinematic supervision by generating serial-arm descriptions from survey-derived geometric priors. We pretrain RoboMorpher on 40 million morphology-state pairs and integrate the frozen tokenizer into a vision-language-action policy for discrete prediction and continuous refinement. We also introduce EmbodiBench, a ten-task benchmark with 30 generated URDFs per task. With downstream URDFs excluded from tokenizer pretraining, the policy achieves 56.40% success on RoboTwin 2.0 and 23.27% on EmbodiBench, exceeding continuous joint-space control by 9.73 and 15.34 percentage points. Removing link-pose supervision reduces EmbodiBench success by 17.94 percentage points, supporting morphology-aware geometric supervision for joint-action representation learning.

赵波老师实验室.title: Baking Gaussian Splatting into Diffusion Denoiser for Fast and Scalable Single-stage Image-to-3D Generation and Reconstruction
赵波老师实验室.authors_text: Yuanhao Cai, He Zhang, Kai Zhang, Yixun Liang, Mengwei Ren
赵波老师实验室.summary: The paper introduces DiffusionGS, a single-stage 3D diffusion model that generates consistent 3D Gaussian point clouds from single views, outperforming existing methods in speed and quality.
赵波老师实验室.debug_abstract: Existing feedforward image-to-3D methods mainly rely on 2D multi-view diffusion models that cannot guarantee 3D consistency. These methods easily collapse when changing the prompt view direction and mainly handle object-centric cases. In this paper, we propose a novel single-stage 3D diffusion model, DiffusionGS, for object generation and scene reconstruction from a single view. DiffusionGS directly outputs 3D Gaussian point clouds at each timestep to enforce view consistency and allow the model to generate robustly given prompt views of any directions, beyond object-centric inputs. Plus, to improve the capability and generality of DiffusionGS, we scale up 3D training data by developing a scene-object mixed training strategy. Experiments show that DiffusionGS yields improvements of 2.20 dB/23.25 and 1.34 dB/19.16 in PSNR/FID for objects and scenes than the state-of-the-art methods, without depth estimator. Plus, our method enjoys over 5$\times$ faster speed ($\sim$6s on an A100 GPU). Our Project page at https://caiyuanhao1998.github.io/project/DiffusionGS/ shows the video and interactive results. The code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/caiyuanhao1998/Open-DiffusionGS . An online Gradio demo with high-quality mesh exportation is available at https://huggingface.co/spaces/CaiYuanhao/DiffusionGS-Object

赵波老师实验室.title: Where Is the Cost of Third-Party API Routers in Agentic Software Development?
赵波老师实验室.authors_text: Donghao Fu, Jingxin Li, Xue Jiang, Yihong Dong
赵波老师实验室.summary: This study investigates the impact of third-party API routers on coding agents, revealing significant vulnerabilities in client-side safeguards against router-side interventions.
赵波老师实验室.debug_abstract: Third-party API routers have become a common layer that unifies access across increasingly diverse LLM providers. In coding-agent workflows, high-autonomy operation is widely adopted because it reduces interaction overhead. As a result, a third-party API router, which sits between the agent and the upstream provider, inevitably occupies the trusted path. It can inspect and modify every request and response, yet no mechanism verifies alignment between the provider's output and the repository-level actions ultimately executed by the agent. Consequently, client-side permission mechanisms may become ineffective in practice. Whether this control gap produces real, hard-to-detect effects on software development tasks remains empirically unmeasured. In this paper, we conduct an empirical study of router-side injection in coding agents, examining four intervention levels of increasing subtlety: Response Substitution (L1), Response Append (L2), LLM-Polished Injection (L3), and LLM-Polished with Distribution Alignment Injection (L4). Moreover, we develop SIDEL, a framework for trace recording, replay, injection, and defense evaluation, with a curated dataset of 400 samples. We evaluate four representative coding agents, and further evaluate whitelist-based execution control and LLM review. Router-side intervention substantially alters repository-level actions and remains difficult for existing client-side safeguards to detect. Without additional mitigations, all evaluated agents achieved a defense success rate of 0 percent across all injection levels. Client-side mitigations and reactive reviews improve resistance but do not fully restore end-to-end control, motivating provider-side output-integrity guarantees. Our code is available at https://github.com/Riyasushin/SIDEL.

赵波老师实验室.title: TOMAS: Topology-Aware Operation Modeling and Adaptive Staging for Egocentric Hand Forecasting
赵波老师实验室.authors_text: Guanzhong Sun, Junyi Ma, Yuxuan Wu, Erhang Zhang, Chenyang Xu
赵波老师实验室.summary: TOMAS introduces a topology-aware framework for egocentric hand forecasting, enhancing prediction accuracy by linking hand movements to object semantics and adaptive staging.
赵波老师实验室.debug_abstract: Forecasting future hand movements from egocentric videos plays an important role in understanding human intentions and hand-object interactions. However, different manipulation intentions can lead to substantially different hand trajectories even when interacting with the same object. Existing methods have not sufficiently explored the intrinsic relationships between articulated hand movements and object semantics to capture such operation-dependent motion patterns. Therefore, we propose TOMAS, a topology-aware operation modeling and adaptive staging framework for egocentric hand forecasting. Specifically, we develop a topology-aware hand-object reasoning mechanism that associates hand skeletal structures and articulation dynamics with object semantics and spatial relationships to jointly infer potential interaction targets and latent manipulation operations. The resulting object-operation representations provide interaction conditions for future hand trajectory prediction, with supervision adapted to the annotations available in each dataset. Furthermore, we introduce an adaptive staging mechanism that organizes future hand movements into ordered latent stages with learnable temporal boundaries. Stage-specific geometric subgoals are then incorporated to guide trajectory refinement according to the underlying manipulation patterns. Experimental results on multiple publicly available benchmarks demonstrate that TOMAS achieves state-of-the-art performance in multi-dimensional and multi-target hand motion forecasting.

赵波老师实验室.title: SemPhys: Semantic-Physical Co-Learning for Humanoid Motion Generation via Differentiable World Models
赵波老师实验室.authors_text: Zejian Kang, Yeqiang Wang, Zekai Chen, Boyang Shen, Mingyu Ma
赵波老师实验室.summary: SemPhys introduces a framework for humanoid motion generation that uses semantic feedback from simulated executions to enhance instruction accuracy during human-robot collaboration.
赵波老师实验室.debug_abstract: In human-robot collaboration, natural language lets people direct a humanoid's whole-body movements without programming joint trajectories. A common approach generates a kinematic reference from an instruction and relies on a tracking controller to execute it. However, as the controller maintains balance under contact constraints, the executed motion can depart from the reference in ways that change the action it conveys. Our central insight is that semantic alignment must be evaluated directly on the complete motion the robot physically executes. Building on this insight, we introduce \textbf{SemPhys}, a framework that trains motion generators using semantic feedback from simulated executions. A differentiable world model and a fixed tracking controller predict a short segment of a recorded execution. SemPhys inserts this prediction at its original position, scores the complete trajectory against the instruction, and backpropagates through the predicted segment. A paired anchoring loss stabilizes adaptation by keeping each generated reference close to its counterpart from the initial generator. On BONES-SEED, SemPhys largely preserves instruction retrieval accuracy from reference to execution and achieves the highest retrieval accuracy on executed motions among the evaluated methods.

赵波老师实验室.title: StrideWorld: Benchmarking Scene Rigidity and Action Consistency in Interactive Video World Model
赵波老师实验室.authors_text: Chuang Wang, Rui Nie, Jie Song, Junyuan Gao, Jiahe Song
赵波老师实验室.summary: StrideWorld introduces a benchmark for evaluating scene rigidity and action consistency in interactive video world models, using fixed references to measure performance against ground-truth geometry and stride.
赵波老师实验室.debug_abstract: Interactive video world models turn user commands into the exploration of a generated scene, which requires the scene to keep its 3D structure as the camera moves and each action to keep a stable effect. Existing benchmarks mostly evaluate these properties against references fitted to the video under test, either a scene reconstructed from its own frames or a camera trajectory aligned to the command path with a free scale. Such references can absorb gradual scene deformation and changes in pace and route length, so these errors can pass undetected. We therefore introduce StrideWorld, a benchmark whose references are fixed before the motion they judge. It evaluates scene rigidity against the ground-truth geometry of the start view, and action consistency against the stride of each action, the camera motion of one command. The stride is measured on the model's first steps and then used to test the steps that follow, so each model is judged only against its own steps. Its measurements are validated on rendered videos with known camera motion, and its scores agree with human judgments. Across \nvideos{} videos generated by \nmodels{} open models from $140$ start views, all models but one deform their scenes as the camera moves, with offsets up to $7.3$ times those of a rigid rendering along the same camera path. Most models keep a steady pace when a single action is held. Along composed routes, several models often stall, and most completed routes end away from the positions predicted by each model's own strides. Only the two models that scale commands by the estimated scene depth bring most routes close to these positions. Fine-tuning two models on a few rendered clips removes most of their mid-route stalls. Code, data, and a leaderboard are publicly available at https://github.com/chuangwang123/strideworld.

赵波老师实验室.title: SCR: Detecting Backdoor-Poisoned Samples through Clean-Reference Residuals
赵波老师实验室.authors_text: Yi Yang, Jinyang Huang, Feng-Qi Cui, Yu-Tong Guo, Sirui Zhao
赵波老师实验室.summary: The SCR method effectively detects backdoor-poisoned samples in deep neural networks by leveraging clean-reference residuals, achieving over 99.5% true positive rates across multiple datasets.
赵波老师实验室.debug_abstract: Deep neural networks are vulnerable to backdoor attacks, in which adversaries manipulate model predictions by injecting poisoned samples into training data. Detecting these samples remains challenging because legitimate semantic variation can obscure poisoning-related signals in learned representations. Consequently, class-level statistics used by existing detectors may flag benign feature deviations while overlooking poisoned samples that blend into the class distribution. In this paper, we propose Semantic Counterfactual Residualization (SCR), which uses a small set of clean reference samples to account for benign variation through sample-specific feature reconstruction. SCR identifies poisoned samples by detecting coherent deviations from these clean baselines, without requiring prior knowledge of the attacks. We evaluate SCR through experiments covering twelve dirty-label and clean-label attacks across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet. With a small clean-reference set, SCR achieves attack-averaged true positive rates above 99.5\% and false positive rates below 2\% on each dataset, outperforming eight representative detection baselines in macro-TPR.

赵波老师实验室.title: BaseRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement of a Base Vision-Language Model via Training-Free Harness Internalization
赵波老师实验室.authors_text: Mingda Zhang, Yuanhao Dong, Qiang Huang, Rui Qian, Yanjin Li
赵波老师实验室.summary: BaseRSI introduces a novel recursive self-improvement method for vision-language models, enabling them to autonomously enhance their performance through training-free internalization of harness improvements.
赵波老师实验室.debug_abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is moving from the harness of prompts and tools around a base model toward the model itself. However, existing RSI still faces key challenges, including harness-bound gains that stay outside the base model, black-box supervision that reads only the model's outputs, and imprecise edits whose site and strength are fixed in advance. To address these challenges, we propose BaseRSI, a new paradigm of Recursive Harness Internalization: the base model improves its harness, then writes what the harness adds into its own weights through training-free edits, round after round on its own responses. To support this paradigm, we introduce ReGap, a mechanism that supervises every transformer block with the high-dimensional activation difference that the harness makes at that block alone, and updates the block's weights along this signal in a low-dimensional subspace. Building on this mechanism, we further propose ReKey, an algorithm that writes this signal by regression into a few key-value neurons of every block, and measures the site and strength of each edit on the model's own responses. Moreover, the base model fills every role of this recursion with forward passes alone, and its edits, written at different sites, compose in one checkpoint without refitting. Experimental results on ten visual reasoning benchmarks show that BaseRSI consistently improves a base vision-language model both in distribution and on held-out benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/beita6969/BaseRSI.

赵波老师实验室.title: Disagree to Prune: Reallocating Visual Tokens Where a Small VLM Dissents
赵波老师实验室.authors_text: Yanchao Li, Jiaqing Xie, Ben Gao, Yusu Zhang, Beilun Wang
赵波老师实验室.summary: The paper introduces PRUDENT, a method that reallocates visual tokens in vision-language models by re-answering questions where a small VLM disagrees, outperforming existing pruning techniques.
赵波老师实验室.debug_abstract: Visual token pruning speeds up large vision-language models (VLMs) by keeping only a part of their visual tokens. Most existing methods improve the ranking of the tokens and then answer every question once with the same budget. With strong rankings, pruning hurts only a few questions, and signals computed on the kept tokens see little of what it removed. We find that, on most of these questions, a small VLM given the full image disagrees with the pruned answer, since it still sees the missing evidence. We propose PRUDENT, which first answers with about half the budget and spends the saved tokens on re-answering the disagreeing questions at twice the budget. We show when such re-answering pays and why the small VLM should read the full image. On 18 benchmarks, PRUDENT outperforms eight existing pruning methods at the same average budget of visual tokens. Its lead widens as the budget tightens, and holds across five InternVL sizes. PRUDENT also has the highest average in two more model families. The disagreement of the small VLM flags most pruning failures of all eight methods, and re-answering on it also improves the two strongest with their own rankings. Other checkers give similar gains, and the extra tokens go where the first pass hurts the answer.
