Existing mechanistic interpretability approaches often rely on superficial text-pattern co-occurrences or capture only short-term effects, struggling to trace the long-horizon, outcome-driven influence of internal components such as neurons or sparse features in multi-step reasoning.In this paper, we introduce Integrated Policy Gradient (IPG), a novel, training-free framework that brings policy-based attribution into mechanistic interpretability for LLM reasoning. Grounded in \textit{outcome-oriented} and \textit{sequential-influence-aware} principles, it backpropagates outcome-level, non-differentiable behavioral signals (e.g., reasoning outcome correctness) through entire inference trajectories, utilizing path integration to isolate outcome-relevant mediators at component level for reliable attribution. This provides a linear approximation of Causal Mediation Analysis (CMA) in reasoning. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that \method achieves precise localization and reveals mechanistic insights by identifying sparse, concentrated subsets of internal components associated with specific reasoning behaviors. Our method also enables modulation of reasoning capabilities, offering a powerful and reliable framework for understanding LLM reasoning. The project page is at https://foundation-model-research.github.io/IPG .

上海科技大学.title: RoboScope Kit: Unified Interfaces for Fast and Scalable Embodied-AI Evaluation
上海科技大学.authors_text: Deng-Ke Wu, Yifan Jin, Yida Yang, Lei Qian, Zhaoye Zhou
上海科技大学.summary: The RoboScope Kit enhances embodied-AI evaluation speed and scalability by unifying interfaces and optimizing resource allocation, achieving up to 25 times faster performance than traditional methods.
上海科技大学.debug_abstract: Simulation benchmarks are the standard way to compare robot policies, but each benchmark brings its own evaluator, observation layout, and action convention, and evaluation is slow: 500 RoboTwin Easy episodes with one simulator and one model on one GPU take 359.7 minutes. Profiling the official StarVLA evaluator shows that simulation occupies CPU cores while the GPU averages 14.3% utilization. RoboScope Kit wraps each model once in a Python class called a Policy, and each benchmark once in an adapter around the benchmark's own evaluator, so the benchmark's rules and scoring stay unchanged. Scheduling runs simulator workers and Policy replicas as separate pools, sizes both from measured probes, and shards work deterministically across GPU instances; runtime optimization renders only the observations an action-chunk Policy reads. Adapters cover six benchmark families. On LIBERO-Long with a StarVLA checkpoint on one 48 GiB RTX 4090, the concurrency search selects twelve simulator workers sharing three Policy replicas, which evaluate 500 episodes 4.45$\times$ faster than the official StarVLA evaluation with equivalent success rates, 2.78$\times$ faster than RLinf, and 1.52$\times$ faster than vla-eval at its tuned configuration. With CUDA MPS, which lets the replicas run their kernels concurrently, the search selects sixteen workers sharing four replicas, 6.16$\times$ faster than StarVLA, 3.85$\times$ faster than RLinf, and 2.10$\times$ faster than vla-eval. On RoboTwin Easy, four GPUs with chunk-boundary observation complete the 500 episodes in 14.4 minutes, 25.04$\times$ faster than the single-GPU baseline, with identical success outcomes and terminal steps.

上海科技大学.title: GazeVLA: Learning Human Intention for Robotic Manipulation
上海科技大学.authors_text: Chengyang Li, Kaiyi Xiong, Yuan Xu, Lei Qian, Yizhou Wang
上海科技大学.summary: GazeVLA leverages human gaze to model intentions for robotic manipulation, enhancing learning from demonstrations and improving task execution across diverse embodiments.
上海科技大学.debug_abstract: Embodied foundation models have significantly propelled the advancement of artificial general intelligence, yet they rely heavily on large-scale data. Recent studies identify human behavior as one of the most scalable sources for fostering robotic physical intelligence. However, the inherent embodiment gap remains a fundamental challenge for effective human-to-robot learning. In this work, we model human intention to enable efficient learning from human demonstrations. Among human behavioral cues, gaze simultaneously encodes high-level task semantics and exhibits a synergistic coupling with low-level action. By modeling intention through gaze, we derive a mid-level representation that facilitates cross-embodiment knowledge transfer. We demonstrate that robots can internalize human intentions to enhance manipulation, even without robotic intention annotations. To capture the synergy between intention and action, we adopt a Chain-of-Thought reasoning paradigm during inference. Our approach enables the execution of long-horizon and fine-grained tasks across diverse embodiments. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms baseline approaches and generalizes to unseen settings. Project page: https://gazevla.github.io .

上海科技大学.title: HaltNav: Reactive Visual Halting over Lightweight Topological Priors for Robust Vision-Language Navigation
上海科技大学.authors_text: Zihui Yu, Pingcong Li, Bichi Zhang, Sören Schwertfeger
上海科技大学.summary: HaltNav integrates lightweight topological maps with reactive visual halting to enhance robustness in vision-language navigation by enabling adaptive local exploration and replanning.
上海科技大学.debug_abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) is shifting from rigid, step-by-step instruction following toward open-vocabulary, goal-oriented autonomy. Achieving this transition without exhaustive routing prompts requires agents to leverage structural priors. While prior work often assumes computationally heavy 2D/3D metric maps, we instead exploit a lightweight, text-based osmAG (OpenStreetMap Area Graph), a floorplan-level topological representation that is easy to obtain and maintain. However, global planning over a prior map alone is brittle in real-world deployments, where local connectivity can change (e.g., closed doors or crowded passages), leading to execution-time failures. To address this gap, we propose a hierarchical navigation framework HaltNav that couples the robust global planning of osmAG with the local exploration and instruction-grounding capability of VLN. Our approach features an MLLM-based brain module, which is capable of high-level task grounding and obstruction awareness. Conditioned on osmAG, the brain converts the global route into a sequence of localized execution snippets, providing the VLN executor with prior-grounded, goal-centric sub-instructions. Meanwhile, it detects local anomalies via a mechanism we term Reactive Visual Halting (RVH), which interrupts the local control loop, updates osmAG by invalidating the corresponding topology, and triggers replanning to orchestrate a viable detour. To train this halting capability efficiently, we introduce a data synthesis pipeline that leverages generative models to inject realistic obstacles into otherwise navigable scenes, substantially enriching hard negative samples. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our hierarchical framework outperforms several baseline methods without tedious language instructions, and significantly improves robustness for long-horizon vision-language navigation under environmental changes.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Infer3D: Inverse Generative Modeling Enables Robust 3D Reconstruction
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Amani Kiruga, Mark Hamilton, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, William T. Freeman, Vincent Sitzmann
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: Infer3D introduces an inverse generative modeling approach for robust 3D reconstruction, enhancing out-of-distribution accuracy by leveraging latent variable recovery and adaptive inference strategies.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Humans can understand the 3D structure of scenes even from highly unfamiliar or extreme viewpoints. Cognitive science suggests this generalization stems from a top-down generative inference strategy. In contrast, state-of-the-art 3D reconstruction neural networks typically rely on amortized, feedforward inference. While fast, this pattern-matching approach degrades when faced with out-of-distribution (OOD) scene conditions unseen during training. Inspired by the generative nature of human vision, we propose Infer3D, an inverse generative modeling framework that recovers the latent variables of a generative model to best match the monocular input. To prevent degenerate flat outputs, we couple the generative image prior with a frozen 3D lifting network that constrains the optimization space to a valid, multi-view-consistent 3D manifold. Across a variety of controlled synthetic and real-world tasks, Infer3D demonstrates superior OOD reconstruction accuracy compared to feedforward networks trained on equal or larger datasets. Furthermore, mirroring how human perception requires more time to process confusing stimuli, we introduce an adaptive inference strategy that expends more test-time compute on ambiguous OOD examples while efficiently routing in-distribution inputs. Project website: https://amanikiruga.github.io/infer3d-site/

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Do Deep Stereo Models Learn Shape Priors?
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Linbo Tang, Aneel Damaraju, Todd Zickler
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: The study reveals that deep stereo models struggle with boundary localization under weak cues, while a new generative model improves accuracy by integrating disparity and distance fields.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Localizing object boundaries is important for embodied visual systems, since small boundary errors can change the inferred geometry of physical surfaces. We study whether deep stereo models produce boundaries consistent with simple shape priors when local image and disparity cues are weak. We create a synthetic stereo dataset consisting of objects drawn from a highly constrained family of shapes, with randomized depth, slant, color and texture. Despite the simplicity of this shape space, we find that several state-of-the-art stereo models retain systematic boundary errors, even when finetuned or trained from scratch on the dataset. We then introduce a simple generative stereo model that jointly predicts disparity and a distance field representing object boundaries. The model improves boundary localization and produces contours that adhere more closely to the underlying shape space. These results expose limitations in the boundary predictions of current stereo architectures when local evidence is weak, and motivate further study of whether generative models can better combine regional grouping evidence with global geometric structure.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: EgoJev: Finding Evidence in Egocentric Video by Reading VLM Decisions
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Chunggi Lee, Hanspeter Pfister
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: EgoJev enhances evidence retrieval in egocentric videos by leveraging a vision-language model to select key frames, improving accuracy significantly without additional training.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Questions about long egocentric video often depend on one brief moment, such as the second a hand puts an object down. A vision-language model (VLM) that sees a few evenly spaced frames usually misses it. Training-free methods rank frames with a separate image-text model or ask the VLM to write a time. In a controlled test, the VLM itself locates the moment better when it chooses among labeled frames, and we read this choice from its output distribution. With the same candidates, this choice lands on the evidence more often than image-text scores or a written time span, and it compares all candidates in one decision. Based on this finding, we propose EgoJev, a training-free frame selector for wearable assistants. EgoJev reads where the evidence is from labeled thumbnails and looks again at the windows it points to. It places its few answer frames at the quantiles of the resulting distribution. One frozen VLM selects, answers and returns the evidence time, with no second model. A wearable device can encode its coarse thumbnails while it records. With Qwen3.5-4B and 8 answer frames, EgoJev raises QAEgo4D accuracy from 51.2% with uniform sampling to 62.0%, and it outperforms recent training-free frame selectors on QAEgo4D and MyEgo. A single-level version runs on a Mac and an iPhone.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: T-WLA: Bridging Slow Vision and Fast Touch with a World-Language-Action Model
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Kaichen Zhou, Yuzhen Chen, Hannah Yao, Chonghe Jiang, Rao Fu
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: T-WLA integrates visual memory with tactile feedback to enhance contact-rich manipulation, achieving significant improvements in motion prediction and task success rates.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: In contact-rich manipulation, contact conditions can change before a visual policy updates its action plan. Recomputing the plan through the visual policy adds latency, while tactile feedback alone does not specify how the ongoing motion should be revised for the task. We introduce T-WLA, a world-language-action architecture that uses shared visual memory to guide both action generation and tactile correction. At each visual update, the visual branch integrates the current image, task instruction, and retrieved history into a visual memory that conditions base-action generation. The same memory is cached for a lightweight tactile editor, which combines it with the active action chunk and incoming touch to predict residual corrections to unexecuted actions without rerunning the visual branch. Future-image and future-pressure prediction provide training-only supervision, encouraging the visual memory and tactile features to capture interaction dynamics relevant to action generation and correction. We evaluate T-WLA on tactile-conditioned hand-motion prediction using EgoTouch and Tachin, and on four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks. On EgoTouch, T-WLA reduces finger-joint MPJPE by 30% relative to the strongest evaluated baseline. Across four real-robot tasks, T-WLA achieves 51.0% mean success versus 23.0% for the baseline, a gain of 28.0 percentage points. Videos and code are available at https://t-wla.github.io/.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: ImpedanceMimic: Learned Impedance as Action Space for Force-Accurate Motion Imitation
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Matthias Jammot, Pembe Gizem Özdil
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: ImpedanceMimic leverages reinforcement learning to optimize joint stiffness and damping for improved motion imitation, achieving superior force and motion fidelity across diverse activities and subjects.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Recovering the forces behind a motion is ill-posed: different controllers can reproduce the same movement while generating different contact forces. Physics-based motion imitation resolves this ambiguity through simulation, but relies on fixed-gain proportional-derivative (PD) control. We show that fixed gains impose a trade-off between motion and force tracking, as contact and swing place conflicting demands on joint stiffness and damping. We introduce ImpedanceMimic, a reinforcement-learning policy that modulates per-joint stiffness, damping, and position setpoints from motion and force measurements, but requires only motion at inference. Across 129 participants and six activities, ImpedanceMimic outperforms matched fixed-gain PD under every integration scheme, direct-torque, muscle-actuated and existing imitation controllers in kinematic and force fidelity, approaching a dedicated motion-to-force regressor. By expressing gains as multiples of inertia-scaled priors, a single policy controls subject-specific biomechanical models without explicit anthropometric input and transfers zero-shot to unseen humans and a humanoid robot. The learned impedance forms a low-dimensional representation of motor state, shared across bodies, that generalizes to withheld activities: stiffness scales with load, and damping anticipates unloading.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Reins: Frontier Multimodal Models Driving Real Robot Arms on Long-Horizon Tasks, Zero-Shot
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Pengfei Ye, Zhiyang Dou, Yuxiang Ma, Haonan Chen, Heng Yang
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: Reins enables frontier multimodal models to effectively control dual-arm robots in long-horizon tasks using 3D perception and continuous scene tracking, achieving 88% success.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Frontier models such as GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 can now plan and call tools, yet they still struggle to drive real robots through long-horizon, contact-rich manipulation, blind while the arm moves and while they think. We present Reins, a harness in which an off-the-shelf model operates a dual-arm robot with 3D perception tools and atomic actions that report contact and grip. The model chains actions in one call, each with a condition that must hold, stopping at the first that fails; a second instance, the narrator, watches the cameras continuously and reports what changed with every result. From images, Reins also builds a simulation-ready twin of the scene for continual policy learning. With natural-language prompts and no task-specific code, GPT-6.1 Sol succeeds in 88% of real episodes on five tasks; without the harness, it fails every shell game, taking 8 times as long. Three frontier models perform alike but differ in tracking a scene that changes while the actor thinks. Code will be released upon publication.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: UGG: Unified Generative Geometry Model
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Amani Kiruga, Zhiyi Li, Ruojin Cai, Hansen Lillemark, Xiaoshan Wu
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: UGG is a unified framework for 4D scene understanding that integrates RGB video and geometric representations, enhancing visual generation and geometric prediction through conditional completion.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Understanding 4D scenes is a core challenge in visual intelligence, requiring models to jointly capture scene geometry, appearance, and dynamics from partial observations. However, existing approaches are subdivided into feedforward models for direct geometric prediction, and generative models for visual synthesis. We introduce UGG, a unified framework for 4D scene understanding that jointly models RGB video and geometric representations such as depth and camera pose. By assigning different noise levels across modalities and time, UGG formulates visual generation and geometric prediction as conditional completion within a single generative model. This flexible formulation enables the model to learn from diverse, heterogeneous datasets with different subsets of geometric and visual annotations. Furthermore, our generative formulation enables inference-time search over multiple plausible scene hypotheses, using geometric evidence extracted from observed RGB frames to improve geometric prediction without ground truth geometry. We demonstrate UGG's effectiveness over non-unified baselines across camera-controlled video generation, depth estimation, and camera pose prediction, including in challenging sparse observation settings. Code and visualizations are available at https://ugg-model.github.io/

Rajpurkar Lab.title: WireSeg-32K: A Physics-Grounded Synthetic Dataset for Wire Instance Segmentation
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Zilin Dai, Lehong Wang, Yi Yang, Xiang Fei
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: WireSeg-32K is a synthetic dataset of 32,000 images for wire instance segmentation, utilizing a co-simulation pipeline for realistic wire deformation and improving model performance in real-world applications.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Deformable linear objects such as wires and cables are difficult to segment because they are thin, highly deformable, and frequently self-occluded, while large-scale instance-level annotations are expensive to obtain in real scenes. Existing resources either focus on cable tracing or semantic segmentation under constrained settings, or generate visually plausible images without physically grounded wire deformation. We present WireSeg-32k, a synthetic dataset for wire instance segmentation with 32,000 RGB images, instance masks, depth maps, and a complementary real-world test set with annotations. To generate this dataset, we develop DeformX, a co-simulation pipeline that couples Cosserat-rod dynamics with photorealistic Isaac Sim rendering, enabling physically plausible, contact-consistent wire shapes, CAD-based wire assets, and diverse visually grounded scenes. As a simple baseline, LoRA fine-tuning SAM3 on WireSeg-32k alone improves real-world mAP@75 by 10.2% over the off-the-shelf model, showing that physically grounded synthetic data can transfer to real wire perception.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Cognitive Foundations for Reasoning and Their Manifestation in LLMs
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Shuyue Stella Li, Priyanka Kargupta, Haocheng Wang, Jinu Lee, Dean Light
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: This paper analyzes cognitive elements in reasoning, revealing differences between human and LLM processes, and proposes a framework to enhance model reasoning accuracy through structured guidance.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Large language models (LLMs) solve complex problems yet fail on simpler variants, suggesting they achieve correct outputs through mechanisms fundamentally different from human reasoning. To understand this gap, we synthesize cognitive science research into a taxonomy of 28 cognitive elements spanning reasoning invariants, meta-cognitive controls, representations for organizing reasoning and knowledge, and transformation operations. We introduce a fine-grained evaluation framework and apply it to 192K traces from 18 models across text, vision, and audio, alongside 1,346 human think-aloud traces on a new, domain-agnostic dataset for human-model comparison. We find that models are able to deploy cognitive elements seen in human reasoning but differ in how they use them. Leveraging these patterns, we develop test-time reasoning guidance that automatically scaffolds successful reasoning topologies, improving the accuracy of the strongest models by 9.7 percentage points on ill-structured problems. Meta-analysis of 1.6K LLM reasoning papers reveals the research community concentrates on easily quantifiable elements but rarely targets self-awareness, whose use differs between human and model reasoning. By establishing a shared vocabulary between cognitive science and LLM research, our framework enables diagnosis of reasoning failures and principled development of models that reason through robust cognitive mechanisms rather than spurious shortcuts, while providing tools to test theories of human cognition at scale.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: XM4D: 4D Reconstruction through Certifiable Geometric Optimization
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Haoyu Han, Jack Benarroch Jedlicki, Jiahui Lei, Heng Yang
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: XM4D presents a certifiably optimal framework for 4D reconstruction, efficiently estimating camera motion and non-rigid deformation through structured QCQP and SDP relaxations.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Accurate 4D reconstruction remains challenging: jointly estimating camera motion, scene geometry, and non-rigid deformation entails highly nonconvex optimization, making global optimality difficult to guarantee. We present XM4D, a framework for accurate and efficient 4D reconstruction built upon certifiably globally optimal geometric optimization. By separating the estimation of camera motion from non-rigid deformation, we formulate both stages as structured quadratically constrained quadratic programs (QCQP) that admit semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations and verifiable global optimality certificates. For camera motion estimation, we lift static point tracks into 3D using foundational depth prediction models and formulate a scaled bundle adjustment problem that jointly estimates camera poses, depth scales, and static landmarks. By analytically eliminating translations and landmarks, we reduce the problem to a QCQP over scaled rotations. For non-rigid reconstruction, we represent dynamic motion using an embedded deformation graph (EDG) and show that its tracking, rigidity, and temporal regularization objectives similarly reduce to a rotation-only QCQP. Both problems admit SDP relaxations that we solve efficiently with a GPU-accelerated Burer-Monteiro solver based on Riemannian optimization. The recovered geometry further initializes dynamic Gaussian splatting for photometric refinement. Extensive experiments across seven benchmarks demonstrate accurate camera motion estimation on both static and dynamic scenes, efficient optimization that scales to thousands of frames, and state-of-the-art novel-view rendering quality.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Hindsight Relabeling is All You Need for Reach-Avoid Learning
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Kevin Li, Marinka Zitnik
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: RADT introduces a novel decision transformer for offline goal-conditioned reach-avoid learning, utilizing hindsight relabeling to dynamically specify avoid-regions without reward supervision, outperforming existing methods.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning methods have shown promise for reach-avoid tasks, where an agent must reach a target state while avoiding undesirable regions of the state space. Existing approaches typically encode avoid-region information into an augmented state space and cost function, which prevents flexible, dynamic specification of novel avoid-region information at evaluation time. They also rely heavily on meticulously designed reward and cost functions, limiting transferability to novel environments and specifications. We introduce RADT, a decision transformer approach for offline, reward-free, goal-conditioned, avoid-region-conditioned RL. RADT encodes goals and avoid-regions directly as prompt tokens, allowing any number of avoid-regions of arbitrary size to be specified at evaluation time. Using only suboptimal offline trajectories from a random policy, RADT can learn reach-avoid behavior in a completely data-driven manner using our novel avoid-region hindsight relabeling approach, without the need for reward/cost supervision. We benchmark RADT against existing offline goal-conditioned RL models across 17 tasks, environments, and experimental settings. RADT generalizes in a zero-shot manner to out-of-distribution avoid-region sizes and counts, outperforming baselines that require retraining. In one such zero-shot setting, RADT achieves 35.7% improvement in normalized cost over the best retrained baseline while maintaining high goal-reaching success. We also apply RADT to cell reprogramming in biology, demonstrating its versatility.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: GRASP: Gradient-Guided Sampling for Contact-Rich Physics-Based Motion Retargeting
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Yang Liu, Tong Wang, Yiming Bao, Heng Yang
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: GRASP introduces a gradient-guided sampling method for effective physics-based motion retargeting in robots, achieving high success rates in complex tasks without task-specific rewards.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: We study physics-based retargeting of human demonstrations for robot learning: finding robot controls that reproduce reference motions under contact dynamics. We propose GRASP (Gradient Recovery from Archived Samples for Proposals), which combines sampling-based exploration with gradient-guided refinement without requiring a differentiable simulator. GRASP-TO extends tempered sequential Monte Carlo by fitting local quadratic cost models to archived rollouts and using their gradients to guide Markov chain Monte Carlo rejuvenation. Metropolis-Hastings correction preserves the target distribution for each fixed proposal kernel, and a population analysis connects the recovered gradients to Gaussian smoothing. GRASP-MPC scales this optimizer to long demonstrations through warm-started receding-horizon planning. Experiments on dexterous hands and humanoids show accurate retargeting with a shared tracking objective and no task-specific contact rewards, including 92.8% success on 1352 bimanual OakInk2 demonstrations. The refined references improve PPO tracking in pen spinning and humanoid-object interaction. We also demonstrate dexterous manipulation and whole-body humanoid motion on real hardware.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Flow Equivariant World Models: Structured Memory for Dynamic Environments
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Hansen Jin Lillemark, Benhao Huang, Fangneng Zhan, Yilun Du, Thomas Anderson Keller
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: The paper presents Flow Equivariant World Modeling, a framework that enhances dynamic environment predictions by utilizing time-parameterized symmetries in a structured latent memory.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Embodied systems experience the world as 'a symphony of flows': a combination of many continuous streams of sensory input coupled to self-motion, interwoven with the dynamics of external objects. These sensory streams and the underlying dynamics of the world obey smooth, time-parameterized symmetries which existing world models ignore. Without a memory that respects this structure, partial observability presents a major obstacle to existing methods: each observation reveals only a fraction of the world, while unobserved regions continue to evolve. In this work, we introduce Flow Equivariant World Modeling, a framework that leverages time-parameterized symmetries within a latent memory for stable and accurate dynamics prediction over long horizons. The latent memory shifts and transforms equivariantly with self-motion and inferred external object motion, keeping information about out-of-view regions aligned as time progresses. We demonstrate the advantage of this framework over state-of-the-art diffusion, memory-augmented, and recurrent world model architectures on 2D and 3D partially observed video world modeling benchmarks. More broadly, our results suggest that predictive representations become more powerful when they are organized in line with the temporal and dynamical structure of the world they model. Project page: https://flowequivariantworldmodels.github.io/

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Towards Trustworthy Physical Intelligence: From Theory to Practice Across Life Cycle
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Yang Wang, Hongxuan Liu, Xinghui Xu, Arjun Menon, Xiaoran Cai
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: The paper establishes a framework for trustworthy physical intelligence, addressing its unique challenges and operationalizing principles for governance throughout its life cycle.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Physical intelligence refers to intelligence systems that understand, reason about and act in accordance with the physical world and its underlying laws, dynamics, and constraints. Unlike conventional AI systems, physical intelligence interacts continuously with uncertain physical environments, and its actions produce consequences that are physically irreversible. As existing trustworthy AI frameworks have been developed primarily for digital AI systems, they do not fully capture the distinctive challenges of Physical Intelligence, such as physical safety, cyber-physical security, and physical manufacturing process. To address this gap, our paper develop a foundation for understanding, operationalizing, and governing trustworthy physical intelligence. First, we characterize the fundamental capabilities of physical intelligence. Second, we investigate the role of physical laws and principles in AI and analyze the associated challenges of physical intelligence. Third, we provide a unified structure of the end-to-end physical intelligence life cycle across five core stages and introduce the Trustworthy Physical Intelligence Operationalization (T-PAIO) framework. Fourth, we formulate the Trustworthy Physical Intelligence (T-PAI) Principles as a theoretical framework that synthesizes key trustworthiness dimensions and establishes a conceptual foundation for the governance of physical intelligence systems.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: BEACON: Cross-Domain Co-Training of Generative Robot Policies via Best-Effort Adaptation
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Antong Zhang, Han Qi, Heng Yang
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: BEACON is a framework for training generative robot policies that enhances robustness and data efficiency by using discrepancy-aware co-training across diverse source domains.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: We introduce BEACON--Best-Effort Adaptation for Cross-Domain Co-Training--a theory-guided framework for training generative robot policies with abundant source demonstrations and limited target demonstrations. BEACON casts cross-domain co-training as a discrepancy-aware importance-reweighting problem, jointly learning a diffusion-based visuomotor policy and per-sample source weights through an objective inspired by the Best-Effort Adaptation (BEA) bound. To make this approach practical for high-dimensional sequence policies, we develop scalable instance-level discrepancy proxies, stochastic alternating updates for policy and weights, and a multi-source extension that balances heterogeneous source domains. Across sim-to-sim, sim-to-real, and multi-source manipulation settings, BEACON improves robustness and data efficiency over target-only, fixed-ratio co-training, and feature-alignment baselines. Without an explicit alignment objective, BEACON also brings source and target representations closer together as an implicit result of discrepancy-aware co-training.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Iterative Gumbel Planning for Continuous Control
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Shaohuai Liu, Weirui Ye, Yilun Du, Le Xie
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: Iterative Gumbel Planning (IGP) aligns continuous control policies with search candidates, enhancing performance and stability in reinforcement learning for robotics.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Search-based planning remains a powerful policy improvement paradigm in reinforcement learning, driving milestone successes in discrete domains. However, extending this paradigm to continuous control exposes a structural mismatch: search evaluates a finite set of action candidates, whereas continuous RL typically relies on Gaussian policies. We show that winner-action distillation into a continuous Gaussian induces a \textit{projection error} and a stepwise variance-expanding gradient tendency when the selected action is sufficiently far from the current mean. Empirically, this tendency is associated with elevated terminal variance and a return gap on the evaluated tasks. To address this, we propose \textbf{Iterative Gumbel Planning (IGP)}. By adopting a per-dimension factorized categorical policy, IGP naturally aligns the policy support with the search candidates, eliminating the projection error and reducing the residual approximation to a bounded discretization error. To bypass the combinatorial explosion of high-dimensional discrete action spaces, IGP pairs Gumbel Top-$K$ candidate sampling with an MPPI-style multi-round iterative search to refine the policy at each state. Empirically, IGP achieves state-of-the-art aggregate performance and sample efficiency on DMControl and HumanoidBench. Furthermore, it produces more stable action sequences with lower temporal variance, demonstrating its practical potential for real-world robotic deployment.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Energy-Based Policy Orchestration
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Weirui Ye, Yen-Jen Wang, Elvis Hsieh, Zhiyang Dou, Shibo Zhao
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: The paper presents EPO, an energy-based policy orchestrator that optimizes runtime selection of policy-goal pairs for robust robot behavior in dynamic tasks.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Hierarchical control scales robot behavior by separating task-level planning from low-level control. In dynamic, high-dimensional tasks, however, a fixed planner-to-policy interface can fail when contacts, balance, or disturbances evolve faster than high-level policy updates. Execution therefore requires choosing not only which low-level policy to run, but also which policy-specific goal should be given to it. We formulate this problem as policy orchestration: runtime selection of a policy-goal pair that is likely to remain feasible while tracking the planner target. We develop EPO, an energy-based policy orchestrator for modular goal-conditioned policy families. For each policy, EPO learns a composite energy over low-level goals, where lower energy corresponds to higher feasibility and more accurate target realization. At runtime, EPO refines each policy's goal and executes the lowest-energy policy-goal pair. Because energies are policy-specific, new policies can be incorporated by learning their own energy models, without retraining the existing policies or a centralized scheduler. In simulation, EPO improves the empirical precision-robustness trade-off by refining policy-specific goals before selectively switching among policies based on energy scores. We further demonstrate sim-to-real deployment of the same frozen policies and energy models on real humanoid loco-manipulation tasks. Project website: https://yewr.github.io/epo

Rajpurkar Lab.title: RCR-Router: Efficient Role-Aware Context Routing for Multi-Agent LLM Systems with Structured Memory
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Jun Liu, Zhenglun Kong, Changdi Yang, Fan Yang, Tianqi Li
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: The RCR-Router optimizes multi-agent LLM systems by efficiently routing role-relevant context, reducing token usage by 35% and runtime by 38% while enhancing performance.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly organized into multi-agent systems for complex reasoning and decision-making tasks. However, scaling such systems can substantially increase inference cost, especially when multiple agents repeatedly process overlapping or role-irrelevant context. Many existing multi-agent frameworks focus on orchestration and role specialization, but still rely on full-context sharing or static context routing, leading to redundant token consumption, increased runtime, and inefficient memory utilization. We present \emph{Role-Conditioned Context Routing (RCR)}, an execution-time layer that allocates role-relevant shared-memory items to agents under token budgets. Given a structured shared memory and a set of role-specialized agents, RCR selectively routes task-relevant memory items to each agent according to its role, optional task-stage metadata, and token budget. RCR integrates role-conditioned relevance scoring, token-budgeted memory selection, and iterative memory updates to reduce redundant context exposure during multi-agent execution. Experiments on multi-hop QA, embodied reasoning (ALFWorld), and web-based decision-making (WebShop) show that RCR reduces token usage by 35\% on average and runtime by 38\% on average relative to Full-Context, while maintaining or improving task performance.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: When Does Test-Time Search Help World Action Models? An Empirical Audit of Candidate Selection and Simulator Integrity
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Jun Liu, Dajie Sun, Zhenglun Kong, Zhenjiang Fan, Peiyan Dong
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: The paper audits test-time scaling in world-action models, revealing limited candidate selection benefits and efficiency gains, emphasizing the need for comprehensive evaluation beyond success rates.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: World-action models increasingly apply test-time scaling, spending extra inference computation on candidate selection and adaptive allocation to improve control. Such gains are credible only when candidates carry exploitable signal, nominal compute savings become real speedup, and evaluation stays reliable. We audit all three on Cosmos Policy and RoboCasa with a premise-first, pre-registered methodology. On clean data, a learned value selector is 1.66 pp worse than random; a hindsight oracle gains only 1.40 pp, with an episode-level interval spanning zero; and 82% of states show identical candidate outcomes, leaving little selection headroom. Token pruning cuts per-forward FLOPs by up to 47% but yields at most a measured 1.15$\times$ end-to-end speedup on the deployed path (1.25$\times$ on a decode-excluded path), short of a 1.5$\times$ target, and our adaptive-allocation experiment is inconclusive under a power gate. We further identify and fix a silent rendering corruption whose rate rises sharply along compute-heavy planning paths while leaving the official direct-policy result unaffected, and release a detector, fix, and scripts. These findings show why test-time scaling should be audited as a chain of premises (decision signal, realized efficiency, evaluationintegrity) rather than by success rate alone. Conclusions are scoped to the tested configuration.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Training language models in simulation for psychiatric intake
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Samuel Schmidgall, Tim Strother, Alex Bijamov, Min Woo Sun, Anil Palepu
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: Training language models in simulated environments significantly enhances their performance in psychiatric intake interviews, improving diagnostic accuracy and patient communication while highlighting the need for clinician oversight.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: In psychiatric practice, the clinical intake interview remains a primary diagnostic instrument, requiring the clinician to establish rapport while disentangling complex, overlapping presentations. Here, we show that multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation environments improves language model performance on structured text-based psychiatric intake, spanning history-taking, differential diagnosis, and initial management planning. In a randomized, double-blind crossover study ($N = 60$ matched scenario pairs, 120 encounters) comparing the RL-trained agent against its identically prompted base model, 32 board-certified psychiatrists role-played standardized patients while a separate panel of 15 independent, board-certified psychiatrists scored the de-identified transcripts. The trained agent outperformed the base model in 76.7% of matched scenario pairs ($p < 0.0001$), with gains on an adapted clinical-examination rubric ($d_z = 0.77$, $p < 0.0001$), patient-centered communication (82.0% vs. 65.2%, $p < 0.001$), and differential diagnosis appropriateness (68.3% vs. 33.3%, $p < 0.001$). Across 127 psychiatrist-validated simulated intake scenarios, the trained agent nearly doubled its base model's clinical rubric score (0.706 vs. 0.379; composite reward 0.564 vs. 0.294, $p < 0.0001$). To systematically probe conversational safety, we established two Delphi-consensus taxonomies, of clinical safety risks and relational competencies, from which 256 challenging adversarial presentations were derived; we find that training in simulation environments more than halved under-triage of acute safety risks (12.9% vs. 30.5%, $p < 0.0001$). Simulation environments thus provide a controlled testbed for training and stress-testing psychiatric conversational agents, with gains that transferred to psychiatrist-enacted encounters, though residual gaps require safeguards and clinician oversight.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Self-Labeled Preference Transfer for Steerable Robot Manipulation
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Kaiwen Hong, Shaoting Peng, Xiangyu Zeng, Pengcheng Wang, Boyuan Tian
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: Self-Labeled Preference Transfer (SPT) enhances robot manipulation by enabling preference adaptation across tasks using self-labeled demonstrations, achieving high accuracy and task success without manual annotations.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can learn to follow execution preferences, such as where to grasp an object or how to move around an obstacle, from demonstrations annotated with preference labels. Providing these annotations for every new task, however, is costly. We study whether learned preference control can transfer to new tasks whose demonstrations contain the desired behaviors but lack preference annotations. We find that a policy trained with preference annotations can follow preferences on a new task before adaptation but achieves limited task success. Fine-tuning on target demonstrations without these annotations improves task success while weakening preference control. Motivated by this finding, we introduce Self-Labeled Preference Transfer (SPT). SPT jointly trains a shared vision-language backbone for preference-conditioned action prediction and preference recognition on annotated source demonstrations. It then freezes the recognizer to preserve its cross-task preference recognition capability and uses it to self-label target demonstrations for policy fine-tuning. Across five types of execution preferences in simulation, the recognizer achieves 96.4% accuracy, and SPT reaches 84.8% preference following and 89.2% task success, compared with 59.4% and 88.0% for naive finetuning. We further extend to multiple preferences, achieving 93.8% preference following compared with 42.5% of baselines. In real-world experiments, SPT increases preference following from 52.5% to 92.5% relative to naive finetuning across two task transfers. These results show that SPT can support preference adaptation across tasks and objects while maintaining success, without additional manual preference annotations.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: UMI-Live for In-The-Wild Bimanual Robotics Data Collection
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Govind Velamoor, Adrian Lin, Sam Jung, Spencer Mateega, Brandon Y. Yang
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: UMI-Live is an open-source bimanual robotics system enabling in-the-wild data collection without external calibration, validated through successful task demonstrations and released datasets.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) devices allow human experts to demonstrate tasks for robot learning without teleoperating physical robots. Using these demonstrations as training data still requires a consistent hardware setup, calibration, and data processing. We present UMI-Live, a full-stack open-source bimanual UMI system for in-the-wild data collection. We design our custom UMI-Live hardware to integrate camera and LiDAR--inertial sensing, onboard compute, and power, without external tracking equipment or calibration within the collection environment. We implement a simple user interface for recording data while an asynchronous pipeline performs parallel SLAM reconstruction and publishes training-ready datasets. We also release software that supports dual-YAM teleoperation and VLA policy training and inference. We validate UMI-Live data quality by fine-tuning $π_{0.5}$ and MolmoAct2, achieving success rates of 10/10 and 8/10, respectively on a bimanual pick-and-place task. Furthermore, we release 40 hours of UMI-Live data across three tasks, and complete hardware designs, software, and reproduction guides at our $\href{https://umi-live.github.io/}{\text{project website}}$.

Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.title: Infer3D: Inverse Generative Modeling Enables Robust 3D Reconstruction
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.authors_text: Amani Kiruga, Mark Hamilton, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, William T. Freeman, Vincent Sitzmann
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.summary: Infer3D introduces an inverse generative modeling approach for robust 3D reconstruction, enhancing out-of-distribution accuracy by leveraging latent variable recovery and adaptive inference strategies.
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.debug_abstract: Humans can understand the 3D structure of scenes even from highly unfamiliar or extreme viewpoints. Cognitive science suggests this generalization stems from a top-down generative inference strategy. In contrast, state-of-the-art 3D reconstruction neural networks typically rely on amortized, feedforward inference. While fast, this pattern-matching approach degrades when faced with out-of-distribution (OOD) scene conditions unseen during training. Inspired by the generative nature of human vision, we propose Infer3D, an inverse generative modeling framework that recovers the latent variables of a generative model to best match the monocular input. To prevent degenerate flat outputs, we couple the generative image prior with a frozen 3D lifting network that constrains the optimization space to a valid, multi-view-consistent 3D manifold. Across a variety of controlled synthetic and real-world tasks, Infer3D demonstrates superior OOD reconstruction accuracy compared to feedforward networks trained on equal or larger datasets. Furthermore, mirroring how human perception requires more time to process confusing stimuli, we introduce an adaptive inference strategy that expends more test-time compute on ambiguous OOD examples while efficiently routing in-distribution inputs. Project website: https://amanikiruga.github.io/infer3d-site/

Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.title: Do Deep Stereo Models Learn Shape Priors?
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.authors_text: Linbo Tang, Aneel Damaraju, Todd Zickler
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.summary: The study reveals that deep stereo models struggle with boundary localization under weak cues, while a new generative model improves accuracy by integrating disparity and distance fields.
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.debug_abstract: Localizing object boundaries is important for embodied visual systems, since small boundary errors can change the inferred geometry of physical surfaces. We study whether deep stereo models produce boundaries consistent with simple shape priors when local image and disparity cues are weak. We create a synthetic stereo dataset consisting of objects drawn from a highly constrained family of shapes, with randomized depth, slant, color and texture. Despite the simplicity of this shape space, we find that several state-of-the-art stereo models retain systematic boundary errors, even when finetuned or trained from scratch on the dataset. We then introduce a simple generative stereo model that jointly predicts disparity and a distance field representing object boundaries. The model improves boundary localization and produces contours that adhere more closely to the underlying shape space. These results expose limitations in the boundary predictions of current stereo architectures when local evidence is weak, and motivate further study of whether generative models can better combine regional grouping evidence with global geometric structure.

Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.title: EgoJev: Finding Evidence in Egocentric Video by Reading VLM Decisions
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.authors_text: Chunggi Lee, Hanspeter Pfister
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.summary: EgoJev enhances evidence retrieval in egocentric videos by leveraging a vision-language model to select key frames, improving accuracy significantly without additional training.
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.debug_abstract: Questions about long egocentric video often depend on one brief moment, such as the second a hand puts an object down. A vision-language model (VLM) that sees a few evenly spaced frames usually misses it. Training-free methods rank frames with a separate image-text model or ask the VLM to write a time. In a controlled test, the VLM itself locates the moment better when it chooses among labeled frames, and we read this choice from its output distribution. With the same candidates, this choice lands on the evidence more often than image-text scores or a written time span, and it compares all candidates in one decision. Based on this finding, we propose EgoJev, a training-free frame selector for wearable assistants. EgoJev reads where the evidence is from labeled thumbnails and looks again at the windows it points to. It places its few answer frames at the quantiles of the resulting distribution. One frozen VLM selects, answers and returns the evidence time, with no second model. A wearable device can encode its coarse thumbnails while it records. With Qwen3.5-4B and 8 answer frames, EgoJev raises QAEgo4D accuracy from 51.2% with uniform sampling to 62.0%, and it outperforms recent training-free frame selectors on QAEgo4D and MyEgo. A single-level version runs on a Mac and an iPhone.

Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.title: T-WLA: Bridging Slow Vision and Fast Touch with a World-Language-Action Model
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.authors_text: Kaichen Zhou, Yuzhen Chen, Hannah Yao, Chonghe Jiang, Rao Fu
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.summary: T-WLA integrates visual memory with tactile feedback to enhance contact-rich manipulation, achieving significant improvements in motion prediction and task success rates.
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.debug_abstract: In contact-rich manipulation, contact conditions can change before a visual policy updates its action plan. Recomputing the plan through the visual policy adds latency, while tactile feedback alone does not specify how the ongoing motion should be revised for the task. We introduce T-WLA, a world-language-action architecture that uses shared visual memory to guide both action generation and tactile correction. At each visual update, the visual branch integrates the current image, task instruction, and retrieved history into a visual memory that conditions base-action generation. The same memory is cached for a lightweight tactile editor, which combines it with the active action chunk and incoming touch to predict residual corrections to unexecuted actions without rerunning the visual branch. Future-image and future-pressure prediction provide training-only supervision, encouraging the visual memory and tactile features to capture interaction dynamics relevant to action generation and correction. We evaluate T-WLA on tactile-conditioned hand-motion prediction using EgoTouch and Tachin, and on four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks. On EgoTouch, T-WLA reduces finger-joint MPJPE by 30% relative to the strongest evaluated baseline. Across four real-robot tasks, T-WLA achieves 51.0% mean success versus 23.0% for the baseline, a gain of 28.0 percentage points. Videos and code are available at https://t-wla.github.io/.

Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.title: ImpedanceMimic: Learned Impedance as Action Space for Force-Accurate Motion Imitation
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.authors_text: Matthias Jammot, Pembe Gizem Özdil
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.summary: ImpedanceMimic leverages reinforcement learning to optimize joint stiffness and damping for improved motion imitation, achieving superior force and motion fidelity across diverse activities and subjects.
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.debug_abstract: Recovering the forces behind a motion is ill-posed: different controllers can reproduce the same movement while generating different contact forces. Physics-based motion imitation resolves this ambiguity through simulation, but relies on fixed-gain proportional-derivative (PD) control. We show that fixed gains impose a trade-off between motion and force tracking, as contact and swing place conflicting demands on joint stiffness and damping. We introduce ImpedanceMimic, a reinforcement-learning policy that modulates per-joint stiffness, damping, and position setpoints from motion and force measurements, but requires only motion at inference. Across 129 participants and six activities, ImpedanceMimic outperforms matched fixed-gain PD under every integration scheme, direct-torque, muscle-actuated and existing imitation controllers in kinematic and force fidelity, approaching a dedicated motion-to-force regressor. By expressing gains as multiples of inertia-scaled priors, a single policy controls subject-specific biomechanical models without explicit anthropometric input and transfers zero-shot to unseen humans and a humanoid robot. The learned impedance forms a low-dimensional representation of motor state, shared across bodies, that generalizes to withheld activities: stiffness scales with load, and damping anticipates unloading.

Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.title: Reins: Frontier Multimodal Models Driving Real Robot Arms on Long-Horizon Tasks, Zero-Shot
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.authors_text: Pengfei Ye, Zhiyang Dou, Yuxiang Ma, Haonan Chen, Heng Yang
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.summary: Reins enables frontier multimodal models to effectively control dual-arm robots in long-horizon tasks using 3D perception and continuous scene tracking, achieving 88% success.
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.debug_abstract: Frontier models such as GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 can now plan and call tools, yet they still struggle to drive real robots through long-horizon, contact-rich manipulation, blind while the arm moves and while they think. We present Reins, a harness in which an off-the-shelf model operates a dual-arm robot with 3D perception tools and atomic actions that report contact and grip. The model chains actions in one call, each with a condition that must hold, stopping at the first that fails; a second instance, the narrator, watches the cameras continuously and reports what changed with every result. From images, Reins also builds a simulation-ready twin of the scene for continual policy learning. With natural-language prompts and no task-specific code, GPT-6.1 Sol succeeds in 88% of real episodes on five tasks; without the harness, it fails every shell game, taking 8 times as long. Three frontier models perform alike but differ in tracking a scene that changes while the actor thinks. Code will be released upon publication.

Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.title: UGG: Unified Generative Geometry Model
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.authors_text: Amani Kiruga, Zhiyi Li, Ruojin Cai, Hansen Lillemark, Xiaoshan Wu
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.summary: UGG is a unified framework for 4D scene understanding that integrates RGB video and geometric representations, enhancing visual generation and geometric prediction through conditional completion.
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.debug_abstract: Understanding 4D scenes is a core challenge in visual intelligence, requiring models to jointly capture scene geometry, appearance, and dynamics from partial observations. However, existing approaches are subdivided into feedforward models for direct geometric prediction, and generative models for visual synthesis. We introduce UGG, a unified framework for 4D scene understanding that jointly models RGB video and geometric representations such as depth and camera pose. By assigning different noise levels across modalities and time, UGG formulates visual generation and geometric prediction as conditional completion within a single generative model. This flexible formulation enables the model to learn from diverse, heterogeneous datasets with different subsets of geometric and visual annotations. Furthermore, our generative formulation enables inference-time search over multiple plausible scene hypotheses, using geometric evidence extracted from observed RGB frames to improve geometric prediction without ground truth geometry. We demonstrate UGG's effectiveness over non-unified baselines across camera-controlled video generation, depth estimation, and camera pose prediction, including in challenging sparse observation settings. Code and visualizations are available at https://ugg-model.github.io/

Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.title: WireSeg-32K: A Physics-Grounded Synthetic Dataset for Wire Instance Segmentation
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.authors_text: Zilin Dai, Lehong Wang, Yi Yang, Xiang Fei
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.summary: WireSeg-32K is a synthetic dataset of 32,000 images for wire instance segmentation, utilizing a co-simulation pipeline for realistic wire deformation and improving model performance in real-world applications.
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.debug_abstract: Deformable linear objects such as wires and cables are difficult to segment because they are thin, highly deformable, and frequently self-occluded, while large-scale instance-level annotations are expensive to obtain in real scenes. Existing resources either focus on cable tracing or semantic segmentation under constrained settings, or generate visually plausible images without physically grounded wire deformation. We present WireSeg-32k, a synthetic dataset for wire instance segmentation with 32,000 RGB images, instance masks, depth maps, and a complementary real-world test set with annotations. To generate this dataset, we develop DeformX, a co-simulation pipeline that couples Cosserat-rod dynamics with photorealistic Isaac Sim rendering, enabling physically plausible, contact-consistent wire shapes, CAD-based wire assets, and diverse visually grounded scenes. As a simple baseline, LoRA fine-tuning SAM3 on WireSeg-32k alone improves real-world mAP@75 by 10.2% over the off-the-shelf model, showing that physically grounded synthetic data can transfer to real wire perception.

Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.title: Cognitive Foundations for Reasoning and Their Manifestation in LLMs
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.authors_text: Shuyue Stella Li, Priyanka Kargupta, Haocheng Wang, Jinu Lee, Dean Light
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.summary: This paper analyzes cognitive elements in reasoning, revealing differences between human and LLM processes, and proposes a framework to enhance model reasoning accuracy through structured guidance.
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.debug_abstract: Large language models (LLMs) solve complex problems yet fail on simpler variants, suggesting they achieve correct outputs through mechanisms fundamentally different from human reasoning. To understand this gap, we synthesize cognitive science research into a taxonomy of 28 cognitive elements spanning reasoning invariants, meta-cognitive controls, representations for organizing reasoning and knowledge, and transformation operations. We introduce a fine-grained evaluation framework and apply it to 192K traces from 18 models across text, vision, and audio, alongside 1,346 human think-aloud traces on a new, domain-agnostic dataset for human-model comparison. We find that models are able to deploy cognitive elements seen in human reasoning but differ in how they use them. Leveraging these patterns, we develop test-time reasoning guidance that automatically scaffolds successful reasoning topologies, improving the accuracy of the strongest models by 9.7 percentage points on ill-structured problems. Meta-analysis of 1.6K LLM reasoning papers reveals the research community concentrates on easily quantifiable elements but rarely targets self-awareness, whose use differs between human and model reasoning. By establishing a shared vocabulary between cognitive science and LLM research, our framework enables diagnosis of reasoning failures and principled development of models that reason through robust cognitive mechanisms rather than spurious shortcuts, while providing tools to test theories of human cognition at scale.

Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.title: XM4D: 4D Reconstruction through Certifiable Geometric Optimization
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.authors_text: Haoyu Han, Jack Benarroch Jedlicki, Jiahui Lei, Heng Yang
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.summary: XM4D presents a certifiably optimal framework for 4D reconstruction, efficiently estimating camera motion and non-rigid deformation through structured QCQP and SDP relaxations.
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.debug_abstract: Accurate 4D reconstruction remains challenging: jointly estimating camera motion, scene geometry, and non-rigid deformation entails highly nonconvex optimization, making global optimality difficult to guarantee. We present XM4D, a framework for accurate and efficient 4D reconstruction built upon certifiably globally optimal geometric optimization. By separating the estimation of camera motion from non-rigid deformation, we formulate both stages as structured quadratically constrained quadratic programs (QCQP) that admit semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations and verifiable global optimality certificates. For camera motion estimation, we lift static point tracks into 3D using foundational depth prediction models and formulate a scaled bundle adjustment problem that jointly estimates camera poses, depth scales, and static landmarks. By analytically eliminating translations and landmarks, we reduce the problem to a QCQP over scaled rotations. For non-rigid reconstruction, we represent dynamic motion using an embedded deformation graph (EDG) and show that its tracking, rigidity, and temporal regularization objectives similarly reduce to a rotation-only QCQP. Both problems admit SDP relaxations that we solve efficiently with a GPU-accelerated Burer-Monteiro solver based on Riemannian optimization. The recovered geometry further initializes dynamic Gaussian splatting for photometric refinement. Extensive experiments across seven benchmarks demonstrate accurate camera motion estimation on both static and dynamic scenes, efficient optimization that scales to thousands of frames, and state-of-the-art novel-view rendering quality.

Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.title: Hindsight Relabeling is All You Need for Reach-Avoid Learning
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.authors_text: Kevin Li, Marinka Zitnik
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.summary: RADT introduces a novel decision transformer for offline goal-conditioned reach-avoid learning, utilizing hindsight relabeling to dynamically specify avoid-regions without reward supervision, outperforming existing methods.
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.debug_abstract: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning methods have shown promise for reach-avoid tasks, where an agent must reach a target state while avoiding undesirable regions of the state space. Existing approaches typically encode avoid-region information into an augmented state space and cost function, which prevents flexible, dynamic specification of novel avoid-region information at evaluation time. They also rely heavily on meticulously designed reward and cost functions, limiting transferability to novel environments and specifications. We introduce RADT, a decision transformer approach for offline, reward-free, goal-conditioned, avoid-region-conditioned RL. RADT encodes goals and avoid-regions directly as prompt tokens, allowing any number of avoid-regions of arbitrary size to be specified at evaluation time. Using only suboptimal offline trajectories from a random policy, RADT can learn reach-avoid behavior in a completely data-driven manner using our novel avoid-region hindsight relabeling approach, without the need for reward/cost supervision. We benchmark RADT against existing offline goal-conditioned RL models across 17 tasks, environments, and experimental settings. RADT generalizes in a zero-shot manner to out-of-distribution avoid-region sizes and counts, outperforming baselines that require retraining. In one such zero-shot setting, RADT achieves 35.7% improvement in normalized cost over the best retrained baseline while maintaining high goal-reaching success. We also apply RADT to cell reprogramming in biology, demonstrating its versatility.

Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.title: GRASP: Gradient-Guided Sampling for Contact-Rich Physics-Based Motion Retargeting
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.authors_text: Yang Liu, Tong Wang, Yiming Bao, Heng Yang
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.summary: GRASP introduces a gradient-guided sampling method for effective physics-based motion retargeting in robots, achieving high success rates in complex tasks without task-specific rewards.
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.debug_abstract: We study physics-based retargeting of human demonstrations for robot learning: finding robot controls that reproduce reference motions under contact dynamics. We propose GRASP (Gradient Recovery from Archived Samples for Proposals), which combines sampling-based exploration with gradient-guided refinement without requiring a differentiable simulator. GRASP-TO extends tempered sequential Monte Carlo by fitting local quadratic cost models to archived rollouts and using their gradients to guide Markov chain Monte Carlo rejuvenation. Metropolis-Hastings correction preserves the target distribution for each fixed proposal kernel, and a population analysis connects the recovered gradients to Gaussian smoothing. GRASP-MPC scales this optimizer to long demonstrations through warm-started receding-horizon planning. Experiments on dexterous hands and humanoids show accurate retargeting with a shared tracking objective and no task-specific contact rewards, including 92.8% success on 1352 bimanual OakInk2 demonstrations. The refined references improve PPO tracking in pen spinning and humanoid-object interaction. We also demonstrate dexterous manipulation and whole-body humanoid motion on real hardware.

Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.title: Flow Equivariant World Models: Structured Memory for Dynamic Environments
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.authors_text: Hansen Jin Lillemark, Benhao Huang, Fangneng Zhan, Yilun Du, Thomas Anderson Keller
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.summary: The paper presents Flow Equivariant World Modeling, a framework that enhances dynamic environment predictions by utilizing time-parameterized symmetries in a structured latent memory.
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.debug_abstract: Embodied systems experience the world as 'a symphony of flows': a combination of many continuous streams of sensory input coupled to self-motion, interwoven with the dynamics of external objects. These sensory streams and the underlying dynamics of the world obey smooth, time-parameterized symmetries which existing world models ignore. Without a memory that respects this structure, partial observability presents a major obstacle to existing methods: each observation reveals only a fraction of the world, while unobserved regions continue to evolve. In this work, we introduce Flow Equivariant World Modeling, a framework that leverages time-parameterized symmetries within a latent memory for stable and accurate dynamics prediction over long horizons. The latent memory shifts and transforms equivariantly with self-motion and inferred external object motion, keeping information about out-of-view regions aligned as time progresses. We demonstrate the advantage of this framework over state-of-the-art diffusion, memory-augmented, and recurrent world model architectures on 2D and 3D partially observed video world modeling benchmarks. More broadly, our results suggest that predictive representations become more powerful when they are organized in line with the temporal and dynamical structure of the world they model. Project page: https://flowequivariantworldmodels.github.io/

Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.title: Towards Trustworthy Physical Intelligence: From Theory to Practice Across Life Cycle
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.authors_text: Yang Wang, Hongxuan Liu, Xinghui Xu, Arjun Menon, Xiaoran Cai
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.summary: The paper establishes a framework for trustworthy physical intelligence, addressing its unique challenges and operationalizing principles for governance throughout its life cycle.
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.debug_abstract: Physical intelligence refers to intelligence systems that understand, reason about and act in accordance with the physical world and its underlying laws, dynamics, and constraints. Unlike conventional AI systems, physical intelligence interacts continuously with uncertain physical environments, and its actions produce consequences that are physically irreversible. As existing trustworthy AI frameworks have been developed primarily for digital AI systems, they do not fully capture the distinctive challenges of Physical Intelligence, such as physical safety, cyber-physical security, and physical manufacturing process. To address this gap, our paper develop a foundation for understanding, operationalizing, and governing trustworthy physical intelligence. First, we characterize the fundamental capabilities of physical intelligence. Second, we investigate the role of physical laws and principles in AI and analyze the associated challenges of physical intelligence. Third, we provide a unified structure of the end-to-end physical intelligence life cycle across five core stages and introduce the Trustworthy Physical Intelligence Operationalization (T-PAIO) framework. Fourth, we formulate the Trustworthy Physical Intelligence (T-PAI) Principles as a theoretical framework that synthesizes key trustworthiness dimensions and establishes a conceptual foundation for the governance of physical intelligence systems.

Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.title: BEACON: Cross-Domain Co-Training of Generative Robot Policies via Best-Effort Adaptation
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.authors_text: Antong Zhang, Han Qi, Heng Yang
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.summary: BEACON is a framework for training generative robot policies that enhances robustness and data efficiency by using discrepancy-aware co-training across diverse source domains.
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.debug_abstract: We introduce BEACON--Best-Effort Adaptation for Cross-Domain Co-Training--a theory-guided framework for training generative robot policies with abundant source demonstrations and limited target demonstrations. BEACON casts cross-domain co-training as a discrepancy-aware importance-reweighting problem, jointly learning a diffusion-based visuomotor policy and per-sample source weights through an objective inspired by the Best-Effort Adaptation (BEA) bound. To make this approach practical for high-dimensional sequence policies, we develop scalable instance-level discrepancy proxies, stochastic alternating updates for policy and weights, and a multi-source extension that balances heterogeneous source domains. Across sim-to-sim, sim-to-real, and multi-source manipulation settings, BEACON improves robustness and data efficiency over target-only, fixed-ratio co-training, and feature-alignment baselines. Without an explicit alignment objective, BEACON also brings source and target representations closer together as an implicit result of discrepancy-aware co-training.

Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.title: Iterative Gumbel Planning for Continuous Control
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.authors_text: Shaohuai Liu, Weirui Ye, Yilun Du, Le Xie
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.summary: Iterative Gumbel Planning (IGP) aligns continuous control policies with search candidates, enhancing performance and stability in reinforcement learning for robotics.
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.debug_abstract: Search-based planning remains a powerful policy improvement paradigm in reinforcement learning, driving milestone successes in discrete domains. However, extending this paradigm to continuous control exposes a structural mismatch: search evaluates a finite set of action candidates, whereas continuous RL typically relies on Gaussian policies. We show that winner-action distillation into a continuous Gaussian induces a \textit{projection error} and a stepwise variance-expanding gradient tendency when the selected action is sufficiently far from the current mean. Empirically, this tendency is associated with elevated terminal variance and a return gap on the evaluated tasks. To address this, we propose \textbf{Iterative Gumbel Planning (IGP)}. By adopting a per-dimension factorized categorical policy, IGP naturally aligns the policy support with the search candidates, eliminating the projection error and reducing the residual approximation to a bounded discretization error. To bypass the combinatorial explosion of high-dimensional discrete action spaces, IGP pairs Gumbel Top-$K$ candidate sampling with an MPPI-style multi-round iterative search to refine the policy at each state. Empirically, IGP achieves state-of-the-art aggregate performance and sample efficiency on DMControl and HumanoidBench. Furthermore, it produces more stable action sequences with lower temporal variance, demonstrating its practical potential for real-world robotic deployment.

Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.title: Energy-Based Policy Orchestration
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.authors_text: Weirui Ye, Yen-Jen Wang, Elvis Hsieh, Zhiyang Dou, Shibo Zhao
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.summary: The paper presents EPO, an energy-based policy orchestrator that optimizes runtime selection of policy-goal pairs for robust robot behavior in dynamic tasks.
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.debug_abstract: Hierarchical control scales robot behavior by separating task-level planning from low-level control. In dynamic, high-dimensional tasks, however, a fixed planner-to-policy interface can fail when contacts, balance, or disturbances evolve faster than high-level policy updates. Execution therefore requires choosing not only which low-level policy to run, but also which policy-specific goal should be given to it. We formulate this problem as policy orchestration: runtime selection of a policy-goal pair that is likely to remain feasible while tracking the planner target. We develop EPO, an energy-based policy orchestrator for modular goal-conditioned policy families. For each policy, EPO learns a composite energy over low-level goals, where lower energy corresponds to higher feasibility and more accurate target realization. At runtime, EPO refines each policy's goal and executes the lowest-energy policy-goal pair. Because energies are policy-specific, new policies can be incorporated by learning their own energy models, without retraining the existing policies or a centralized scheduler. In simulation, EPO improves the empirical precision-robustness trade-off by refining policy-specific goals before selectively switching among policies based on energy scores. We further demonstrate sim-to-real deployment of the same frozen policies and energy models on real humanoid loco-manipulation tasks. Project website: https://yewr.github.io/epo

Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.title: RCR-Router: Efficient Role-Aware Context Routing for Multi-Agent LLM Systems with Structured Memory
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.authors_text: Jun Liu, Zhenglun Kong, Changdi Yang, Fan Yang, Tianqi Li
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.summary: The RCR-Router optimizes multi-agent LLM systems by efficiently routing role-relevant context, reducing token usage by 35% and runtime by 38% while enhancing performance.
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.debug_abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly organized into multi-agent systems for complex reasoning and decision-making tasks. However, scaling such systems can substantially increase inference cost, especially when multiple agents repeatedly process overlapping or role-irrelevant context. Many existing multi-agent frameworks focus on orchestration and role specialization, but still rely on full-context sharing or static context routing, leading to redundant token consumption, increased runtime, and inefficient memory utilization. We present \emph{Role-Conditioned Context Routing (RCR)}, an execution-time layer that allocates role-relevant shared-memory items to agents under token budgets. Given a structured shared memory and a set of role-specialized agents, RCR selectively routes task-relevant memory items to each agent according to its role, optional task-stage metadata, and token budget. RCR integrates role-conditioned relevance scoring, token-budgeted memory selection, and iterative memory updates to reduce redundant context exposure during multi-agent execution.
